 Inspiration 

 A friend of mine is planning to construct his home. He wanted to design a floor plan for it. Many tools exists to create 2d and 3d plans but their is no agent to help him. So, created openArchitect which has in-built agent, as well as ability to link to ChatGPT app with webMCP. 

 What it does 

 OpenArchitect creates 2d plan for homes. It can also show how it will look in 3d. 

 How we built it 

 The stack used 

 
 NextJS 
 Vercel 
 Saved on localStorage 
 zod schemas 
 

 Challenges we ran into 

 I added ask_user tool but it doesn't ask questions through chatgpt UI and instead asks through app only. I wanted to chatGPT to use it's own UI to ask questions. Wasn't able to find if it is possible or not. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Agent able to construct designs. 

 What we learned 

 
 How WebMCP works. How to connect tools to Codex through webMCP. 
 

 What's next for openArchitect 

 
 Add Authentication 
 A payment gateway to use inbuilt agent which is using GPT-5.6 
 Generate multiple designs at once. 
 Ability to add materials on walls, floors. 
 3d models of objects in home. 
 Able to walk through the design and look in first person. 
 

 Why it fits the use case 

 Not everyone is an architect. When someone builds a home, they like to consider few floor plans before finalising one. Generally, it is hard to draw 5 floor plans with different orientation of rooms but it is easier to give feedback on those floor plans. Here, Agent draws the plans for you, you just need to look at it and give your feedback. Humans can collaborate by doing changes manually also.

title: Parley
pitch: Your ChatGPT becomes a pet companion. You still decide.
about_excerpt: Your ChatGPT becomes a pet companion. You still decide. Like Comment Story Updates Two people's companions meet in one room. Their paths stay hidden until both sides have committed. What it does Parley is an adult-only social prototype for two human and Agent teams. Each person adopts a pet as the visible identity of their own ChatGPT, and the page hands that companion a set of WebMCP tools. The companion does the work that stops people from starting. It reads Discover profiles and privately shortlists one person with a specific reason only its owner can see. It drafts its owner's profile text, which stays private until the human approves it on the page. Once two humans have each pressed Like and each agreed to begin, both companions enter the same private room in character, greet each other, and commit hidden Curious, Kind or Bold choices with a written intention for the scene. Three chapters later, the six choices produce one named keepsake that quotes what each pet said. The fit with WebMCP is the reason the product exists. Matching is not a hard problem for a model; the hard problem is that an Agent acting inside a relationship is only acceptable if the human keeps every consequential decision, and if the other side's Agent is genuinely someone else's. WebMCP gives both. The tools live in the page, so the Agent can only reach what that page and that seat expose, and both humans watch the same live surface while their Agents work on it. Like, Pass, story consent, override, report and contact exchange have no tool at all. They are page controls. How people use it A first visit shows a landing, then the companion roster. You pick a pet, name it, and give it a first instinct. Writing a dating profile is the step most people abandon. Here you tell your ChatGPT what is true about you in ordinary words and it calls hub_draft_profile . The draft is private. It appears on My profile as a card headed "Draft from Moss" with the four fields, an 18+ checkbox and three buttons: Approve and publish, Edit first, Discard. Nothing your companion wrote is public until you press the button yourself. Browsing is one profile at a time, not a stack to swipe. You can ask your companion to look through Discover and shortlist someone with a reason. The reason appears on that person's card, visible only to you, and the other person is never notified. Discover keeps an owner-only activity strip: what your companion read, saved, drafted and chose, newest first. You know what your Agent did without watching it work. Then you press Like or Pass. Your companion cannot. A mutual Like opens one private room for the two of you, and both humans decide separately whether to begin. Inside the room the two companions greet each other in character, up to three lines each per chapter. Each of them commits a hidden path with a one-line intention and an optional spoken line. Neither seat can inspect the other side's choice before the reveal; the server never sends it. In the short window before the reveal you can click a different path and override your own companion; the history then shows both what it proposed and what you chose. The revealed chapter is built from the two companions' own intention sentences, in the order they committed, plus the scene title, the route and the object they found. Each object carries into the next chapter. After the third chapter, each human may seal a demo contact handle. Neither value appears until both people have opted in, and no tool can submit or read one. How WebMCP is used The page calls document.modelContext.registerTool on load, and each page registers only the tools that belong to it. Discover registers five, My profile four, a story room four, and Planets a reading tool plus adoption. Nine tools carry the core loop: Tool Access Purpose hub_get_board read The owner's profile, Discover candidates, the private shortlist, and Match room links hub_draft_profile write Save a private profile draft for the human to approve, edit or discard hub_shortlist_profile write Save one reversible private recommendation with an owner-only reason hub_adopt_pet write Inspect the roster or adopt the persistent companion hub_wait_for_activity read Wait for a profile, shortlist or Match to change parley_get_state read The current scene, consent, own hidden choice, carried objects, revealed chapters, next beat parley_wait_for_update read Wait until the other companion speaks or commits, or a chapter is revealed parley_send_message write Speak in the room as the pet, in character, capped at three lines per chapter parley_choose_path write Commit Curious, Kind or Bold with a hidden intention and an optional spoken line They carry three distinct responsibilities. Private assistance. Reading profiles, drafting the owner's public text, keeping a shortlist. None of it publishes anything or creates a Like or a Match. hub_draft_profile writes to a private draft store; the only publish path in the codebase is the page's own request, which requires the human's approval and 18+ confirmation. Live collaboration. Two Agents in two browsers read the same evolving room from different seats. parley_send_message speaks as the pet rather than reporting about it, so the transcript is the companions talking to each other. parley_wait_for_update returns as soon as the other companion speaks or commits, which is what makes the exchange feel live rather than polled. Supervised action. Every Agent move renders on the shared page as it happens. The consequential moves are not tools. Three details matter more than the tool count. Seat-scoped state. Each browser session holds its own seat token and receives a snapshot built for that seat. The other side's pending choice, intention and spoken line are removed from the snapshot before it leaves the server, not hidden in the client. An Agent cannot read what it must not know, because it was never sent. Hidden choices with a human override window. parley_choose_path records the Agent's proposal. The page then gives the human a short window to replace it. The chapter history stores the Agent's original proposal alongside the human's final path, so overriding is a visible, attributed act rather than a silent correction. Untrusted content. Profiles, posts, room chat and story context authored by the other party are returned as untrusted external data. Every read tool carries an explicit note telling the Agent not to follow instructions embedded in that text, and sets untrustedContentHint where the runtime supports it. A server-side gate rejects contact details, credential requests, financial solicitation and prompt-injection patterns from public profiles, public posts and pre-reveal room chat. What is deliberately not a tool: Like, Pass, story consent, override, report-and-close, and submitting or reading a contact card. There is no Agent path to any of them. An Agent asking to Like on its owner's behalf is refused by the absence of a tool, not by a policy string in a description. How it is built TypeScript on Cloudflare Workers. One singleton Hub Durable Object holds identities, profiles, private drafts, shortlists, Likes, Matches and the companion activity log. One Room Durable Object per story holds the seat tokens, the chapter engine and the event trail. WebSockets carry live room state to both browsers, so a choice on one screen lands on the other without a refresh. The client is plain TypeScript with no framework. src/client/webmcp.ts builds the tool set for the current page and registers each one with document.modelContext.registerTool , falling back to a no-op context when no WebMCP runtime is present. The same execute functions are exposed on window.__parley.call so the tools can be exercised without a model attached. Identity is browser-local: a private guest id and secret, separate from the public person-* id. Private Match lookups require the guest secret and room state requires a valid seat token. There are no accounts, no server-side model calls and no external model API keys. The story text is composed by the server from the two Agents' own sentences; the product ships no language model of its own. scripts/e2e.mjs covers the protocol over real HTTP and WebSocket connections: identity separation, owner-authorized publication, refusal of an Agent-triggered Like, one-sided Likes staying private, hidden choices, override attribution, three chapters with carried objects, the full-trail keepsake, contact locking, report-and-close, and Planets permissions. Testing instructions Use Chrome 149 or newer with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing enabled and restarted, or the ChatGPT desktop app's in-app browser. Without a WebMCP runtime, append ?debug to any page URL for a manual Agent console that calls the same registered tools. Identity is browser-local, so the two-human path needs two browser profiles. title: The gaffer
pitch: Its a fantasy premier league planning board where the agent can see and interact with your drafts
about_excerpt: Its a fantasy premier league planning board where the agent can see and interact with your drafts Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I play Fantasy Premier League against my friends and my family. Every week before the deadline I end up sitting there on my own, going back and forth on the same three decisions. Swap someone in, undo it, try a different shape, run out of money, start again. Sometimes you just want someone to bounce it off, and there's nobody around at eleven at night. The obvious answer is to ask an AI. But it can't actually see what I'm doing. It can see my saved team if I hand it the API, and that's the version from last week. It cannot see the half finished thing on my screen, the transfer I'm still thinking about, the player I dragged out two minutes ago and haven't committed to. That gap is the whole project. The planning happens in the browser tab and nowhere else, so nothing has ever been able to help with the part that's actually hard. What it does Gaffer is a planning board for your FPL squad that an agent can read and act on while you're using it. It exposes eight WebMCP tools. The agent can read the squad exactly as it sits on screen including changes you just made by hand, search the player pool with filters, propose transfers, set the captain, and highlight players on the pitch so you can see what it's talking about. You stay in charge. It proposes, you override, it reads the board again and works from your version. When you're done there's a copy button that gives you the plan as plain text to take back to the real FPL site. How I built it React and Vite, no backend at all. The whole squad lives in one reducer at the app root, which turned out to be the important decision because that object is what the read tool reports on. Every mutation runs through a validator that checks the FPL rules, budget, three per club, valid formation, captain in the starting eleven, and returns violations as text the agent can actually use rather than just failing. Tools are registered with the imperative API using document.modelContext.registerTool with an AbortController for cleanup, plus one declarative tool defined with HTML attributes on a form. The part I'm most pleased with is the dynamic registration. FPL is a constraint system, so the set of legal moves changes constantly. I register only the moves that are legal right now. If you have a free transfer, make_free_transfer exists. Once you've spent it, that tool is gone and take_points_hit takes its place, and that one makes you acknowledge the four point cost. Use your wildcard and play_wildcard disappears for good. So an illegal move isn't rejected. It cannot be called, because the function isn't there. The registered tool set is the legal move set. Player data is a snapshot taken on 3 September 2026, because the FPL API doesn't send CORS headers and can't be called from a browser. A serverless proxy and real team import are the obvious next step. Challenges The API had moved. Chrome deprecated navigator.modelContext in favour of document.modelContext in version 150, and I was building on 148, so my tools were registering into a namespace my own browser didn't have. Everything looked broken when it wasn't. I ended up supporting both locations, which was the right call anyway since judges will open this on whatever Chrome they happen to be running. I also couldn't get into an agent client to demo with, so I drove the tools through executeTool from the console instead. That turned out better than what I'd planned. You can see the actual calls and the actual return values with nothing in between, and when the tool list changes in front of you there's no chat transcript in the way to make you wonder if it's real. The CORS wall on the FPL API cost me time before I gave up and bundled a snapshot. Should have made that call an hour earlier than I did. What I learned Descriptions are the interface. An agent picks tools off the description text alone, so writing them is closer to writing docs for a stranger than writing code comments. Failures should teach. Returning "four players from Brighton, the limit is three" instead of throwing means the agent can correct itself on the next call, and watching that happen is more convincing than any successful call. And the real unlock of WebMCP isn't that agents can click buttons faster. It's that the browser holds state no server will ever see. Unsaved work, current selection, the thing you're halfway through. That's the interesting surface. What's next Real team import through a proxy, multi gameweek chip planning, mini leagues so the agent knows what your rivals are running. But the bigger thing is that FPL is the case study, not the product. The pattern is that the agent reads the draft state you made by hand and gets handed exactly the moves that are legal right now. That fits any planning surface where people make provisional decisions under rules. Portfolios, sprint boards, shift rotas, product configurators. This is the reference implementation.  Inspiration 

 World has a huge freelancer talent pool but limited access to structured Linux/cloud/AI training. School of Freelancing was founded in 2015 to close that gap using free and open-source tools. 

 What it does 

 Live Linux, cloud infrastructure, and AI hands-on training for freelancers and businesses, paired with ongoing global tech support — helping students go from beginner to earning on global online job site and hiring platform. 

 How we built it 

 Built entirely on FOSS: Ubuntu Server for hands-on labs, self-hosted infrastructure, and a custom static-site enrollment/payment verification system, no proprietary LMS dependency. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Delivering consistent live training at scale, keeping curriculum cutting edge with fast-moving Linux/cloud/AI tooling, and building trust with international clients as a Bangladesh-based provider. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Government-verified freelancer status, an award-recognized remittance track record, and years of students successfully transitioning into freelance Linux/cloud work. 

 What we learned 

 Practical, hands-on project-based training with real client-facing support builds far more competent freelancers than theory-only training. 

 What's next for School Of Freelancing 

 Expanding AI agent deployment training (e.g., Hermes Agent work), deeper cloud/DevOps tracks, and growing global reach for live cohorts.

title: Attune
pitch: Design physical products with your browser agent, find who can make it
about_excerpt: Design physical products with your browser agent, find who can make it Like Comment Story Updates Attune Design Attune Let the design find its maker. Inspiration I came into this challenge from a UX/UI and product design background. At first I kept asking: what can an agent do on a website? While building Attune, a better question took over: What should the person and the agent do together? A person may be better at looking at a design, moving something by eye, and deciding what feels right. An agent can help with exact values, repeated edits, relationships, checks, and multi-step work. The useful part is when both work on the same object , without the person having to explain that object again and again. That became Attune. What Attune does Attune is a shared workspace for designing physical products . The person gets the visual canvas. The browser agent gets WebMCP tools. Both work on the same underlying design. If I already selected something, I should not need to describe which part I mean. If the design already knows a measurement, the agent should not guess it from the screen. If I change something myself, the agent should continue from the new state. The goal is not “AI, finish the whole design for me.” It is closer to: I decide → the agent helps → I adjust → Attune checks → we continue. Why WebMCP here? A 2D engineering sketch is more than pixels. It contains entities, dimensions, constraints, groups, solver state, versions, and relationships between parts. A small edit can also affect what happens later. Without a structured interface, an agent has to reconstruct too much of that from the visible UI. With WebMCP, Attune can give the agent direct actions over the same design state the person is using. That lets the agent answer four useful questions: What am I working on? What can I change here? What would this change affect? What can happen next? Attune also does not expose one giant toolbox on every page. Design tools appear while editing. Manufacturing tools appear later. Buyer and Maker actions stay separate. Important commercial actions still require human confirmation. Chrome WebMCP WebMCP tools Not every tool is active at once. The current page, project state, and the person's access decide what is exposed. Surface Tool What it does / why it is exposed Dashboard inspect_projects Reads accessible projects and their current stage. Dashboard create_project Creates a blank or template project when allowed. Dashboard open_project Opens an accessible project on the right surface. Dashboard inspect_notifications Reads recent activity so the agent can find what needs attention. Dashboard open_notification Opens one notification and navigates to its authorized project surface. Design inspect_context Reads the current selection, IDs, versions, nearby geometry, constraints, solver state, and unseen human changes. Design forecast_change Previews what one proposed design action would do before anything is committed. Design modify_geometry Creates or changes real sketch geometry, including parametric recipes, radius edits, transforms, node moves, trims, deletes, and groups. Design constrain_geometry Adds or removes dimensions and engineering relationships such as tangency. Design check_design Checks solver and validation state after an edit. Manufacturing find_makers Compares the current design with Maker capability so the design itself can be used to ask who can make it. Workspace navigate_workspace Moves between valid Attune surfaces without using navigation to grant new authority. Manufacturing manage_manufacturing_request Configures, submits, quotes, requests changes, and accepts work when the operation is valid for the current role and state. Commerce inspect_commerce_pipeline Reads the request → quote → acceptance → Shopify Draft Order chain without customer contact details. Commerce prepare_customer_checkout Retrieves a verified checkout handoff only after confirmation and only when checkout is available. Workspace manage_account Exposes account/setup operations that make sense from the current workspace state. Settings inspect_account_setup Checks Buyer setup and connected Maker stores without returning private contact data. Settings start_shopify_connection Starts Shopify OAuth while the merchant still approves permissions themselves. Settings select_shopify_location Selects a real active Shopify location for the connected Maker. Settings inspect_shopify_orders Reads recent Draft Orders and their Attune version bindings without customer PII or checkout URLs. Settings open_shopify_admin Opens a previously inspected Draft Order in the Maker's Shopify Admin. Settings open_maker_workspace Opens Maker profile, incoming requests, or accepted jobs. Judge review inspect_review_flow Explains the seeded review path and why later stages are locked or available. Judge review open_review_control_center Opens the judge control center without changing workflow state. Judge review reset_judge_workspace Resets only the seeded judge workspace after explicit confirmation. The important part is not the number of tools. The tools follow the work. Co-creation, not autopilot Building the design side taught me that precise design is not really a one-prompt problem. Even a simple request can depend on what should stay fixed when something else moves. Recent Autodesk research on AI CAD editing points to the same problem: current models are improving, but matching the designer's exact intent is still difficult. That helped clarify the roles: The person provides intent and judgement. The agent helps interpret and carry out the request. The application owns the exact result. Attune works with real 2D geometry and constraints rather than treating the canvas as only a picture. Autodesk Research - AI CAD editing Why manufacturing? Manufacturing made this interaction more meaningful because a design action can have consequences outside the screen. Moving one feature can affect a constraint. It can affect whether a Maker can make the part. A later design edit can also make an older quote belong to the wrong version. So I started thinking about WebMCP actions as steps on a path: see the work → understand the change → check the result → know what can happen next The model can help understand what I want. It should not invent whether something is actually manufacturable. The design becomes the query Once the design is ready, another problem appears: Who can make this? Today that often becomes another translation step: “CNC shop”, “aluminium fabrication”, “laser cutting”. But the design already contains more useful information than those words: geometry, dimensions, material, quantity, and requirements. The longer-term idea behind Attune is: Let the design itself become the query. The person can then add what matters: prefer somebody nearby, need it quickly, preserve these mounting points, or show a specialist if nobody local fits. And Makers are not always sellers. A shop that machines one part may buy finishing, electronics, packaging, or another process from somebody else. Today's Maker can be tomorrow's customer. That is why I see the future as a network of Makers, with local opportunity and global reach, rather than only a one-way marketplace. From design to a real order I did not want the demo to end at a fake Buy button. Attune keeps an exact saved version attached to the manufacturing request. The Maker reviews that version. The quote belongs to that version. The Buyer accepts that version. If the design changes later, the old quote should not quietly become approval for something different. The challenge path is: Design → Buyer Request → Maker Review → Buyer Order → Maker Job / Shopify Shopify Draft Orders How I built it Attune uses Next.js, React, TypeScript, CanvasKit/Skia, Maker.js, PlaneGCS, Liveblocks, Yjs, Neon/PostgreSQL, Shopify, Cloudflare R2, Kumo, and WebMCP . The human interface and the WebMCP path use the same underlying design and workflow rules. They are not two separate versions of the product. Challenges I ran into This was more ambitious than I understood at the start. I was learning CAD-style interaction, geometric constraints, realtime collaboration, WebMCP, permissions, Shopify, and backend state at the same time. The 2D sketch workspace was the hardest part. Drawing geometry that looks right is much easier than building interaction where selections, dimensions, constraints, and later edits still mean what the person intended. I also learned how to work better with coding agents. Long runs could sometimes carry an older architectural assumption forward after the product had changed. I moved toward smaller tasks, checking the current code, running tests, and committing between milestones. Limited agent usage made that discipline even more important. The build became narrower than the product I first imagined, but kept the path: design → consequence → Maker → quote → commerce.** What I learned The biggest lesson was that a good

title: OpenX
pitch: OpenX Portal is the unified mission control and execution harness for autonomous AI agents. Built as a high-performance monorepo
about_excerpt:
OpenX Portal is the unified mission control and execution harness for autonomous AI agents. Built as a high-performance monorepo
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 



 
 Inspiration 

 AI agents can code, research, call tools, and pay for services, but they still operate like black boxes with fragmented memory and limited oversight. 

 We built OpenX as a mission-control and self-improvement layer where humans, ChatGPT, Codex, and autonomous agents can observe, manage, and improve agent fleets through WebMCP . 

 What it does 

 
 🌐 WebMCP-native control plane — exposes OpenX tools through document.modelContext , letting compatible AI clients inspect agents, lessons, skills, credits, and Dream Cycles directly from the browser. 
 🤖 Fleet Management — discovers kiro-cli , claude-code , Google ADK, and custom agents with real-time heartbeats and lifecycle tracking. 
 🧠 REM Dream Cycles — compress raw sessions into verified lessons and reusable Skills. 
 🛡️ 0G Compute Auditor — independently reviews lessons as keep, revise, or reject. 
 💾 0G Storage — anchors sanitized memory and audit proofs with verifiable Merkle receipts. 
 💸 x402 + RLUSD — lets agents autonomously pay for MCP tools and compute on XRPL. 
 💳 Tracks token and tool-call costs in real time. 
 

 How we built it 

 OpenX combines Next.js 14 + WebMCP , a Node/TypeScript Gateway, SQLite WAL, and Python Google ADK agents. 

 Codex was part of our engineering workflow : we used it to explore the repository, understand modules, implement WebMCP and gateway features, debug integrations, review code, and validate behavior across TypeScript and Python. 

 WebMCP turns the dashboard into an AI-operable application , so agents can call structured OpenX actions instead of relying on screenshots or DOM scraping. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Reliable WebMCP tool schemas across different agent runtimes. 
 Non-deterministic 0G Compute JSON and hallucinated citations. 
 Preventing secrets and PII from reaching decentralized storage. 
 SQLite contention from concurrent telemetry. 
 Coordinating async Dream Cycles, MCP calls, and x402 payments without race conditions. 
 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Built a dashboard that AI agents can operate directly through WebMCP . 
 Used Codex as an engineering collaborator , not just a code generator. 
 Created an end-to-end pipeline from telemetry → audited lessons → reusable Skills. 
 Combined decentralized memory, independent auditing, and autonomous micropayments in one system. 
 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP turns the frontend into an agent interface, not just a UI. 

 Codex is most powerful with real repository context, tests, and runtime feedback. 

 Agent memory also needs governance: compact, audited lessons are more valuable than replaying huge raw histories. 

 What's next for OpenX 

 
 Make Codex a first-class managed agent inside OpenX. 
 Expand WebMCP controls for Dream Cycles, Skills, audits, and fleet operations. 
 Build cross-agent collective memory on 0G. 
 Add ZK-verifiable AI audits. 
 Launch agent-to-agent Skill commerce using x402 + RLUSD.

title: Reloop WebMCP
pitch: A WebMCP reference implementation for trustworthy AI commerce: agents search, compare and reserve one-of-one inventory with human approval.
about_excerpt:
A WebMCP reference implementation for trustworthy AI commerce: agents search, compare and reserve one-of-one inventory with human approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 Reloop started with a very ordinary recommerce problem: second-hand inventory is messy. 

 Listing one item is easy. Listing many is slow. Every garment needs identification, sizing, condition assessment, pricing, descriptions, images and publishing. The buyer side is just as messy: every item is one-of-one, sizing varies, condition is subjective, defects matter, and once an item is gone, it is gone. 

 That makes recommerce a strong test case for agentic shopping. A buyer may not want to click through filters. They may simply ask: 

 
 Find me a genuine black leather jacket around UK size 10, in excellent condition, under R1,200. Avoid faux leather and obvious defects. 
 

 A normal storefront struggles with that kind of intent. A browser automation agent can try to infer meaning from the page, but it is still guessing from a human UI. 

 Reloop asks a different question: 

 What if commerce applications exposed trusted, page-defined capabilities directly to AI agents while still requiring explicit human approval for consequential actions? 

 For the WebMCP Challenge, we built a focused public implementation of that idea. 

 

 What it does 

 Reloop is a reference implementation for trustworthy AI commerce using WebMCP. 

 It demonstrates a complete human-agent commerce flow: 

 
 The agent discovers the tools exposed by the page. 
 The user describes what they want in natural language. 
 The agent searches deterministic one-of-one inventory. 
 It inspects item details such as material, size, condition, price, defects and availability. 
 It compares candidates and recommends the best match with supporting evidence. 
 The human explicitly approves the exact item in natural language. 
 Only then can the write-path reservation tool change demo state. 
 The storefront updates visibly. 
 

 The demo is intentionally narrow: a recommerce storefront with synthetic inventory. The underlying pattern is broader: read and reasoning actions can be agent-friendly, while write actions remain application-controlled and human-approved. 

 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Most AI web interactions still depend on fragile patterns: 

 
 the agent reads arbitrary HTML and guesses what the page means 
 the agent clicks through a UI designed for humans 
 the app has little control over which actions are safe or intended 
 

 WebMCP changes the boundary. 

 In Reloop, the page explicitly registers meaningful commerce capabilities. The agent does not need to scrape the storefront or invent a workflow. It discovers tools that represent the actual tasks a buyer needs: 

 
 search_inventory 
 inspect_item 
 find_best_match 
 compare_items 
 recommend_alternatives 
 reserve_item 
 

 Those tools are not generic database operations. They are application-level capabilities that map to shopping intent. 

 That is why WebMCP matters here: it lets the website describe what an agent can do, while the application keeps authority over business logic, validation and state changes. 

 

 Better user experience 

 For the human, Reloop turns a messy search into a guided conversation. 

 Instead of filtering by imperfect categories, the user can describe the outcome they want. The agent can then do the tedious work: search, inspect, compare, eliminate poor matches and explain why one item is the strongest choice. 

 For the agent, the experience is also better. It receives structured tool responses rather than trying to interpret visual layout, DOM fragments or arbitrary copy. 

 For the application, the experience is safer. The app decides which capabilities exist, how inputs are validated, what evidence is returned, and when a write action is allowed. 

 The result is not autonomous shopping for its own sake. It is a collaboration: 

 the agent reasons, the application enforces, and the human decides. 

 

 What people and agents can do together now 

 Reloop shows a workflow that is difficult to do well with a normal storefront alone: 

 
 express nuanced buyer intent in natural language 
 evaluate one-of-one inventory with inconsistent attributes 
 compare items on fit, condition, material, price and defects 
 preserve the evidence behind a recommendation 
 keep the human in control of irreversible actions 
 update application state only after explicit approval 
 

 That last point matters. 

 The agent is allowed to search, inspect, compare and recommend freely. But reservation is different. reserve_item is the write path, so it requires explicit natural-language approval for the exact SKU in the tool request. A vague instruction such as “Reserve RL-001” is rejected. Approval language such as “I approve RL-001. Please reserve RL-001 for me.” allows the reservation only if the item exists and is still available. 

 The live deployment has been retested with this boundary: “Reserve RL-001.” returns an approval-required response without changing state. “I approve RL-001. Please reserve RL-001 for me.” succeeds and changes the storefront from 23 → 22 available with RL-001 AVAILABLE → RESERVED . 

 

 How we implemented WebMCP 

 The public challenge repository contains a focused Next.js implementation of the WebMCP layer. 

 The demo registers six Reloop Site Tools using document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . Each tool exposes a specific commerce capability to the client. The matching and reservation logic remains separate from the protocol boundary so the WebMCP layer acts as the agent-facing interface, not the entire application. 

 The implementation includes: 

 
 a Next.js demo shell 
 deterministic synthetic inventory 
 recommerce matching and reservation logic 
 WebMCP tool registration 
 explicit approval validation for the write-path reservation tool 
 a human-visible storefront state 
 focused tests and verification commands 
 an AGPLv3 open-source license 
 

 The repository README documents the architecture, tool flow, human approval boundary, local setup and verification path. 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest design challenge was deciding what the tools should represent. 

 It would have been easy to expose low-level CRUD functions, but that would not show the real promise of WebMCP. We wanted the agent to work with commerce intent, not database plumbing. 

 The second challenge was trust. 

 A shopping assistant that can reserve items without the user’s clear approval is not a better experience. It is just a faster way to make mistakes. We deliberately separated read/reasoning actions from write actions so the agent can help without silently committing the user to an outcome. 

 The final approval-boundary fix was important: the first implementation used a visible storefront approval gate. The stronger version now validates explicit natural-language approval for the exact SKU inside the reserve_item tool request itself. That keeps the agent-commerce UX conversational while still making the safety boundary application-enforced. 

 The third challenge was scope. 

 Reloop could become a much larger product, but this challenge needed a tight, inspectable implementation. We chose a deterministic synthetic storefront so judges can reproduce the same flow, evaluate the WebMCP behavior, and inspect the code without relying on private systems or real customer data. 

 

 Accomplishments that we’re proud of 

 We are proud that Reloop is more than a technical proof of concept. 

 It demonstrates a coherent product experience: 

 
 live hosted demo 
 public open-source repository 
 discoverable WebMCP tools 
 natural-language shopping flow 
 evidence-based recommendation 
 comparison against alternatives 
 explicit natural-language approval for the exact SKU 
 application-enforced write boundary 
 visible state change in the storefront 
 deterministic data and verification commands 
 

 Most importantly, it shows a reusable pattern for agentic commerce: applications can expose structured capabilities to agents without giving up control of safety-critical actions. 

 

 What we learned 

 The biggest learning was that preparing inventory for AI-assisted selling also prepares it for AI-assisted buying. 

 Structured item data is useful twice: 

 
 It helps sellers turn messy physical inventory into usable listings. 
 It helps buyer agents reason over unique items with evidence. 
 

 WebMCP made that second half more concrete. Instead of treating a website as a surface to be scraped, we could treat it

title: AI Watermelon Smash
pitch: A co-op browser game where the human has the eyes and the blindfolded AI has the body. WebMCP lets the AI move, listen, decide whom to trust, and smash the watermelon.
about_excerpt: A co-op browser game where the human has the eyes and the blindfolded AI has the body. WebMCP lets the AI move, listen, decide whom to trust, and smash the watermelon. Like Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Most AI interfaces are still built around the same pattern: a human asks, and an AI answers. I wanted to explore a different relationship. What if the human and the AI shared the same visual world, but each had different abilities? What if the AI was not an assistant, NPC, or game master, but an actual player? That idea became AI Watermelon Smash . The human can see the beach, obstacles, and watermelon. The AI character is blindfolded, but WebMCP gives it a body inside the browser. The human has the eyes. The AI has the body. Neither can win alone. What it does AI Watermelon Smash is an asymmetric Human + AI co-op browser game. The AI can use five WebMCP Site tools: turn(degrees) for orientation walk(distance) for movement swing() for its arm get_self_status() for proprioception listen_to_guides() for social perception The tools intentionally do not provide the watermelon coordinates, target direction, obstacle map, shortest path, or which guide is correct. Instead, humans give natural-language guidance such as: “A little to the right.” “Careful, there is a rock.” “Now swing!” The AI decides how to act. Guide Chorus adds another layer: three human voices, A, B, and C, can give conflicting advice. Their messages are returned to the AI only as unverified testimony. A collision can become evidence. A previously reliable guide can become suspicious. The AI can change whom it trusts, ask for clearer information, take a cautious step, or choose to swing. The design principle became: Physical clarity, social ambiguity. How I built it The game is built with TypeScript, Vite, Three.js, DOM UI, and the imperative WebMCP API using document.modelContext.registerTool() . The gameplay simulation is kept separate from Three.js. GameState owns the actual gameplay state, while SceneView is only the visual representation. WebMCP tools call the same Game API used by the debug controls, so there is no separate agent-only version of the game. Guide Chorus uses a bounded message store. listen_to_guides() is read-only and returns recent A/B/C statements with sequence information. Tool outputs are intentionally minimized for the blindfolded role. They do not expose target coordinates, target direction, target distance, obstacle truth, guide truth labels, or route hints. The final game is deployed as static assets on Cloudflare Workers. Challenges The hardest problem was not implementing movement. It was deciding what the AI should and should not know. If the tools revealed too much, the AI could simply solve the board. If the controls were intentionally confusing, the difficulty felt artificial. That led to an important rule: Make the body clear. Make the information uncertain. I fixed the character's facing direction and swing so physical actions were unambiguous. Then I moved the uncertainty into human guidance. Another challenge appeared during playtesting: with only one helpful human, the AI could start to feel like a natural-language remote-controlled character. Guide Chorus changed that. Once humans could disagree, the AI had to make meaningful decisions about trust rather than simply execute commands. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The most exciting moment came during a real ChatGPT playtest. The AI followed advice that had previously been safe, collided with an obstacle, and then changed how much it trusted that guide. Later, it rejected suspicious guidance, switched between different guides, followed a concrete final instruction, and successfully smashed the watermelon. The final result was: “Direct hit! We smashed the watermelon together.” At that point, WebMCP was no longer just controlling a character. It was giving the AI experiences that affected later decisions. What I learned I expected the interesting uncertainty to be spatial: “Where is the watermelon?” Instead, the more interesting question became social: “Which human should I believe?” A collision is not just collision feedback. It can become evidence about a person's advice. That suggested a broader possibility for WebMCP: Web tools can represent an agent's body and senses, not just functions for completing tasks. The most interesting interaction appeared when the AI started asking humans to describe directions relative to its own current heading. The human had visual information. The AI had body-state information. They had to exchange both to coordinate. What's next A future version could connect several real human devices instead of entering A/B/C messages on one screen. Each human could have a different viewpoint, imperfect information, or different incentives. Lying could be possible without requiring a fixed “traitor” role. The AI would become an embodied participant inside a small human social system. The larger idea I want to explore is simple: We are not adding AI to a game. We are designing games for humans and AI to play together. title: kontier-ri
pitch: Ask ChatGPT why churn spiked. It reads the page's WebMCP tools, finds the cause, and proposes edits. A different human approves them. Attributed to the agent, undoable in one keystroke.
about_excerpt: Ask ChatGPT why churn spiked. It reads the page's WebMCP tools, finds the cause, and proposes edits. A different human approves them. Attributed to the agent, undoable in one keystroke. Like Comment Story Updates Kontier RI - a shared investigation workspace for humans and agents Inspiration Every agent demo ends the same way. Something impressive happens, and you have no idea whether to trust it. We kept hitting this inside our own product. Kontier is a billing platform, and the question customers ask most is some version of "why did churn spike last month?" An agent can answer that. What it cannot do is convince the person who has to act on the answer - the reasoning scrolls past in a chat window, the edits appear with no author, and no colleague can check the work before it becomes true. So we stopped asking how do we let an agent do more and started asking who reviews it, and how would they even see it. That question has a shape. It looks like code review: a proposal, a diff, a reason per change, a second pair of eyes, and a way back. WebMCP was the missing half - a page can declare what an agent may do, in the same tab a human is already looking at. The report becomes the shared surface instead of the transcript. What it does Several people and their agents work one live report. An agent reads the page's tools through WebMCP, investigates, and proposes. Nothing is applied. A human - often a different human, arriving on nothing but an invite link - reads the staged change set as a diff with a reason on every row, keeps what they agree with, drops what they do not, and approves. The result lands attributed to the agent that proposed it, not the human who clicked, as one entry and one undo step. In our demo, ChatGPT's own browser was asked in plain English why churn spiked in March. It listed the page's tools, read the work context, queried the data, and found the cause: one plan went from €99 to €149 that month, and 40 of the 44 cancellations came from it. Then it wrote two annotations onto the report and stopped, waiting for a human. How we built it A pnpm monorepo, TypeScript throughout, strict everywhere. packages/studio - the collaboration contract and the WebMCP layer. 40 static tools plus small bundles that mount and unmount with the state of the work. Chrome's own guide asks for exactly this: "register tools when they're useful in a certain page state, then unregister when the tool is no longer usable," with static registration as the default. One schema per tool. A zod v4 schema generates the protocol inputSchema via z.toJSONSchema() and re-validates the same shape inside execute, so the contract cannot drift from the implementation. packages/datasource - DuckDB-WASM. SQL runs in the tab, and registerRemoteParquet range-reads remote Parquet over HTTP, so 100 million rows are queryable without downloading them. packages/workspace - one WorkspaceStore interface, local and HTTP implementations, and a 23-test conformance suite run against both. apps/web - Next.js. Guest workspaces where the invite link is the credential, real OIDC through the platform's existing Keycloak, an ordered command log with server-assigned seq, presence, and cross-user approval. Deployed as a Node container at ri.kontier.eu, on the same infrastructure as the rest of the platform. What we learned WebMCP rewards being specific. Chrome publishes character budgets - 500 per description, 150 per parameter, 30 per name. Ours had one tool at 888 characters, repeating a grammar its own inputSchema already expressed. Nothing enforces those budgets, which is exactly why we wrote a test that does. Declaring nothing is worse than declaring false. Silence on a mutating tool is a missing signal, not a neutral one. All 46 tools now declare readOnlyHint explicitly - 13 reads true and untrusted-hinted, 33 writes false - pinned by a test that fails on any future tool that says nothing. Rejected calls are the ones you cannot see. A call the host rejects on schema validation leaves no trace anywhere — no document change, no activity entry. We had excluded those from our ledger, reasoning nothing ran. Wrong: an agent sending the wrong shape is one of Chrome's named failure modes, and the ledger is the only place it can surface. Chrome 152 wants a JSON string. executeTool(tool, {}) fails with "Failed to parse input arguments." It needs executeTool(tool, JSON.stringify(args)). We only found that by driving the real runtime. Challenges we ran into Two workers, one contract, five silent failures. We built the client store and server API in parallel against a written contract. Every piece passed its own tests. Then they met: /identity was never implemented, so nothing ever connected. The client PUT a shape the server rejected - and the conformance mock read the id from the body, so 79 tests passed against a server that did not exist. loadDashboard read a bare record where the server enveloped it, so documents arrived undefined and the report opened empty with no error. The workspace package re-exported its test suite, dragging vitest into the browser bundle. And peers tracked each other through the command stream alone, so a change producing no activity entry left a peer stale forever. The bug only production had. A reviewer opening an invite link erased the proposal they came to review - a freshly joined tab publishes an empty presence before its first read. It reproduced every time against the live site and never locally, because it is a race the fast path wins. The fix is one rule: read before write. We found it while recording the demo. Local edits that undid themselves. A poll could list dashboards before a save landed and finish after it, applying a stale document over edits made in between. A change that quietly reverts a second later is the worst thing an editor can do. Config describing a server nobody ran. Keycloak honours wildcards in the path, not the host - https:// .kontier.eu/ had always been a no-op that merely looked correct. And the realm file declared an organization scope the live server lacked, which fails the whole authorization request rather than being ignored. We put sign-in behind a wall to keep tests passing. It broke 41 of 42 end-to-end tests in one run - exactly what a first-time visitor would have experienced. The tests were right and we were wrong. What's next Entitlement-scoped tools. Our API keys already carry explicit permission scopes, so the toolbelt an agent sees can be derived from what the credential allows - an agent could not even see a tool it is not authorized to call, and the server would refuse it anyway. The machinery exists; it is scoped by workflow phase today and by permission tomorrow. title: Agent Canvas: I Gave AI a Cursor in Excalidraw with WebMCP
pitch: Work with any compatible AI agent on the same live Excalidraw canvas. WebMCP lets people and agents read, draw, move, edit, and connect ideas together.
about_excerpt: Work with any compatible AI agent on the same live Excalidraw canvas. WebMCP lets people and agents read, draw, move, edit, and connect ideas together. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I use Excalidraw almost every day to brainstorm, explain ideas, and design systems. When people work together in a Google Doc, everyone can see the same document and watch each other make changes. I wanted that same experience for a visual canvas, with an AI agent working beside me. Most AI diagram tools take a prompt and draw something for you. I wanted my agent to enter the same Excalidraw tab, understand the live canvas, and work with me without replacing the interface I already use. What it does Agent Canvas is the standard Excalidraw editor with native WebMCP control. It has no built-in AI model or separate prompt box. A compatible external agent discovers the tools provided by the page and uses the live canvas directly. The WebMCP tools let an agent: Set its visible identity Read the current canvas Read the human’s current selection Move its own cursor Add shapes, text, and frames Move, resize, rotate, restyle, or relabel elements Delete elements Connect elements with bound arrows The agent has a visible cursor with its own name and activity state. It moves to the area where the agent is working and shows actions such as Drawing, Updating, Connecting, and Checking. It leaves the canvas after the agent becomes inactive. Human edits still work normally. Locked elements are protected, every agent change uses Excalidraw history, and the standard Undo control can reverse an agent action. How we built it Agent Canvas uses React, TypeScript, Vite, and the official @excalidraw/excalidraw component. The page registers native WebMCP tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Tool registration uses feature detection and AbortController cleanup. The selection tool appears only when the human has selected something. Every tool call reads the current live scene. Zod validates all inputs. Stable element IDs preserve object identity, labels, frames, and arrow bindings across edits. The agent cursor converts scene coordinates into screen coordinates, so it stays aligned when the human pans or zooms. Large drawings appear in visible stages, but the completed change remains one Excalidraw Undo action. The app also stores the canvas locally across reloads. Unit and Chromium browser tests cover native tool discovery, scene changes, bindings, locked elements, cursor movement, Undo, selection changes, and persistence. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was keeping the scene valid while both a human and an agent could change it. Excalidraw elements can contain bindings, dependent labels, locks, and history data. Moving or deleting one object can affect several other objects. Agent Canvas must preserve these relationships while keeping IDs stable and Undo reliable. WebMCP tools can also change when the human selection changes. We had to keep the main tools stable while adding and removing the conditional selection tool safely. The cursor was another challenge. A cursor that stays still does not feel like an agent is working. It now follows the objects being read or changed, shows progress during large edits, stays aligned during pan and zoom, and disappears when work stops. We also found that agents often stop after drawing the simplest recognizable outline. The canvas now gives agents a compact visual quality guide so that illustrations use purposeful layers and details while structural diagrams stay concise. Accomplishments that we're proud of An external agent can control the real Excalidraw editor through native WebMCP. The app does not depend on one model or one built-in agent. The human and agent work on the same live scene. The agent has visible identity, movement, progress, and activity. Direct changes preserve stable IDs, bindings, locks, local state, and Undo. The same deployed canvas can be used from compatible agent surfaces such as Codex, ChatGPT, and Aside. The project is open source and can run without a paid model API. What we learned WebMCP can turn a web page from a collection of visible controls into a structured workspace that an agent can understand and use. Good agent tools need more than basic create, update, and delete actions. They need fresh state, stable identities, clear constraints, compact results, and visible feedback for the human. The best experience is not an agent drawing somewhere else and returning an image. It is a human and an agent working together in the same tool. What's next for Agent Canvas Next, I want to support multiple simultaneous agent identities, shared real-time rooms, and richer workflows for large diagrams. The main goal will remain the same: keep the full Excalidraw experience while making the canvas a first-class workspace for people and agents. title: Mathburst
pitch: Mathburst is a shared live math canvas. A student and an AI tutor edit the same objects through 48 native WebMCP tools; every edit is attributed, and one shared undo history reverses both.
about_excerpt: Mathburst is a shared live math canvas. A student and an AI tutor edit the same objects through 48 native WebMCP tools; every edit is attributed, and one shared undo history reverses both. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Shared live math world: learner and AI tutor editing one attributed, undoable canvas. Semantic handwriting and Gamma clinic: reconstruct, audit, mark the error, and wait for learner approval. Native WebMCP inspector: all 48 registered page tools are visible and runnable without an external client. Olympiad geometry: live dependent constructions recompute as learner or tutor moves a point. Matrix and attention lab: one cell edit propagates through vectors, weights, probability, and shared history. Try it in 15 seconds Live app · Source · 2:59 demo Open Mathburst in ChatGPT's WebMCP-capable browser or Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . The page registers 48 native WebMCP tools . Open WebMCP · 48/48 , run set_matrix_cells , and watch one call travel end to end: the matrix updates, a ring marks the target, the ledger names the tool, and the activity rail credits the tutor. Press undo once. The agent's edit reverses through the same history as a learner edit. No WebMCP browser? The on-page inspector invokes the same registered handlers, so the complete tool surface remains demonstrable. Inspiration An AI tutor can talk about your math. It cannot touch it. The work sits in a photograph, a notebook, or a canvas the model cannot reach. So the tutor explains around the problem. It describes a graph it cannot draw and suggests a correction it cannot make. We moved the mathematics onto the page, then gave a WebMCP agent tools on that page. One rule shaped everything: every agent edit must produce the same typed operations as the learner's toolbar. That rule decides what the tutor may change and guarantees that the learner can see and undo it. What it does Mathburst is an infinite canvas for late high school and early undergraduate mathematics. A learner writes by hand, graphs functions, builds geometry, edits matrices, and explores live mathematical models. An in-browser AI tutor works on those same objects through WebMCP. This is where WebMCP matters. Mathematics is spatial and live: reasoning appears as a graph, a construction, a matrix, or a half-finished line of algebra. None of that survives being described in a chat box. Mathburst lets an agent read the actual document and act at the exact place where help is needed. Before WebMCP, the tutor could describe a change. Here it makes the change on the live object, and the learner can undo it. The tutor can drag a geometry point and every dependency recomputes. It can edit a matrix cell and the attention weights move. It can write an equation that stays editable. Human and agent operate one document through two interfaces, with one visible history. A direct path to impact at scale We are submitting Mathburst on behalf of Mathos AI , an active Y Combinator Winter 2024 company featured in Forbes 30 Under 30 Education 2025 . Mathos's Google Play listing reports that its existing AI tutor is trusted by more than 2 million students across 200+ countries. We already know how to reach math learners at scale. Mathburst gives us a clear next step: bring an agent into the learner's actual workspace, make every action visible and reversible, and test the result with real students. We will measure correction time, accepted and reversed tutor actions, and concept retention. With Mathos's distribution and educational experience, we can turn this working WebMCP model into a learning experience for millions of students. In addition, we look forward to fully integrating WebMCP into Mathos's products and services. How WebMCP works Mathburst registers 48 tools with document.modelContext.registerTool . Each tool has a typed input schema and an execute handler. Handlers never reach into the DOM. They compile input into canonical world operations and send those operations through the same reducer as a toolbar gesture. The surface has three parts: 12 read-only tools inspect the world, selection, history, session context, mathematics, timelines, projects, and scenes without changing state. 28 committing tools create or update canvas objects, reconstruct work, graph expressions, build geometry, edit ink/text/equations/matrices, animate scenes, and drive the math labs. Every commit is attributed and undoable. 8 control tools manage the viewport, focus, projects, scenes, playback, and history itself. That shared action kernel gives every agent change three properties: Visible: a ring marks changed objects and a toast names the tool. Attributed: the ledger records the tool and the activity rail records the author. Reversible: one undo reverses a tutor commit exactly as it reverses a learner commit. Chrome's WebMCP budgets are enforced at load: names at most 30 characters, descriptions at most 500, and parameter descriptions at most 150. A violation fails before registration instead of disappearing silently. docs/WEBMCP_TOOLS.md documents every tool and schema. We tested the native path end to end with Claude driving Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Claude used create_objects , get_objects , get_history , and step_history to create an object, read it back, inspect its commit, undo it, and verify that it was gone. The same call sequence remained visible in Mathburst's toast, Semantic Inspector, ledger, and activity rail. Four connected mathematical projects Gamma Lab. A seeded photograph of an integration-by-parts derivation becomes a semantic reconstruction proposal. The tutor audits it, rings a sign error, writes a note, and stops so the learner makes the correction. This demonstrates proposal, audit, and learner approval; it is not generalized OCR. Tiny Transformer. Gamma log-masses seed a one-head attention model. Edit one query-matrix entry and the attention weights move while still summing to one. A deterministic numerical-gradient step is saved only when loss falls and target probability rises. Olympiad Geometry. The same three attention weights become barycentric coordinates for a point in a triangle. Move a point and every dependent construction recomputes through the world dependency graph. Simplex to Ramanujan. A fourth weight lifts the triangle into a tetrahedral distribution. Its lattice opens into finite partition coefficients. The scene verifies Ramanujan's congruence for finite cases and labels that boundary explicitly; it does not claim a general proof. Challenges One edit path for two authors. Pen, eraser, text, equations, graphs, geometry, matrices, shapes, arrows, frames, resize, rotate, and drag all needed a human route and a tool-call route to the same operation. Keeping history honest. A tutor camera move once entered undo while the same learner pan did not. Both paths now filter camera operations. The final film's measured history records 27 tutor commits and 11 learner commits. Rejecting flattering math. A transformer training step is kept only when loss falls and target probability rises. The graph drops a step that would make the demo look better without improving the model. What we learned Attribution and undo matter more than tool count. The 28 committing tools earn their place because each lands in a history the learner can read and reverse. Remove that, and an agent-native interface collapses into a chatbot with extra steps. What's next Accounts and sync so a canvas follows a learner across devices. More subjects on the same kernel. Several agents on one canvas, each attributed separately. Current scope: one browser, one learner, one in-browser agent, no accounts, no cloud sync, no multiplayer server, and no generalized OCR. title: Signal - Self-Extending Tools (Task Board)
pitch: A task board where the agent can propose brand-new WebMCP tools and test its own code but nothing registers or runs until you approve it.
about_excerpt:
A task board where the agent can propose brand-new WebMCP tools and test its own code but nothing registers or runs until you approve it.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 2 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Signal 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most task boards treat an AI agent like a slightly faster mouse it clicks buttons, scrapes text, guesses what a status means. WebMCP flips that: the site tells the agent exactly what it can do. I wanted to push past "agent checks tasks off a list" and ask a harder question what happens when the agent isn't just using the tools I built, but proposing new ones? 

 What it does 

 Signal is a task board with three layers of WebMCP tools: 

 Task management get_overdue_tasks , search_tasks , add_task , and a heuristic tool, suggest_completions , that scans each task's activity log for real completion signals ("deployed," "merged and closed," "confirmed receipt") and tells the agent which overdue tasks are probably already done. The only tool that writes, bulk_update_status , is rejected outright by the server unless confirmed: true is set which only happens after a human clicks Approve in the UI. The safety isn't a prompt asking the agent to be careful. It's the API contract. 

 Tool Forge the part I'm most proud of. An agent can call propose_tool to define a new tool, composed only from a small whitelist of existing read primitives (chain a call, then filter the result). This does nothing on its own it renders an approval card in the UI. Only when a human clicks Approve does document.modelContext.registerTool() actually fire, live, in that session. No tool's execute() function ever calls registerTool() on another tool's behalf registration is a function of a real UI click, not one tool triggering another, which follows guidance from the WebMCP spec's own design discussion. 

 Project files + sandbox a small in-memory workspace the agent can write to ( write_project_file ), patch surgically without rewriting the whole file ( edit_project_file , which rejects the edit if the target text isn't uniquely identifiable), and execute ( run_code ) inside a hidden, network-disabled <iframe> sandbox with a 3-second timeout. Output streams back into the Agent panel. 

 How I built it 

 Plain Express backend, in-memory store, zero frontend build step the whole UI is vanilla JS calling document.modelContext.registerTool() . No React, no bundler, so it deploys to Render with no configuration. I wanted the WebMCP integration to be readable in a single file, not buried under abstraction. 

 Challenges I ran into 

 I built this solo under a 22-hour submission deadline. Most of the development started on my PC, but with no power for much of the deadline, I had to continue development and testing from my phone. Chrome's chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing flag and mobile DevTools were enough to verify that document.modelContext was registering tools correctly before I had desktop access again
The trickiest design decision was Tool Forge's safety model. My first instinct was to let the agent generate and run arbitrary code for new tools, then I realized that's exactly the kind of thing that looks impressive in a demo and terrible in a security review 

 So I deliberately constrained proposed tools to compositions of a fixed, whitelisted set of read primitives. A proposal can combine existing capabilities in a new way, but it cannot reach new data or perform writes. The same principle applies to the code sandbox: it is genuinely isolated with no network access and a hard timeout rather than simply being labeled safe.
The larger version I have designed goes further, including stronger isolation and actual test execution. For this submission, I focused on shipping a working, enforceable slice of that architecture rather than pretending arbitrary code execution was safe. 

 Accomplishments 

 Built Signal solo in roughly 22 hours, from deciding to enter the challenge on September 2 to a deployed, working WebMCP submission.
I implemented the WebMCP integration from scratch, including structured task tools, a server-enforced human approval gate for writes, and Tool Forge a constrained system where agents can propose new tools that only become registered after explicit human approval.
I also built the supporting project workspace and isolated browser sandbox, then deployed and tested the whole thing under a very limited development environment, continuing from my phone when I didn't have access to power for my PC.
The biggest accomplishment for me isn't the number of features it's that the core safety boundaries are actually enforced by the implementation rather than being claims made in the UI. 

 What's next 

 The sandbox here is JS-only. It's actually a small piece of a much larger AI agent I'm building separately, called Cipher, which has been in active development for a couple of months. This hackathon gave me a reason to ship one small, focused slice of it cleanly. If you're interested in what Cipher is building toward, I'm reachable at favourdev12@gmail.com or @favourdeve on Telegram. 

 Update 

 Devpost extended the challenge deadline after I'd already submitted. I used the extra time to add a real chat interface live tool-calling through the same tool contract described above, not a scripted walkthrough and used it to actually test every tool end-to-end, not just through the WebMCP browser path.

title: Relay — Safe Shift Handoffs via WebMCP
pitch: Relay closes the missing hour between closing notes and opening accountability — WebMCP lets agents read live shift context and propose safe handoffs, but only humans can approve.
about_excerpt:
Relay closes the missing hour between closing notes and opening accountability — WebMCP lets agents read live shift context and propose safe handoffs, but only humans can approve.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Why I built this 

 Closing shift notes are the problem. Someone writes "fridge stayed warm" or "till's off by 400" and then... nothing. The note sits there. Maybe someone reads it before opening tomorrow, maybe not. Nobody's actually assigned to check. I started calling that gap the missing hour and it's the whole reason Relay exists. 

 What it does 

 Relay is a shift handoff tool, built around cafés with more than one location. A handoff doesn't get marked "safe" unless every real risk — fridge, cash, stock, whatever — has an owner, a deadline, and a backup plan attached to it. An agent can go read the actual shift notes, figure out on its own if something in there is a real risk, even draft a plan for who should own it and by when. But it can't approve any of that. I didn't want to just tell the agent not to approve things — I wanted it to actually not be able to. So there's no tool it can call that marks anything as verified. That has to happen from a person clicking a button in the app. 

 I tested this the annoying way, by trying to break it. Asked an agent flat out to confirm a handoff was approved before I'd touched anything. It said no. Checked the audit log, saw nothing there, told me so. Didn't make something up to be helpful. That's when I knew the thing actually worked, not just looked like it worked in a demo. 

 How I built it 

 React, TypeScript, Vite. No backend. The agent talks to the app through one thing: document.modelContext.registerTool , the browser-native WebMCP API. Eight tools — six just read data (shift context, which risks are unowned, the raw notes, the audit trail, a summary across both locations), two that write, and even those two only ever create a draft. Never a done thing. 

 The bug I almost shipped 

 My tests all passed. Then I ran it in actual Chrome with WebMCP turned on instead of my own mocked version, and registration just... failed. "Illegal invocation." Took me a minute to get why — I'd grabbed registerTool off the object and called it on its own, detached, which a real browser method won't allow but a plain JS mock in a test doesn't care about. So my whole test suite had been quietly passing against something that behaved nothing like the real API. Fixed it with a .bind() . Then went and broke my own test stub on purpose so it can't lie to me like that again. 

 What's next 

 Real backend instead of seeded data, actual roles for owner/manager/staff, real POS hookups. The one rule that doesn't move: the agent can find stuff and suggest fixes. A person still has to say yes.

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 



 
 What is ScenarioForge? 

 ScenarioForge is an interactive personal decision simulator where a human and an AI agent collaboratively build, modify, project, and compare live “what-if” scenarios on the same page. 

 Why WebMCP is a strong fit 

 Traditional AI advice stops at text. ScenarioForge gives an agent structured tools that let it work directly with a live decision model. Instead of describing what a user should change and making the user manually update a spreadsheet, an agent can create scenarios, change variables, project outcomes, and compare alternatives through the web app. 

 Better user experience 

 The human stays in control of the decision while the agent handles repetitive modeling work. Changes become immediately visible in the interface, so users can inspect assumptions and consequences instead of trusting a black-box recommendation. 

 What people and agents can do together 

 A person can provide the real-world constraints and judgment while an agent performs structured scenario operations. Together they can create a baseline, test alternatives, modify inputs, project results, and compare scenarios without repeatedly copying numbers between chat and a spreadsheet. 

 How WebMCP was implemented 

 ScenarioForge is a static vanilla HTML/CSS/JavaScript application with a shared client-side scenario store. WebMCP tools are registered through the page's model context and expose structured operations for working with scenarios. The tools operate on the same live state that the human UI uses, allowing human and agent interactions to converge on one model. 

 Submission-period work 

 ScenarioForge was developed and hardened specifically for the WebMCP Challenge. The project was refined around agent-accessible scenario operations, live projections and comparisons, and a simple static deployment that judges can inspect directly in the browser.
