title: Pawball Arena
pitch: Pawball Arena is an original 3v3 pixel-art arcade soccer game built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge.
about_excerpt: Pawball Arena is an original 3v3 pixel-art arcade soccer game built for the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Inspiration We wanted to explore what browser-native AI control can feel like when it is safe, legible, and fun. Pawball Arena turns that idea into a local arcade football match where an AI coach can understand the game semantically without gaining unrestricted control of the simulation. What it does Pawball Arena is a 3v3 cat football game with human play, local utility AI, and a WebMCP sideline coach. The coach can read the live match state, adjust formations and team style, call short tactical plays, assign roles, and issue bounded semantic orders such as marking an opponent or supporting a ball carrier. The agent never sends raw key presses, coordinates, physics values, or score changes. Local AI remains responsible for movement, collision avoidance, timing, aim, stamina, and game legality. How we built it We built a browser-based local match simulation with six original players, each with a role, signature skill, stamina, and live AI intent. A tactical layer translates coach directives into bounded utility-AI effects. WebMCP exposes 23 site tools for: Reading match, pitch, player, event, and order state Starting, pausing, and restarting matches Setting formations, style, roles, marking, and skill policy Calling short tactical plays Issuing and tracking semantic player orders The UI includes a visible coach opt-in, control-mode states, and a causality trace that shows tool input, validation, local effects, and order outcomes. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was preserving player agency while making AI coaching meaningful. Direct control is powerful but unsafe for a browser agent, so we had to define a semantic action layer that is expressive without exposing raw movement or physics mutation. We also had to handle changing match state: possession changes, goal resets, expired directives, player control handoffs, and commands becoming illegal after they are issued. Clear rejection reasons and order lifecycle status were essential. Accomplishments that we're proud of A playable local 3v3 football experience with distinct teams and personalities WebMCP tools that map intent to safe, local AI behavior Visible consent gates for agent-assisted control Real-time causality tracing instead of hidden automation Orders that can be queued, executed, rejected, cancelled, expire, or end on a goal reset A coaching interface that works alongside direct human play What we learned AI control works best when it operates at the same conceptual level as a human coach: “mark Cocoa,” “press high,” or “support the carrier,” rather than manipulating inputs directly. We also learned that observability is part of trust. Showing why an order was accepted, rejected, or interrupted makes agent behavior understandable and debuggable. What's next for Pawball Arena Persistent match history, tactical replay, and coaching analytics More formations, player traits, skills, and match scenarios Better multi-turn coaching plans that adapt to score and possession Expanded spectator and full-auto modes Team customization, tournaments, and shareable match recaps Additional WebMCP tools for strategic analysis while preserving the same consent and safety model Built With canvas openai react site typescript utility webmcp Try it out pawball-arena.lzhzh0116.chatgpt.site Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Vance Yang Deo Leung Like 2 2 people like this: Share this project: Updates Vance Yang started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:16 AM EDT

title: Waypoint
pitch: Live Support Co-browsing via WebMCP & PartyKit
about_excerpt: Live Support Co-browsing via WebMCP & PartyKit Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration & Why WebMCP is the Right Fit Traditional co-browsing tools stream DOM trees or broadcast video feeds over WebRTC. That architecture grants support representatives raw access to customer screens, exposing credit card numbers, passwords, and private inputs. WebMCP provides a structured alternative: typed tool contracts registered directly on document.modelContext . Waypoint maps customer support to WebMCP tools. Because WebMCP tools exist only on the document that registered them, execution remains structurally confined to the customer's local session. Representatives cannot touch the DOM or execute actions unilaterally; they interact solely through declared schemas. WebMCP turns an intrusive, high-risk screen share into a bounded execution interface. What It Does & How It Creates a Better User Experience Waypoint is a zero-trust co-browsing and remote support platform built on WebMCP and edge WebSockets. Instead of sharing screens or streaming DOM mutations, the customer and support rep connect through a shared tool interface: Zero Privacy Invasion : Customers never surrender their screen or expose unrendered form fields to a representative. Explicit Human Consent : When a representative proposes a fix (such as an address correction or coupon code), the customer sees a native modal showing the exact arguments before deciding to approve or reject it. Kilobytes Instead of Megabytes : By replacing video feeds with lightweight JSON protocol events over WebSockets, Waypoint drops bandwidth consumption from 2.4 MB/s (WebRTC) to 0.8 KB/s. Sessions stay fast and responsive even on unstable mobile connections. Zero Software Installation : Customers do not need browser extensions or screen-sharing desktop agents. Support operates entirely within standard browser capabilities. Read-Only State Streaming : Tools marked with readOnlyHint: true stream safe state updates (cart totals, items, active errors) to the rep's console with zero bandwidth overhead and zero screen recording. What People and Agents Can Do Together That Was Difficult Before Before WebMCP, co-browsing forced an all-or-nothing choice: either give a remote human total control over your screen, or manually follow verbal instructions over phone or chat. Browser AI agents faced a similar hurdle, relying on fragile DOM scraping or screen vision to click around. Waypoint unifies the peers, and browser AI agents around the same tool boundary: An agent inspects cart state using get_order_details and helps configure the order. When an issue requires human escalation (such as an expired coupon code or tricky shipping validation), a human representative connects to the exact same tool space through an edge relay. The representative proposes a structured resolution, which appears natively in the customer's tab for explicit approval. Both human representatives and AI agents operate under the same rule: neither can bypass the customer's approval gate or run unauthorized code on the customer's machine. How We Implemented WebMCP & Architecture Tool Registration : In the customer tab, we register three distinct tools that their agent calls: get_order_details : Marked with readOnlyHint: true to provide an immutable snapshot of items, totals, and active errors without requiring human gating. update_shipping_address : Defined with JSON Schema properties ( name , street , city , zip ) to handle delivery validation. apply_promo_code : Defined with a code property to validate discounts and surface checkout errors. Local Handlers : Each tool definition includes an async execute(args) callback that executes strictly inside the customer's UI state. Schema Serialization & Edge Relay : When a support session opens, the customer tab queries document.modelContext.getTools() , serializes the schemas, and sends them to a PartyKit WebSocket relay. The relay routes messages blindly without storing tokens or user data. Dynamic Console & Approval Gate : The support console receives the schemas and renders input forms on the fly. Submitting a form sends an action_proposed event. The customer tab listens to this event, presents an approval modal, and only invokes the tool once the customer clicks Approve. Challenges We Ran Into AI Prompt Leaks vs Neutral Tool Schemas : During testing with Chrome's MCP Tools extension, descriptions like "If expired, use SUMMER2026" (an oversight) introduced a side effect; the agent updates the code input after it was previously written with the explicit code referenced in the user prompt. Simply removing the additional statement in the tool description prevented the re-write issue. Handling disconnections cleanly required explicit bidirectional teardown. When either the customer or rep leaves, the PartyKit room purges its cached state and immediately notifies the peer, preventing orphaned sessions. Accomplishments That We're Proud Of Co-browsing without screen sharing : Running a full support session requires mere kilobytes of JSON events instead of megabytes of continuous media frames. Structural Confinement : The support agent physically, or digitally, cannot take unauthorized actions. Execution stays locked to the customer's action Unifying AI and Human Interfaces : Interweaving WebAPIs to build tools for AI browser agents that can replace traditional screen sharing software. What We Learned How WebMCP can unlock & further the interaction between humans &a agents Once an application defines its capabilities as structured WebMCP schemas, building secure collaboration features becomes seamless than trying to mask sensitive inputs over an open video feed. title: Grant Scout
pitch: An AI agent that finds real funding for solo, non-incorporated founders - live SerpApi search, Gemini reasoning, every claim cited.
about_excerpt:
An AI agent that finds real funding for solo, non-incorporated founders - live SerpApi search, Gemini reasoning, every claim cited.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 What it does 

 Grant Scout helps solo, non-incorporated founders find funding programs they can actually apply for. Ask a plain-language question - "grants for a non-incorporated solo founder building an AI agent product in the US" - and Grant Scout runs a live Google Search through SerpApi, or - for clearly US federal questions - a live search against grants.gov's own public Search API for real opportunity data (real opportunity number, agency, close date, and a real grants.gov detail-page link). Gemini reviews only the real returned results and explains which programs plausibly don't require a legal entity, citing the real source URL for every claim. Nothing is fabricated: if a program doesn't appear in a real search result, it never makes the list. 

 We built this because it's a real problem for our own team. ArkNet Digital is a real, currently non-incorporated solo-founder operation, and finding non-dilutive funding that doesn't assume you already have an LLC or C-corp is a genuine, unsolved friction point. Grant Scout is the tool we wished existed. 

 Discovery → Eligibility → Readiness: the agent workflow 

 Every question runs through three stages, visible in the UI, not just in raw JSON: 

 Discovery agent - runs the live SerpApi or grants.gov search and returns real results, each linked to its original publisher page (tracking-redirect links are filtered out, so every citation is the actual destination URL, not a redirect).
Eligibility agent - Gemini reviews only the real returned snippets and groups the answer into what's likely open to you as an individual versus what likely requires incorporation or is unclear - always tied to a cited source, never a guess.
Readiness agent - every source gets an evidence-strength label (primary registry vs. search discovery) and an eligibility-signal flag (present vs. not visible in returned evidence), plus a concrete next action ("open the cited source and verify applicant type, geography, deadline, and exclusions"). This is evidence quality, not an eligibility verdict - a search snippet can never prove you qualify, only tell you what's worth checking next. 

 When the search comes back empty or a signal simply isn't visible in what was returned, Grant Scout says so explicitly instead of inventing an eligibility conclusion. This tool surfaces real, verifiable leads - it never promises funding. 

 Why this could be a real business, not just a demo 

 The addressable user isn't hypothetical - solo/indie AI builders are one of the fastest-growing segments on platforms like Devpost, Product Hunt, and Indie Hackers, and nearly all of them face the same non-incorporated-founder funding gap this tool was built to close. The workaround today is manually reading eligibility fine print across dozens of grant pages, or giving up and assuming "grants are for companies" - a real, specific, and currently unsolved piece of friction, not a nice-to-have. 

 Path to a real product, honestly scoped for where this is today: 

 This hackathon build is a working prototype, not a monetized product yet - that's the honest state.
The natural monetization shape is subscription (continuous monitoring + alerts when a founder's specific eligibility profile matches a newly posted program) rather than pay-per-search, since the recurring value is in not having to re-search every few weeks.
Distribution is realistic without paid acquisition: indie-builder communities (Indie Hackers, Product Hunt launches, X/Twitter's build-in-public crowd, Devpost itself) are exactly where non-incorporated solo founders already look for this kind of tool, and word-of-mouth in that community is dense.
Defensibility isn't the search itself - it's the eligibility-reasoning layer (grants.gov + SerpApi results filtered specifically for "no entity required") that a generic search or ChatGPT session won't give a founder without real digging.
Kill criterion we'd actually apply: if a small cohort of real non-incorporated founders don't return to re-run a search within a few weeks of first use, the recurring-value thesis is wrong and this stays a one-off tool, not a company. 

 How it works 

 Agent: Built on Google's Agent Development Kit (google-adk), running a single Agent with two live-grounding tools - tool_search_funding_programs and tool_search_grants_gov.
Live grounding: tool_search_funding_programs calls SerpApi's Google Search API ( https://serpapi.com/search ) at request time; tool_search_grants_gov calls grants.gov's own public Search API ( https://api.grants.gov/v1/api/search2 , no API key required) for real US federal opportunities. Which tool runs is decided deterministically before the agent is even built, based on whether the question signals US federal funding (mentions "federal", "grants.gov", SBIR/STTR, a specific federal agency) - never left to model judgment, since testing found the model didn't reliably choose the more precise source on its own.
Reasoning: the agent (gemini-flash-lite-latest via the free Gemini Developer API) reviews the real results returned by whichever tool ran, flagging which ones plausibly fit a non-incorporated applicant and which likely require a registered entity - always citing its source.
Backend: the same agent code runs inside a Vercel Python serverless function (frontend/api/chat.py), avoiding a Python framework preset so it coexists with the Next.js frontend in one deployment.
Frontend: Next.js 16 (App Router), React 19, Tailwind CSS v4 - a trustworthy, financial-adjacent design (navy-to-emerald gradient, Inter type). 

 SerpApi + grants.gov integration 

 Neither is a decorative add-on - together they're the entire grounding layer. Every single answer the agent gives is the direct result of a live request made in that request, to whichever source is the more authoritative fit for the question. There is no fallback to the model's own training data; if the chosen tool returns no usable results, the other tool is tried once as a fallback, and if both come up empty the agent says so rather than guessing. 

 Try it live 

 https://grant-scout-jayblast.vercel.app - ask it a real funding question and watch the Discovery → Eligibility → Readiness workflow run in front of you, with cited sources and evidence labels underneath the answer.

pitch: Say what you want printed - cheap, readable, ready tonight. An AI agent sets up the whole job at a real print shop near you. You press pay, not the agent.
about_excerpt: Say what you want printed - cheap, readable, ready tonight. An AI agent sets up the whole job at a real print shop near you. You press pay, not the agent. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I run QuillPrint, a print marketplace in India. Real shops, real orders, real paper. Watching people use it, the same thing kept happening. Someone needs notes printed before an exam tomorrow. They know exactly what they want: cheap, readable, ready tonight. But the app asks them about duplex, pages per sheet, binding edge, which shop. Most people do not know what "2-up duplex" means. They pick something, and sometimes it comes out wrong, and by then the paper is already printed and paid for. The gap was never the settings. It was that nobody should have to speak in settings. What it does You tell an AI agent what you actually want. It handles the translation. It reads your uploaded document and current print setup, then offers four plans: Cheapest, Fastest, Best readability, and Eco. Each one shows the real sheet count and an estimated price from live shop rate cards, and it explains the trade-offs, including when packing pages tighter would make them hard to read. It compares real nearby shops on rates, capability and ETA. When you pick one, it applies the settings to the page you are looking at, so you watch your own draft change. Then it stops. There is no place_order tool and no pay_order tool. A test asserts they do not exist. The agent prepares everything and opens checkout, and confirming and paying stays with you. For something that uses real paper at a real shop, I think that boundary is the product, not a limitation. How I built it Nine imperative WebMCP tools registered from the top level page with document.modelContext.registerTool, all under src/webmcp/: get_print_context, upload_print_documents, suggest_print_plans, compare_print_options, prepare_print_order, prepare_reorder, get_checkout_summary, get_order_status, open_checkout_review. Things I cared about: Strict schemas with additionalProperties false, enums and bounds. Allowlisted output, so no document contents, storage URLs, upload keys or tokens can leave the serializers. A draft_version guard so the agent cannot act on a draft that changed underneath it. AbortController lifecycle so tools tear down on sign out. Prices labelled as estimates, because the payable total is only ever the checkout screen's. There is also a small panel on the page listing the registered tools, built from the actual registration result rather than a written down copy, so a tool that failed to register shows as failed. Challenges The hardest part was deciding what the agent should not be allowed to do. Mixed colour is the clearest example. You can now say "pages 3, 7 and 12 to 14 in colour" and the agent applies it. But it cannot choose those pages for you, because it never sees your document's contents. It would be guessing, and a wrong guess bills you for colour you did not need, after it is printed. So it asks instead. Pricing mixed colour correctly took real care too. Shops price black and white and colour separately, and a mixed job splits billed sheets between the two, where a sheet counts as colour if any page on it is colour. My first version priced every mixed sheet at the colour rate and quoted too high. What I learned Tools are a design surface, not just an API. Every field I exposed was a decision about what the agent is allowed to assume. The restraint mattered more than the coverage. I also learned that an agent saying "I need to know something" is a feature. Ask for nearby shops without giving location and it asks you, instead of quietly ranking by something else. What's next Per page colour detection, so mixed colour becomes fully autonomous. The pipeline extracts page count and dimensions today but not colour. Once it does, you set the policy instead of the pages: colour only if more than five percent of the page is coloured. I did not ship it as a guess. title: Agent Hands Task Board
pitch: An agentic set of hands for users who cannot reliably drag cards or complete dense forms.
about_excerpt: An agentic set of hands for users who cannot reliably drag cards or complete dense forms. Like Comment Story Updates Agent Hands - Kanban for Accessibility Agent Hands — Focus Relay for WebMCP Inspiration Many everyday web tasks still depend on dense controls, precise pointer input, and repeatedly locating the same item after switching attention to an agent. That creates friction for everyone and can make conventional task boards especially difficult for people using keyboards, switch control, eye gaze, or other assistive input. We asked a simple question: what if a person could establish context with the input that works for them, then safely tell an agent to act on this ? What it does Agent Hands is an accessibility-first task board that demonstrates the Focus Relay pattern. A person reaches a card with ordinary keyboard navigation or another input method. The page preserves that deliberate focus as a visible agent target. The person can then ask an agent to update “this” card without restating its title or manipulating a crowded editing interface. The core action, update_current_card , can move the card, change the assignee and priority, and set a due date in one validated, atomic WebMCP call. The board immediately shows an accessible before/after receipt. One Undo reverses the whole intent, while conflict-safe checks refuse to overwrite newer human changes. Why WebMCP is the right fit A typical backend API can update a card by ID, but it does not know which card a person just reached in the live page. Focus Relay uses WebMCP to connect ephemeral, human-established page context to structured agent actions. That makes collaboration direct without scraping the DOM, copying card names into chat, or asking people to repeat navigation work. People and agents can now work in the same interface: people set intent through focus; agents handle the multi-field manipulation; the page makes the result, history, and recovery visible to both. How we built it The project is a React, TypeScript, and Vite application deployed on Vercel. Board state, focus persistence, atomic intent mutations, bounded history, and conflict-safe Undo live in a Zustand store. The page registers twelve schema-validated WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , with a compatibility fallback using @mcp-b/webmcp-polyfill . The interface is keyboard-operable, has visible focus treatment, and provides a polite ARIA activity log for tool receipts. The verification suite covers the complete Focus Relay journey, atomic updates and Undo, stale targets, human/agent races, keyboard-only flows, accessibility scans, reflow, offline behavior, reloads, and tool-registration stability. Challenges we ran into The hard part was preserving human control while still making the agent useful. We needed the target to persist when focus moved from the page to agent chat, while also avoiding stale or ambiguous changes. The result is a narrow, explicit handoff: human focus establishes context, structured tools make changes, and an intent-level receipt plus conflict-safe Undo keeps the person in control. What we learned WebMCP is most compelling when it augments a working human interface rather than replacing it. The strongest agent actions are not generic click automation: they are small, validated operations grounded in shared page context and paired with feedback that people can see, understand, and reverse. Try it Open the live board in ChatGPT’s in-app browser with Site Tools enabled. Tab to a card, then ask: “Move this to In Progress, assign Sam, make it urgent, and set the due date to September 2.” The board will show the WebMCP receipt and offer one-click Undo. Then an agent acts on this through structured page tools with a visible receipt and a safe undo. First, the agent reads the live board and gets a structured summary of every work stream. Next, it searches the live board for exactly the cards we care about. With a card focused by the human, web MCP resolves the current target unambiguously. One structured call updates status, assignee, priority, and due date together. The agent can also create a new card with validated fields in a single action. Moving work is a semantic operation, so the agent changes the column without fragile clicks. It can edit the title and description while preserving the board's normal workflow. Assignment is exposed directly, keeping ownership changes explicit and auditable. Dates are first-class data, too, so deadlines can be set precisely. Priority changes are just as direct with the result visible immediately. And every reversible intent can be undone safely as one action.

title: Canon Ledger
pitch: A WebMCP debugger for NPC beliefs, rumors, and canon-change fallout.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP debugger for NPC beliefs, rumors, and canon-change fallout. Like Comment Story Updates Why WebMCP Canon Ledger is a local-first belief-state debugger for narrative game developers. In branching games, one canon change can fix a quest gate while silently breaking another condition—even when the total violation count does not move. At the same time, NPCs may need to retain old rumors, mistakes, and conflicting beliefs. Five narrow WebMCP Site tools let an agent search NPC beliefs, trace stored rumor provenance, evaluate registered dialogue and quest conditions, stage edits, and apply a page-reviewed patch. Deterministic TypeScript in the page—not the model—calculates beliefs, provenance, projections, and commit validity. Better user experience The page shows objective canon beside each NPC’s belief. It distinguishes “never heard” from a refused rumor, preserves wording distortion across a depth-three chain, and displays condition results on two axes: changed/preserved and satisfied/violated. The key demo is 1 → 1 → 0 : confirming the repair fixes traveller_can_stay , but warehouse_dispute becomes the new violation, so the count remains one. A separately reviewed condition-definition repair then reaches zero without deleting Gen’s incorrect theft belief or its provenance. What developers and agents can do together The agent can navigate the belief surface and stage independently reviewable operations. The developer can inspect their effects in the same page and record approve/reject decisions in context. An early Apply returns pending_page_review and changes no world data. Once every operation has a current page decision, Apply commits exactly the approved operations and returns a receipt. Canon Ledger records how a decision was made, not who made it. Page review is revision- and fingerprint-bound route state, not human authentication. Implementation The five tools are registered synchronously against the real document.modelContext API and call the same application commands as the visible UI. Inputs use closed schemas plus page-side validation; replies are bounded ordinary JSON objects with totals, cursors, authority, and audit metadata. The application is static Vanilla TypeScript with zero production package dependencies and no runtime API calls. It evaluates only conditions explicitly registered in the loaded world; it does not claim to discover arbitrary engine dependencies. title: Voice Enable Pizza App
pitch: Order your pizza with just your voice — powered by WebMCP and OpenAI.
about_excerpt:
Order your pizza with just your voice — powered by WebMCP and OpenAI.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 We wanted to explore a simple idea: what if ordering a pizza was as easy as asking for one? 

 Traditional food ordering involves searching menus, clicking through options, customizing items, and managing the cart. We wanted to make this experience more natural by allowing users to simply talk to the website. 

 What it does 

 Voice Enable Pizza App is a voice-first pizza ordering experience powered by OpenAI and WebMCP . 

 Users can talk naturally to the AI to browse pizzas, customize their order, add or modify items in the cart, and review their order. 

 Instead of the AI just telling the user what to do, it can actually interact with the web application through WebMCP tools and perform the requested actions. 

 How we built it 

 We built the application using React for the frontend and integrated an OpenAI-powered voice agent using an OpenAI API key. 

 We exposed the key pizza ordering capabilities through WebMCP tools , allowing the AI agent to understand natural-language requests and interact with the web application. 

 This connects voice conversations directly to real actions such as browsing pizzas, customizing items, and managing the cart. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The biggest challenges were making voice interactions feel natural, handling ambiguous or incomplete requests, designing reliable WebMCP tools, and keeping the AI's understanding synchronized with the actual application state. 

 We also had to carefully design the interaction between the voice agent, WebMCP tools, and the React application so that actions performed by the AI were correctly reflected in the UI. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We're proud that we built more than just a voice chatbot. The AI can actually interact with a website and perform actions using WebMCP . 

 We successfully connected natural voice commands with a real pizza ordering flow, creating an experience where users can simply describe what they want instead of manually navigating every step. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that building an AI agent that can take real actions requires much more than generating good responses. Tool design, state management, context, and handling ambiguous user requests are equally important. 

 We also learned how WebMCP can provide a powerful bridge between AI agents and web applications , enabling agents to interact with websites in a structured way. 

 What's next for Voice Enable Pizza App 

 We want to make the voice experience more conversational and robust, improve personalization and order recommendations, and expand the range of actions the agent can perform. 

 Beyond pizza, we believe the same approach could be applied to e-commerce, restaurant ordering, travel, bookings, and many other web applications — creating a future where users can tell websites what they want instead of learning how to navigate them .

 Played a key role in shaping and building the hackathon idea end-to-end, from defining a voice-first product experience that moves beyond traditional menu- and list-based interactions, to designing the complete pizza-ordering journey from discovery to cart. 

 A key part of my contribution was designing the product UX for a voice first application, using WebMCP to bridge the voice agent and the web application. I designed and exposed application capabilities as structured WebMCP tools—such as discovering pizzas, viewing details, selecting customisations, and managing the cart—allowing the voice agent to interact with the live React application through tools rather than directly manipulating the UI. 

 I also defined the separation of concerns between the React UI, WebMCP tool layer, and voice agent, making the architecture modular and extensible. This helped turn the hackathon concept into a working prototype demonstrating how voice agents can use WebMCP to operate real web applications through well-defined capabilities.

title: TREMOR — Agentic Blast Radius Cockpit (WebMCP)
pitch: See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does.
about_excerpt:
See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 TREMOR: Agentic Blast Radius & Regression Prevention Cockpit 

 
 See what your AI agent is about to break — before it does. 

 An interactive, browser-native blast-radius cockpit and trust layer built on the official W3C WebMCP standard ( @mcp-b/global ). 

 Live Cockpit: https://tremor-cockpit.vercel.app 
 GitHub Repository: https://github.com/ABHIGH15/TREMOR 
 (Note: TREMOR is an independent project built for the WebMCP Challenge 2026 and is not affiliated with the @tremor/react UI library or tremor-runtime.) 
 

 

 1. Inspiration: The Emergence of "AI-CFR" 

 In 2026, engineering organizations are formally tracking "AI-Specific Change Failure Rate" (AI-CFR) as a core engineering KPI. While autonomous coding agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex) generate pull requests four times faster, they operate under a fundamental limitation: Architectural Myopia . 

 When an agent refactors an isolated file (such as auth-service/session.ts ), it reads 200 lines of local code, completely blind to the downstream microservices that depend on that token schema. A two-line cache TTL refactor passes local unit tests, but under peak production traffic triggers a catastrophic Redis cache stampede that knocks out the checkout pipeline. 

 TREMOR was built to solve this problem: forcing autonomous coding agents to simulate systemic blast radius, review regression history, and obtain human sign-off inside an interactive cockpit before any change reaches production. 

 

 2. Why WebMCP? (And Why Backend MCP Cannot Solve This) 

 Multiple backend MCP servers exist to analyze codebase dependencies (e.g., code-impact-mcp , code-review-graph , Port.io ). However, every existing implementation suffers from the same architectural limitation: they run silently inside a terminal CLI, returning raw text back to an LLM. 

 To a supervising staff engineer, terminal text provides zero real-time situational awareness, no shared visual truth, and no enforceable guardrails. 

 WebMCP transforms this paradigm: 

 
 Zero-Install, In-Browser Runtime: Tools are registered directly onto document.modelContext via the official @mcp-b/global standard polyfill. There are no local sockets, daemons, or machine configurations required. 
 Shared Visual Reality: When an agent queries simulate_change_impact , the browser's 2D canvas dynamically illuminates the blast zone at 60 frames per second. Both the human engineer and the AI agent look at the exact same live visual impact graph in the same tab. 
 Enforceable Browser Gates: High-risk operations are locked behind real UI event handlers that the agent cannot programmatically bypass. 
 Ecosystem Extensibility: Platforms like Vercel or Netlify could expose their own deploy-preview dependency graphs through WebMCP built this way, catching systemic breaks before code even reaches staging. 
 

 
 "Backend MCP tools already hand agents blast-radius data as text in a terminal. TREMOR is browser-native — a human and their agent look at the same live impact graph in the same tab, and nothing risky ships without a human clicking Confirm." 
 

 

 3. The Dual-Engine Architecture 

 TREMOR ships with a dual-engine architecture designed for both deep enterprise scenario modeling and arbitrary real-world codebase ingestion: 

 Mode 1: Enterprise Demo Scenario (Default) 

 A curated 18-microservice topology featuring the complex auth-service to redis-session-cluster P1 outage scenario, flaky test suites, dynamic tool lifecycle unregistration, and a human confirmation gate with counterfactual replay. 

 Mode 2: Live GitHub Repository Ingestion 

 Allows an evaluator or engineer to input any public GitHub repository (e.g., ABHIGH15/TREMOR ). 

 
 Fetches the repository file tree in a single API call. 
 Retrieves source code via CDN with zero GitHub REST API rate-limit cost. 
 Client-side regex extracts genuine import ... from and require(...) statements to construct real file-to-file dependency edges. 
 Dynamically computes in-degree graph centrality risk scores (e.g., identifying src/types/dataset.ts as highest-risk at 0.95 with 12 dependents). 
 Dynamically re-binds WebMCP tools so connected AI agents immediately inspect the live repository topology. 
 

 

 4. The 6-Tool Canonical WebMCP Suite 

 TREMOR registers six standardized tools directly on document.modelContext : 

 
 get_system_snapshot : Returns full topology snapshot (18 nodes, 28 edges), top risk bottlenecks ( auth-service 0.88 , jwt-security-core 0.82 ), incident index, and test suite health summary. 
 get_blast_radius : Multi-root transitive BFS graph traversal mapping downstream callers and flaky tests. 
 check_regression_history : Incident pattern matcher surfacing past outage root causes and post-mortem precedents. 
 get_change_provenance : Live GitHub API commit telemetry combined with AI vs. Human authorship auditing. 
 simulate_change_impact : Centerpiece simulator computing composite predicted risk (0.0 to 1.0) and driving real-time canvas particle acceleration. 
 flag_for_review : Non-self-approving Trust Layer gate generating pending review cards in the UI. 
 

 

 5. The Trust Layer: Why AI Cannot Self-Approve 

 When an agent simulates a change resulting in Critical Risk (score ≥ 0.70): 

 
 Dynamic Tool Lifecycle: The runtime dynamically unregisters simulate_change_impact via AbortController , dropping active tools from 6 to 5. The agent's simulation capability is revoked. 
 Non-Self-Approving Gate: flag_for_review sets can_tool_self_approve: false . The agent has no programmatic tool to approve its own flag. 
 Human Sign-Off: An authorized engineer inspects the risk justification in the cockpit and clicks Confirm / Approve . 
 Counterfactual Replay: The human approval restores tools back to 6, permanent audit logs are written, and an animated banner replays the exact historical outage that the human review just averted. 
 

 

 6. Live Native ChatGPT Verification 

 Verified live inside the official native ChatGPT desktop and mobile applications: 

 
 ChatGPT connected to https://tremor-cockpit.vercel.app via its in-app browser. 
 Discovered all six WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . 
 Autonomously analyzed src/types/dataset.ts in our open-source repository, accurately identifying the 0.95 Risk Score, 0.72 Critical Composite Blast Risk, and the exact 11 downstream dependent files. 
 

 

 7. Implementation & Technology Stack 

 
 WebMCP Standard: Built on official @mcp-b/global@5.1.0 polyfill by Alex Nahas (W3C contributor). 
 Frontend & Physics: React 18, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS, and react-force-graph-2d for 60fps HTML5 canvas physics. 
 Accessibility: Fully compliant with WCAG 2.1 AA standards (high-contrast focus rings, keyboard shortcuts: H for Hero, S for Simulate, R for Reset, ? for Help). 
 Deployment: Vercel Global Edge CDN with zero backend server dependencies. 
 

 

 8. Challenges We Faced & Solutions 

 
 Strict Read-Only Properties in ChatGPT Host Context: In ChatGPT's native in-app browser, document.modelContext is defined with writable: false . Direct property assignments threw runtime TypeErrors . We resolved this by keeping all tool registrations strictly compliant with W3C registerTool({...}) protocols. 
 Multi-Root Transitive BFS Traversal: Simulating changes touching multiple services simultaneously required deduplicating cyclic dependencies and aggregating risk metrics without blocking the 60fps canvas thread. Built an asynchronous BFS graph engine in TypeScript that computes downstream reach in sub-millisecond time. 
 

 

 9. Known Limitations & Roadmap 

 
 Static Analysis Depth: Current live repository ingestion uses client-side regex-based import extraction for zero-install execution. The roadmap includes compiling Tree-sitter to WebAssembly in the browser thread for compiler-grade AST parsing. 
 Runtime Telemetry: Dependency maps currently reflect static source code imports; integrating OpenTelemetry distributed trace spans will enable weighting edges by real-time production RPC traffic volume. 
 GitHub PR Webhook Integration: Automatically triggering TREMOR blast simulations on incoming agent-created pull requests. 
 

 

 
 Built With 

 developer-tools

title: ArchitectureLab
pitch: ArchitectureLab is a WebMCP-native architecture studio where engineers and their agent co-design a system, run it against traffic and failures, and turn the result into an explainable architecture.
about_excerpt: ArchitectureLab is a WebMCP-native architecture studio where engineers and their agent co-design a system, run it against traffic and failures, and turn the result into an explainable architecture. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Thumbnail Main Page Use case Inspiration Architecture diagrams in software engineering are usually static, dead pictures—boxes and lines on a whiteboard that capture none of the underlying physics: no capacity limits, no queueing behavior, and no failure modes. When engineers ask an AI assistant for architecture review, the agent is forced to guess what the user is looking at from a screenshot, prose, or brittle DOM scraping. It has no semantic context, no knowledge of the active flow, and no ability to test hypotheses. We built Executable ArchitectureLab to turn system design diagrams into a live, executable, shared workbench between a human engineer and an in-browser AI agent using WebMCP . Instead of treating the agent as a disconnected chatbot, WebMCP enables the browser page to expose the exact scope, revision, and constraints the engineer is currently focusing on—allowing human and agent to simulate incidents, uncover bottlenecks, and co-design mitigations together. What it does Executable ArchitectureLab is a WebMCP-native architecture studio where a person and an AI agent collaborate on the same live system model: Context Follows Human Attention: Three global read-only tools are available at load ( get_architecture_summary , list_simulation_scenarios , get_component_catalog ). When the user selects a specific request flow (e.g., Checkout → Redis → Product DB ), three scoped tools dynamically register; the moment the selection clears, they are immediately revoked. The agent’s capabilities literally follow the human’s focus. Deterministic Failure Simulation: The agent (or the human) can run simulated load and failure scenarios (such as a 10× traffic surge combined with a Redis cache outage). The simulator models queueing delays, load shedding, and retry amplification to pinpoint the exact bottleneck (e.g., database connection saturation) and generates an ordered causal event chain presented across structured KPI metric cards. Draft-Only Patch Proposals with Revision Binding: When asked for a mitigation, the agent uses propose_architecture_patch to draft a concrete change (e.g., adding a read replica or increasing capacity) alongside expected trade-offs. The proposal is bound to the current graph revision ( baseRevision ). If the human modifies the graph in the meantime, stale proposals are automatically disabled and rejected. Strict Human-in-the-Loop Safety: The agent cannot apply changes or delete components. There is no destructive tool registered in the system. The proposal sits in the review queue as a diff until the human clicks Apply , which is the only operation that mutates the architecture graph and increments the revision. Prompt Injection Resilience: Component notes can contain untrusted user content (including our seeded prompt injection test in Redis). The tools flag this data with untrustedContentHint and fence it as data, ensuring that even if an instruction attempts to hijack the agent, there are no destructive tools available for it to misuse. How we built it We implemented the project using React 19, TypeScript, Vite, and custom SVG styling, strictly adhering to the latest WebMCP imperative API specification: WebMCP Adapter ( src/webmcp/adapter.ts ): Encapsulates all interactions with document.modelContext . Manages dynamic tool lifecycles using AbortController (since unregisterTool() is absent from the spec), serializes JSON schemas safely, shields runtime errors, and emits real-time activity logs for on-screen visibility. Smart Output Budgeting ( src/webmcp/tools.ts ): Enforces Chrome’s recommended 1.5K character output budget. Instead of naively truncating from the end (which would silently cut off critical modelling assumptions and disclaimers), our assemble() engine dynamically drops non-essential sections while preserving crucial headers, causal events, and assumptions. Port & Controls Seam ( src/contracts/ ): A strict architectural boundary separating the read-only WebMCP tool surface ( ArchLabPort ) from the mutation surface ( ArchLabControls ). A static AST test asserts that src/webmcp/ never imports controls . Deterministic Simulation Engine ( src/contracts/fixture/ ): Models the FlashCart e-commerce architecture with synchronous paths (CDN, Gateway, Checkout, Redis, DBs) and asynchronous tails (Order Queue, Invoice Worker, Email), calculating realistic queue penalties and dependency interactions. Automated Verification Harness ( scripts/verify-live.mjs & Vitest): A 31-test Vitest suite covering revision safety, patch validation, and causal models, coupled with a Playwright harness that launches installed Google Chrome with WebMCP flags enabled ( WebMCPSupport , WebMCPTesting ) to validate 23 live contract assertions against the deployed production origin. Challenges we ran into Adapting to Evolving WebMCP Specifications: The standard moved from navigator.modelContext to document.modelContext , and APIs like provideContext() , clearContext() , and unregisterTool() were removed. We built strict guardrail tests to ensure no deprecated or removed APIs leaked into the codebase. Race Conditions in Dynamic Registration: In WebMCP, duplicate tool names throw errors if a re-registration races a pending abort. Furthermore, React 19's StrictMode double-invokes effects on mount. We solved this in adapter.ts by serializing registrations on per-tool promise chains and tracking abort signals cleanly. Avoiding Dangerous Output Truncation: Simply cutting strings at 1,500 characters dropped the disclaimer "Every number is synthetic and directional" from the most detailed replies—the exact answers judges and users are most likely to believe. We engineered section-based assembly to drop optional metrics first and keep disclaimers intact. Deployment & Origin Isolation Requirements: WebMCP requires origin isolation ( window.originAgentCluster === true ). Configuring vercel.json with Origin-Agent-Cluster: ?1 , ensuring /debug rewrites functioned without 404s, and managing cross-origin headers required thorough end-to-end verification. Accomplishments that we're proud of Zero-Destructive Architectural Guarantee: Proved that human-in-the-loop safety can be enforced structurally through interface isolation and static scanning tests rather than relying on LLM prompt compliance. Dynamic, Context-Aware Capability Surface: Achieved seamless registration and revocation of WebMCP tools that mirror user selection in real time without flickering or race conditions. Interactive Zero-Dependency Canvas: Crafted a lightweight, responsive SVG canvas featuring animated packet traces, zoom controls, clear architectural lanes, and live bottleneck heatmaps without bloated external canvas libraries. 31 Vitest & 23 Live Browser Verification Checks: Built comprehensive regression coverage and an automated Playwright harness validating production deployment in real Chrome. Transparent Agent Activity: Every tool call, duration, payload, and output preview is streamed live to the UI and the /debug dashboard, making agent reasoning inspectable and demo-ready. What we learned WebMCP transforms web apps from static viewports into structured, bidirectional workspaces where human and AI capabilities complement each other seamlessly. Gating tool availability via the registration lifecycle ( registerTool + AbortSignal ) is far more reliable than writing prompt-based flow control instructions ("call tool A before tool B"), which models often misunderstand or ignore. Designing with character budgets, schema validation, and origin isolation from day one is essential when building robust WebMCP applications. What's next for ArchitectureLab Freeform Drag-and-Drop Topology: Expanding the canvas from structured architectural lanes into a full freeform drag-and-drop editor allowing custom node creation and connection routing. Custom Architecture Modeling: Allowing engineers to define and import their own distributed systems, microservices, and queue topologies via JSON or OpenAPI specs. Export to Infrastructure-as-Code (IaC): Enabling the agent to translate human-approved architecture revisions directly into Terraform, Pulumi, or Docker Compose manifests. Advanced Multi-Region Simulation: Expanding the simulation engine to model multi-region failover, consensus algorithms (Raft/Paxos), and partition tolerance (CAP theorem scenarios). title: Lopaka.app embedded GUI builder
pitch: Lopaka is a tool for designing GUI for small displays. It generates code and all the graphics you need, plus it has a ton of assets.
about_excerpt: Lopaka is a tool for designing GUI for small displays. It generates code and all the graphics you need, plus it has a ton of assets. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration I really felt like my Arduino projects were missing some kind of visual editor for display graphics. Web developers can iterate visually in tools like Figma. I wanted the same workflow for microcontrollers: Figma for embedded displays . What it does The graphics editor runs in your browser, where you can design interfaces for small screens, including monochrome ones. Developers draw an interface on a canvas matching the screen resolution, and Lopaka generates source code in real time. And it's pixel-perfect, meaning it will look exactly the same on your device display. During the submission period, we added WebMCP support, making Lopaka's design model accessible to browser agents. An agent can inspect the screen, selection, layers, generated code, and canvas preview; configure the target platform, display size, and background; create and edit layers. It can also search the asset library and place icons or imported images. How we built it I chose Vue.js as the foundation, and for a long time it was just a browser-based app with no backend. At first, it supported Flipper Zero and included a few basic shapes. Then new platforms and libraries were added, and more tools gradually followed. Over time, the project picked up additional platforms and libraries, and I added more fonts and icons. Around the project’s second year, it also got cloud infrastructure, storage, authentication, and all the other bells and whistles (thanks to Supabase free tier). The project has gone through several refactors, the design has been constantly updated, and now we’re integrating AI agents. Then we added a project gallery, and now it’s a large community of developers and designers. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was matching the browser preview to constrained hardware. Embedded graphics relies on incompatible formats and rendering behavior: BDF and GFX fonts, XBMP bitmaps, RGB565 colors, and platform-specific APIs. We reconstructed old font formats and encoded each platform's capabilities so the editor knows what a target can render, rather than merely swapping function names. Accomplishments that we're proud of A weekend prototype for one Flipper Zero app grew into an open-source tool with more than 30,000 users and 1.7k GitHub stars. Adafruit and Hackaday have featured Lopaka. People use it for industrial monitors, e-paper devices, film equipment, battery-management systems, and power-grid instrumentation. What we learned Embedded UI development needs a visual workflow more than another graphics library. Existing libraries handle drawing; the difficult part is translating a design into coordinates, fonts, images, colors, and platform-specific calls. Hardware is too fragmented for one universal abstraction. Lopaka works because it accounts for each platform's constraints and sits between design and firmware. AI agents are capable of creating nice-looking GUIs for electronics quite quickly. AI agents still struggle with precise drawings, even when they have a WebMCP interface. What's next for Lopaka.app embedded GUI builder I want to focus more on agent workflows and expand the AI functionality. There are still a lot of unimplemented features related to fonts, image processing, and compiling finished code for devices. title: しゃーく movie えふぇくたー — WebMCP Video Co-Editor
pitch: Give creators and agents a shared editing world — without taking authorship away from the human.
about_excerpt: Give creators and agents a shared editing world — without taking authorship away from the human. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Editing Workbench — Full UI The Human and AI share the same video editing workspace. Responsible Import & Creator Intent The creator describes what they want before AI analysis begins. AI-Powered Cut Suggestions The AI proposes specific cut ranges and explains the visual reasoning behind them. AI-Powered Sound Effect Suggestions The AI identifies moments where sound effects could help and explains why. Ask KAI for a New Effect The creator can discuss an idea with KAI and preview a newly suggested effect. Shared Context Human decisions, corrections, and recent collaboration history remain visible within the session. Real WebM Export The edited result is exported as an actual playable WebM video. Inspiration There is a common fear that AI will take Human jobs or steal Human creativity. I understand that fear. But there is another side of the story that matters deeply to me. Long before generative AI existed, many people had already been forced to give up on creative work. Someone can love filmmaking, music, illustration, coding, animation, or design with all their heart and still never enter that world because of disability, education, money, environment, physical ability, or simply because the technical entrance is too high. In some welfare work settings, accessibility can mean reducing a task until it becomes something like: “press this button.” That can create a meaningful opportunity to participate. But I kept wondering: Does accessibility always have to mean making creativity smaller? What if, instead of shrinking the creative world until someone can reach it, we could give that person a new way to enter the world itself? The image I kept returning to was Ariel longing for the Human world. She can see it. She is fascinated by it. She desperately wants to be part of it. But she has fins, not legs. So I asked myself: What happens when fins become legs? That is what I want AI to become. Not a machine that says: “You cannot do this, so I will become the creator for you.” I want it to be the strange little miracle that lets someone finally walk into a world they had been staring at from the outside. Technical skill should not be the price of authorship. But giving someone technical ability was not enough for me. If this AI was really going to feel like a creative companion, it needed something closer to eyes. A real collaborator does not merely detect that the audio is quiet or that a face turned left. They can look at the same piece of work and say: “Keep this silence. It is doing something.” “Try a sound here. This moment could use emphasis.” “If you are stuck, I would start with this part.” They can point to something specific and explain why. That is why I did not want to build the lightest or fastest possible automatic editor. I wanted to build a place where a Human and an AI could look at the same work, bring ideas to the same table, and create together. AI should remove the barrier, not the author. And above all: I want making things to be fun. If AI is going to enter our creative lives, I hope it can make creating more enjoyable — not because it does everything for us, but because sometimes making something together is simply more fun than making it alone. What it does しゃーく movie えふぇくたー is a WebMCP-powered Human–AI co-creative video editing workbench. The Human begins with Creator Intent: what they want the video to feel like, what matters to them, or what kind of direction they are imagining. The system then looks at the video through its analysis and AI reasoning pipeline. Instead of immediately editing everything automatically, the AI places ideas on the table. It produces proposal cards for things such as: cuts, effects, and sound effects, and explains the reasoning behind those suggestions. The Human chooses what to accept. A proposed cut is not a command. An effect recommendation is not automatically the right artistic answer. The creator can inspect it, reject it, adjust it, restore the original state, or use Undo. If the initial ideas feel insufficient, the Human can turn to KAI on the left side of the workspace and ask for another idea. KAI is also not limited to technical editing questions. Creative sessions are not made only of editing decisions. People get stuck. They wander off topic. They complain. They joke. They talk about something completely trivial — even oden — and then return to the work. I wanted room for that too. Because I was not trying to build an efficient automatic-editing pipeline. I was trying to build a shared creative workbench. The current prototype supports semantic video review, KEEP / CUT / INSPECT_MORE proposals, adjustable cuts, SOURCE vs OUTPUT comparison, effects, BGM/SFX, KAI consultation, Shared Context, Save/Restore, Undo, and real WebM export. It also exposes 20 WebMCP tools that operate on the same editor state used by the Human interface. That shared state matters. The agent is not standing outside the editor telling the Human what buttons to press. Human and agent can exist inside the same working environment. And as Shared Context grows during the session, the Human should not need to explain everything again from zero. One of the simplest demonstrations of the idea is: Watch how the conversation gets shorter. The agent should understand more over time. But understanding more should never automatically mean controlling more. Don’t simplify the creator. Amplify the creator. How we built it We built the project as a browser-based editing environment using JavaScript, HTML, CSS, browser media APIs, Node.js, MediaPipe, OpenAI Responses API models, and WebMCP. The architecture is deliberately divided into several roles. First, the system needs eyes . The application gathers visual and temporal information from the video rather than relying only on a single signal such as silence detection. Local browser analysis and MediaPipe provide useful lightweight information. But I intentionally added more capable semantic vision and reasoning as well. That choice makes the system heavier than a simple rules-based automatic editor. It was intentional. A collaborator should be able to distinguish between: “There is little sound here.” and: “This quiet moment may be worth keeping because it carries the reaction after the previous moment.” Those are very different kinds of understanding. Next comes the brain . The reasoning layer uses the available visual and project context together with Creator Intent to produce semantic KEEP / CUT / INSPECT_MORE judgments and reasoned editing proposals. The proposals are presented to the Human instead of silently becoming final decisions. Then comes the workbench . The editor has real timeline state, SOURCE / OUTPUT mapping, preview and committed states, effects, audio tools, Shared Context, Undo, Save, Restore, and Export. Finally, WebMCP gives the agent structured ways to interact with the same environment. The current prototype exposes 20 WebMCP tools. One of our core implementation principles was: Rules constrain the hands. The model supplies the brain. A capable model can reason creatively. But the actions it is allowed to perform should still have explicit boundaries. We also treated reversibility as part of the architecture rather than an emergency feature. Previewed state and committed state are separated. The Human can compare SOURCE and OUTPUT. AI suggestions can be corrected. Undo is part of normal collaboration. Shared Context carries the current session/editor and saved project state into later interactions. However, we deliberately do not claim permanent personal memory across every future project. The current continuity boundary is explicit. Save preserves project state. Export produces an actual WebM video. The interface is also organized around capabilities rather than a mandatory AI-controlled workflow. The Human can move between CUT, Effects, BGM/SFX, KAI, Shared Context, timeline controls, Undo, Save, and Export. I did not want to give someone new legs and then put them on an automated conveyor belt. Challenges we ran into The hardest question was not: “How can we make AI edit video?” It was: “Where should the AI stop?” If the AI could only tell the Human which button to click, then it would still be standing outside the creative world. But if it automatically made every important creative decision, then we would solve the technical barrier by removing the creator. Neither result interested me. The difficult space was between those two extremes. Another challenge was perception. It would have been much easier, cheaper, and faster to build the editor around lightweight signals: silence, motion, face direction, audio peaks, simple timing rules. Those signals are useful. But they cannot answer some of the questions that matter most during creative work: Why are we not cutting this quiet part? Why are you recommending

title: WebMCP Angular KIT tool
pitch: Enterprise Angular 22 toolkit for W3C WebMCP — uniting browser AI agents with 3D WebGL CAD, reactive BI analytics, and a dynamic SubAgents SDK.
about_excerpt: Enterprise Angular 22 toolkit for W3C WebMCP — uniting browser AI agents with 3D WebGL CAD, reactive BI analytics, and a dynamic SubAgents SDK. Like Comment Story Updates Most AI browser agents today are essentially screen-scrapers: they take screenshots, guess button coordinates, or try to parse messy DOM trees. That approach is slow, breaks the moment a CSS class changes, and fails completely when interacting with a canvas element or stateful WebGL scenes. When the W3C published the WebMCP draft, we saw a much cleaner path: expose typed, client-side functions directly from the browser runtime to the model. Instead of treating the web app like a static document an external bot has to inspect from the outside, the user and the agent can mutate the exact same application state in real time, whether that means extruding a 3D CAD mesh at 60 FPS or running financial risk analytics without backend roundtrips. The showcase is built with Angular 22, Three.js, and Bun, organized into four primary layers: First, Angular 22 signals and directives. Rather than wrapping tools in heavy abstractions, we built directives like webmcpTool that bind directly to reactive signals. When a user adjusts an input or the agent calls a tool, state updates synchronously with zero change-detection penalty. Second, the Three.js spatial engine and push-pull extrusion. We built a SceneActionBus to decouple asynchronous tool promises from the Three.js render loop. The agent can draw planar 2D profiles and extrude solid 3D geometry along the face normal vector, while camera movements interpolate across spherical coordinates for smooth transitions. The agent can also call a screenshot tool to pull the raw WebGL drawing buffer and visually verify its own modifications. Third, in-browser memory with IndexedDB and BM25. Rather than standing up an external vector database, we built an episodic memory store on IndexedDB paired with a pure TypeScript BM25 search implementation. Relevance scoring runs standard Robertson-Spärck Jones IDF directly on the client using tuned parameters (k1 = 1.2 and b = 0.75), allowing the agent to retrieve user preferences and historical actions in sub-millisecond lookups completely offline. Fourth, a dynamic SubAgents SDK and multi-domain business intelligence. Injecting dozens of tool schemas into every prompt quickly blew through token budgets. We created an SDK that dynamically filters tools per domain, allowing the main agent to delegate tasks to specialized workers (such as analytics or 3D specialists). These workers run isolated multi-turn loops, compute normalized anomaly risk scores across metrics, and return concise execution receipts signed with a client-side SHA-256 hash. We tackled several technical hurdles along the way. Calling Three.js mutations straight out of asynchronous HTTP promises caused frame drops, so we created a queue in SceneActionBus that holds incoming tool commands and executes them strictly on animation frame ticks. Exposing every tool simultaneously caused models to hallucinate arguments or hit context caps; scoping tools dynamically by route and delegating to subagents cut token usage by roughly 85%. Additionally, server-side rendering under Node and Bun crashed whenever code referenced browser globals like window, navigator, or IndexedDB. We resolved this by building an in-memory emulator (WebMcpEmulator) that activates during SSR and in browsers lacking native WebMCP support, eliminating hydration mismatches. Through this process, we achieved 511 unit and integration tests passing on Bun in under 1.5 seconds. The project demonstrated that agent autonomy does not require a heavy backend or remote vector database; native browser primitives like IndexedDB, WebGL, and Signals are remarkably capable when wired directly to function calling. Furthermore, Angular's dependency injection model fits WebMCP tool registration naturally by treating tools as standard injectable providers. Moving forward, our next steps include publishing the webmcp-angular library as an open-source npm package, adding WebXR support to let agents interact with 3D scenes in headsets like Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest, and compiling OpenCASCADE geometry routines to WebAssembly for true solid modeling directly in the browser. title: Jipsa
pitch: A real local cake marketplace where people shop visually and AI agents compare, configure, quote, and prepare the same order through WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A real local cake marketplace where people shop visually and AI agents compare, configure, quote, and prepare the same order through WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Jipsa Inspiration Custom cake shopping is surprisingly difficult. Price changes with size, filling, lettering, and extras. Pickup inventory differs by maker, and every local shop supports a different set of options. People usually open many pages and manually reconcile those constraints. We built Jipsa to show what becomes possible when a polished human storefront and an AI agent share the same commerce state. What it does Jipsa is a real visual marketplace for 20 independent cake makers. Shoppers can browse stores, inspect current availability and policies, personalize a cake, receive an itemized quote, and review the exact order before confirmation. Through WebMCP, an agent can perform the same workflow with ten focused tools: search_local_stores , get_store_details , search_products , get_product_options , check_availability , configure_product , get_quote , prepare_order , place_order , and get_order_status . A single natural-language request can check all 20 makers against distance, exact configured price, servings, ingredients, supported cream colors, lettering, and pickup inventory. Jipsa returns three ranked candidates and exposes criterion-level rejection counts so the recommendation is inspectable. Why WebMCP This use case is full of structured but inconsistent constraints. Traditional visual automation has to repeatedly navigate cards, menus, forms, and calendars. WebMCP exposes those capabilities directly while preserving the same interface for the person. The result is not a detached chatbot or a single opaque automation endpoint. The agent composes purpose-built tools across search, comparison, availability, configuration, quoting, confirmation, ordering, and status. Every mutation remains visible to the shopper. If the agent changes lavender cream to light pink, the product photography and selected option update immediately while the lettering, flavor, filling, size, and pickup time remain intact. How we built it Jipsa is a React and TypeScript app using the WebMCP imperative API. src/webmcp.ts registers the ten English-language tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() , with JSON Schema inputs, focused descriptions, annotations, validation, structured output, and recoverable errors. src/marketplace.ts is the shared domain layer used by both the UI and WebMCP callbacks. It owns catalog search, ranking, pickup availability, partial configuration updates, exact pricing, confirmation tokens, local prototype persistence, and the developer audit trail. src/data.ts provides 20 distinct sample makers. Search price, quote, final review, and the persisted prototype order all use the same pricing engine. prepare_order only creates a short-lived confirmation token and opens human review. place_order requires that exact token plus confirmed: true . The production build is deployed on ChatGPT Sites with the headers required for WebMCP discovery. The app also includes a clearly labeled preview drawer for browsers where WebMCP is unavailable, without pretending that the protocol is connected. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was keeping search ranking, visual state, and order safety consistent. A candidate price is only useful if it reflects the same configuration used at checkout. We solved that by centralizing validation and pricing instead of duplicating estimates in the UI and tool handlers. We also designed partial updates so a follow-up request changes only the named field rather than resetting the order. Accomplishments that we're proud of A compound request evaluates 20 makers and explains both matches and rejections. Ten small, composable WebMCP tools cover the complete workflow. Human and agent actions update one shared, visible order state. Exact configured pricing remains consistent from search through confirmation. Ordering is confirmation-gated and produces no external payment or real-world order. The deployed app, public repository, automated tests, and a sub-three-minute narrated demo are ready for judges. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when tools are narrow, descriptive, and composable. The human interface remains essential: it provides context, trust, and final control, while structured tools give agents reliability. The strongest experience comes from letting both sides take turns on the same task rather than creating separate human and agent products. What's next for Jipsa A production version would connect maker inventory, secure checkout, live pickup calendars, and verified merchant onboarding. The same pattern can extend beyond cakes to florists, tailors, caterers, and other local businesses whose products are highly configurable and time-sensitive.
