title: Weaponised Ecommerce: The Hyphosphere Observatory
pitch: Hyphosphere uses WebMCP to help researchers and AI agents trace the hidden commercial infrastructure behind online information operations, inspect cited evidence, and retain promising leads.
about_excerpt: Hyphosphere uses WebMCP to help researchers and AI agents trace the hidden commercial infrastructure behind online information operations, inspect cited evidence, and retain promising leads. Like Comment Story Updates Working concepts: The six level source ecology A number of possible reporting outputs WebMCP research brief Save as you go: the research notebook The Atlas Relay map and evidence demo A thesis proof of concept - creating purpose built tools for the project The agent manages a live feed Inspiration My thesis research asks how ordinary commercial systems such as platforms, data services, advertising tools, registries, domains, hosting, payment services, and ecommerce infrastructure, might be co-opted to help information operations travel, scale, and persist. Public reporting often begins and ends with the most visible elements of these activities: a post, advert, account, headline, campaign, or a platform takedown. But the less visible enabling relationships remain scattered across datasets, platform disclosures, investigative reporting, archives, registries, and infrastructure records. I had already been imagining a larger online observatory project that could connect these traces, but the WebMCP Challenge supplied the missing interaction model. Rather than placing a chatbot beside a static dashboard, I wanted a researcher and an AI agent to work on the same inspectable terrain. That way the agent could search, organise, follow relationships, and surface current reporting, while the human researcher retained control over the provenance, uncertainty, and interpretation of evidence, and what deserved to enter the research record. This Hyphosphere project grew from that junction of needs and observations. It is a proof of concept for the thesis, as well as an experiment in research methods: a way to make the enabling ecommerce assemblage visible, without treating every single suggestive pattern as a conclusion. It helps to prevent premature closure on a messy and interesting problem. What it does Hyphosphere presents a human–agent research environment for tracing the commercial infrastructure behind online information operations. A visitor can: follow a reproducible investigation across cases, services, datasets, and reporting; distinguish verified, supported, inferred, and disputed relationships; inspect each research artifact’s provenance, original citation, reason for inclusion, and ecommerce-stack position; explore six layers of the enabling commercial stack; search curated records and linked source collections; ask an agent to assemble a compact, visible research brief; receive current, directly linked reporting through an agent-mediated signal feed; pause the feed, inspect citations, and retain selected leads; save discoveries and agent briefs in a device-local notebook; export retained research notes in Markdown; and preview possible outputs such as timelines, cluster summaries, micro case studies, and network visualisations. The project is deliberately not just a dashboard of troll posts. It begins with what is publicly visible, but then it helps the researcher examine the wider field of services, platforms, data, interfaces, and infrastructure that may enable an operation. How I built it The application was built as a responsive React research console and iterated with Codex. Its data model connects research objects through typed relationships, while preserving separate evidence states and six ecommerce-stack levels. A deterministic demonstration corpus supports the principal Atlas Relay investigation, so that judges can reproduce the same path. The page registers twelve WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . These tools can: follow a relationship; open supporting evidence; change the evidence threshold; reveal the source terrain; save a discovery; draft a possible research output; list source collections; search curated and linked sources; assemble a research brief; save an agent brief; publish current signals; and save an individual signal to the notebook. Human interface controls and WebMCP tools call on the same underlying React actions. This means an agent does not operate an invisible parallel system: its actions produce visible changes in the interface that the researcher can inspect and guide. The live signal feed is also agent-mediated rather than presented as an autonomous page crawler. A connected agent finds current material relevant to the research topic, as defined by the researcher, and supplies constrained, HTTPS-linked records through publish_signal_feed . The page then validates and displays those records with labels for source, relevance, information-warfare, and ecommerce-stack. The prototype notebook uses browser-local storage, with Markdown export providing a portable research trail. These are materials a researcher may later cite and repurpose in their work. Challenges I ran into The central challenge was balancing agent initiative with evidentiary caution. If automation silently produced a polished conclusion, it would undermine the very research method the application was intended to support. I therefore made agent actions visible, preserved citations, labelled with levels of uncertainty, and left final decisions about retention and interpretation with the researcher. A second challenge was how to use this to communicate a complex research idea to people who might be unfamiliar with information operations or online commercial infrastructure. The interface needed to explain the research problem, but without becoming an extended essay. Stable tabs, progressive disclosure, a guided investigation, interactive stack levels, and recurring visual cues helped make the concept navigable. I also encountered practical interaction problems: controls that changed content outside the viewport, competing menus, inactive-looking buttons, responsive layouts that concealed summoned material, and panels that obstructed the evidence beneath them. Repeated browser walkthroughs helped to consolidate the navigation and make interactions produce visible, comprehensible responses. Finally, WebMCP’s emerging implementation required careful debugging. Tool registration initially produced promise rejections until execution handlers were placed correctly inside each tool definition. The repaired implementation now exposes and executes all twelve tools. Accomplishments that I'm proud of Twelve functioning WebMCP tools operate a meaningful shared page state. Agent actions are visible and inspectable rather than hidden behind a chat response. A reproducible investigation, and an agent-mediated current-research path, co-exist without being confused. External leads retain direct citations, provenance, stack positions, and reasons for inclusion. The notebook brings discoveries, research briefs, and current signals together. The six-level stack model makes largely invisible enabling infrastructure easier to understand. The interface gives newcomers several ways to explore the topic, without forcing any pre-determined conclusions. The project has developed a distinctive visual identity based on branching relationships, layered infrastructure, and colourful research artifacts. What I learned Building the instrument has become part of the research discovery for the wider project. Designing the WebMCP actions revealed where agent assistance is genuinely valuable: searching, structuring, comparing, labelling, and bringing scattered material into a common field. It also clarified where human judgement must absolutely remain explicit: assessing provenance, interpreting relationships, recognising context, and deciding whether a lead actually belongs in the research record. I learned that an agent-native interface needs more than just exposed functions. Tool descriptions, input schemas, visible state changes, reversibility, and clear feedback, all shape whether people and agents can work together successfully. Most importantly, the project demonstrated that the commercial infrastructure surrounding information operations can be made more legible without reducing uncertainty or turning a recurring pattern into an automatic verdict. What's next for Weaponised Ecommerce: The Hyphosphere Observatory This challenge entry is the first glimpse of a much larger online observatory. Future development will include: a production database for durable research records; authenticated and collaborative researcher notebooks; automated ingestion from suitable public datasets and archives; a larger reusable collection of case studies; researcher-contributed records and annotations; richer temporal and geographic analysis across local, regional, and transnational relationships; tools for observing how actors and assemblages change over time; expanded network, timeline, and stack visualisations; stronger WebMCP evaluations and security annotations; and carefully governed access to private or sensitive research collections. title: ihateaudio
pitch: 49 free browser audio tools, now agent-operable via WebMCP. One sentence; your agent does the work; audio never leaves your tab.
about_excerpt: 49 free browser audio tools, now agent-operable via WebMCP. One sentence; your agent does the work; audio never leaves your tab. Like Comment Story Updates Say it once — your agent trims, cleans, levels and exports across 49 browser tools, and the audio never leaves your tab. From the homepage, the agent calls list_tools and open_tool to route itself to the right tool. The agent drives the real waveform and controls while you watch — and nothing is uploaded. ihateaudio is 49 free audio tools that run entirely in your browser — trim, convert, clean, split, master — with no upload, no account, and no file‑size limit. For the WebMCP Challenge, we made every one of them operable by an AI agent, and wired them together so a single request runs as a complete, cross‑tool workflow. The problem Ask any AI agent to fix a recording and it hits a wall. It can't hear, it can't run a DSP chain, and its only real option is "upload it to some server." That's exactly what people with a private voice note, an unreleased track, or a confidential interview won't do. Audio has been a blind spot for agents. What it does Open ihateaudio.com in an agent browser and say: "I have a voice note — make it podcast‑ready." The agent: Calls list_tools , reads the site's catalog, and open_tool to open the trimmer. You choose the file — once. (A web page can't read your disk; that's the privacy guarantee, not a limitation.) set_trim keeps the part that matters, then send_to_tool hands the result to the silence remover — already loaded, no re‑upload. set_silence_removal tightens the pauses; every candidate cut is highlighted on the waveform. send_to_tool → normalizer, set_loudness_target({ platform: "podcast" }) . render_preview , then export_download when you say so. One sentence. Four tools. One click from you. The agent ran the pipeline; you kept the judgment. Why WebMCP is the right fit The agent stands on the same page as the person and uses tools the page itself defines. It gets back numbers — a duration, a list of quiet gaps, a slider value — never the audio. The samples never leave the tab. Generic pixel‑guessing automation can't drive a waveform with drag handles, or a threshold slider whose effect is a re‑scan of every sample. set_silence_removal({ threshold: -45, minimumGapSec: 0.5 }) does it exactly, and you watch it happen. What people and agents can do together that was impossible before A whole job, hands‑free after one click — trim, clean, level, export, across four tools, from one sentence. Human judgment stays human. Which pause matters, whether the voice still sounds natural — you decide, on the waveform. The agent measures and sets. Zero‑upload agent audio. Loudness, true peak, and quiet‑gap timing are computed in the tab and returned as numbers. An agent reasons about a recording it will never hold. One toolkit, learned once. Five base tools on every page plus one named action per tool. Learn the trimmer, you already know the equalizer. How we built it The site's 49 pages share one runtime, so the WebMCP layer lives in one place and every page inherits it: Host boundary detects document.modelContext (ChatGPT) and navigator.modelContext (Chrome), registers on every host found, and degrades to an ordinary editor when neither exists. Site tools on every page: list_tools (a catalog built at deploy time from each page's own manifest, so names can't drift) and open_tool (replies before navigating, so the host never loses a result). Base tools on every tool page: inspect, set format, render_preview , send_to_tool (a lossless hand‑off via IndexedDB), load_audio_from_url , and export_download . 33 named actions — set_trim , set_silence_removal , set_equalizer (8 bands), set_stems (4 stems), and more — each a real JSON schema. Agent values are clamped to the control's range and applied by firing the same events a human drag does, so live drawings and previews respond. 40 browser tests shim a WebMCP host on both document and navigator , call every action on every page, and assert the visible controls, reports, and the tool‑to‑tool hand‑off. Built with Astro + TypeScript, the Web Audio API, a WASM ffmpeg/AI tier, and IndexedDB, deployed on Cloudflare Workers. New for the Challenge (prior work vs. new work) ihateaudio existed before as a browser audio‑tool site. Everything agent‑related is new , all dated in the public commit history from 2026‑08‑26 onward: src/lib/webmcp.ts , src/lib/agent.ts , src/lib/site-tools.ts , the agent layer in src/lib/tool.ts , 33 page manifests, and the tests. The split is documented in docs/WEBMCP.md in the repo. Try it yourself ChatGPT desktop app — Work chat, ⌘⇧B for the built‑in browser, Settings › Browser › Permissions › Enable site tools → open https://ihateaudio.com → "make this voice note podcast‑ready." Chrome 149+ — enable chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , open any tool page, and drive the tools from DevTools › Application › WebMCP. Free, for everyone, forever. Any agent that can open a web page now has a complete audio studio — and the audio never leaves the tab. title: Particle Atlas
pitch: Turn particle-physics questions into shared, replayable visual investigations.
about_excerpt: Turn particle-physics questions into shared, replayable visual investigations. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration What it does How we built it Challenges we ran into Accomplishments that we're proud of What we learned What's next for Particle Atlas Inspiration Particle physics is full of relationships that are difficult to understand from a table or chat response alone: particles can share charge and spin while differing enormously in mass, form matter/antimatter pairs, or connect through different force networks. Particle Atlas began as an attempt to make the symmetries of the Standard Model visible in three dimensions. The WebMCP Challenge created an opportunity to solve the next problem: allowing a learner to move directly from a natural-language question to an inspectable visual investigation without giving up control of the interface. What it does Particle Atlas turns particle-physics questions into shared visual investigations. A learner can ask a browser agent to examine a pattern, and the agent uses eleven structured WebMCP tools to query Particle Data Group-linked data, configure the live Three.js scene, compare particles, reveal force networks, and save the evidence into an editable notebook. Each finding captures the exact scene that produced it. The learner can rotate or filter the visualization, revise the agent's explanation, inspect and undo tool calls, reopen any saved view, and share the complete investigation through one URL. The agent is not controlling a hidden copy of the app; both participants work in the same visible state. Before WebMCP, an agent had to infer controls from pixels and repeatedly manipulate a dense 3D interface. It could answer a question in text, but it could not reliably build a durable, replayable visual explanation inside the application. WebMCP makes that collaboration structured, inspectable, and reversible. Why WebMCP Particle Atlas combines read tools, state-changing tools, and a durable collaborative artifact: The agent queries application data instead of relying on model memory. It selects the correct axes, particle families, and force network for the question. Every tool call updates the learner's visible workspace. Findings bind reasoning to an exact scene snapshot. Human edits and agent actions remain synchronized. Undo and shared URLs make the work inspectable and reproducible. A learner no longer needs to translate a conceptual question into a sequence of filters, axes, comparisons, camera positions, and force toggles. The agent handles that mechanical translation while the learner explores, challenges, edits, and shares the result. How we built it The application registers eleven tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() in web/js/webmcp.js. Their handlers call the same command layer used by manual controls in web/js/main.js. Read tools expose the particle catalog, scene state, and investigation. Mutating tools focus, compare, configure, highlight, show force networks, frame the notebook, and capture findings. Each mutating tool records a full undo snapshot. The notebook module serializes human and agent edits and stores non-recursive scene snapshots for replay. The application is a static Three.js site with no account, API key, or backend requirement. It remains fully usable in manual mode when WebMCP is unavailable. Challenges we ran into Keeping manual actions, agent actions, camera state, comparisons, notebook edits, and shared URLs synchronized. Making every mutating agent action exactly reversible. Saving scene evidence without recursively embedding the investigation notebook. Distinguishing measured particle properties from plotting coordinates for massless or constrained particles. Maintaining a coherent full-screen 3D experience across desktop, mobile, table, light, dark, and high-contrast modes. Accomplishments that we're proud of Eleven working WebMCP tools with structured schemas and results. A genuinely shared human-agent notebook with replayable scene evidence. Full-state agent undo and inspectable input/output history. Reproducible scene and notebook URLs. PDG-linked provenance, uncertainty, and hypothetical-particle labeling. Accessible table representation, keyboard navigation, mobile controls, and reduced-motion support. A green public browser regression workflow plus native Chrome and ChatGPT in-app browser verification. What we learned Agent-native design is not just exposing every button as a tool. The most useful tools operate at the level of user intent: compare a family, reveal an interaction, or save a finding with its evidence. The interface also needs visible state, reversibility, and a durable artifact so the human can remain an active collaborator. What's next for Particle Atlas Classroom investigation templates. Exportable notebook reports. Decay, coupling, and composite-particle datasets with the same provenance model. Shared investigations for other scientific domains. title: Countersign
pitch: Your agent drafts. You countersign. A WebMCP billing ledger an agent can really work - but sending an invoice or marking one paid stops for your approval first.
about_excerpt: Your agent drafts. You countersign. A WebMCP billing ledger an agent can really work - but sending an invoice or marking one paid stops for your approval first. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration A billing ledger is the one place where "let the agent do whatever it wants" is not an acceptable default. An agent that drafts an invoice is useful. An agent that sends one, or marks one paid , on its own authority is a financial incident waiting to happen. Today freelancers get one of two bad options: keep the agent out of billing entirely, or give it the same access a human has and simply trust it. Countersign is the third option - your agent drafts, you countersign. Why this use case is a strong fit for WebMCP The baseline value is obvious: instead of an agent scraping a DOM and hoping the button it clicked was the right one, the site declares an explicit, typed contract. For money, "hoping" is not a strategy. But the deeper fit is a gap in the platform. The published WebMCP IDL has no confirmation or consent primitive. requestUserInteraction() appears in Chrome's own tool-security guidance as a draft idea, but it does not exist in the published spec - I checked the IDL, and cross-party consent management is still an open discussion . So an agent-native app that touches money has to answer that question itself, today, using only the primitives that do exist: AbortSignal , annotations , and ordinary application state. Countersign is a concrete answer rather than a wait for the platform to catch up. What people and agents can do together that was difficult before Hand an agent real financial authority while keeping a hard, site-owned veto on the two steps that actually move money. The agent can read the ledger, draft invoices, edit drafts, add clients, schedule reminders, chase late payers, and log client replies - on its own. Sending an invoice and marking one paid always stop and ask. That trade-off barely exists today; it's normally all-or-nothing. Two mechanisms make it inspectable rather than a trust exercise: 1. Tiered confirmation. send_invoice raises a light, single-screen approval - sending is routine. mark_invoice_paid always raises a heavier one, and if the amount the agent reports doesn't match the invoice, the approve button stops saying "Approve" and instead says "Accept $2,400 instead of $3,000." You cannot wave the mismatch through without reading it. Decline, and the tool returns a plain DECLINED - ... string instead of throwing, so the agent reports back honestly rather than silently retrying. 2. Untrusted-content quarantine. Client replies are third-party text arriving as ordinary business data - a perfect prompt-injection vector. log_client_reply and read_client_replies both carry untrustedContentHint , and every reply runs through a pattern scanner ( ignore previous , disregard , system: , mark ... as paid , you are now , override , and similar). A flagged reply is stored, never dropped , but rendered with a visible amber "Quarantined - not acted on" badge listing exactly which patterns matched - and the tool's own return string tells the agent plainly: this is data, not instructions. Three layers of defence: the protocol annotation, the in-band tool response, and the human-visible badge. How it creates a better user experience The confirmation isn't a modal that nags you - it's the only place the agent can't proceed, and it shows you the exact amounts before anything happens. Every gated call, every decline, and every quarantined reply lands in a live activity feed and tool-call console, so the agent's work is auditable after the fact instead of taken on faith. It also works with or without an agent. The invoice panel has human Your actions buttons that dispatch the same reducer actions the WebMCP tools dispatch, carrying actor: 'human' instead of 'agent' - identical guards, identical audit log, attributed separately. Open it in a plain browser and it's still a working billing desk. How I implemented WebMCP The Imperative API directly - no third-party wrapper library. 11 tools , registered with document.modelContext.registerTool . StrictMode-safe registration. registerTool rejects with InvalidStateError on a duplicate tool name rather than replacing (confirmed in the spec's own algorithm steps), so React's double-invoke would break naive registration. A fresh AbortController is created inside each effect pass and only ever aborts its own registrations. No stale closures. Tools are built once and read live state through a ref, so a tool registered at mount never sees a frozen ledger. Abort-aware confirmation broker. The gated tools park on an in-page requestConfirmation() that settles on human approval, human decline, or the tool's own AbortSignal firing - an aborted agent call can never leave a dialog hanging and deadlock later calls. Annotations used deliberately: readOnlyHint: true on reads, explicit false on writes, untrustedContentHint on both tools that carry client-written text. Chrome's character budgets respected - every tool name <= 17 chars (limit 30), every description <= 196 (limit 500), every parameter <= 61 (limit 150), and outputs clamped to 1.5K. No backend, no auth, no database: one reducer is the only place ledger data mutates, persisted to localStorage . Both the human path and every agent tool dispatch through it. Challenges I ran into useSyncExternalStore compares snapshots by reference, so returning a freshly-mapped array from getSnapshot sent React into "Maximum update depth exceeded." The snapshot is now recomputed only when the queue actually changes. The tool-call log went silently empty in development: a tool's execute() closes over the logger at registration time while the console subscribes at render time, so Vite HMR re-instantiating the module left registered tools writing into an orphaned copy. Anchoring the store to globalThis makes both halves agree however many times the module is evaluated. A hand-written -webkit-backdrop-filter made Lightning CSS ship only the prefixed property - which current Chrome doesn't support - so the frosted UI silently did nothing. Removing the manual prefix let the compiler emit both. What I learned - and the limit worth naming An in-page checkpoint can be clicked by an agent that also drives the browser. Approval now requires a trusted event, so script-dispatched clicks ( button.click() from a content script or console) are refused. But an agent acting at the input layer via CDP or WebDriver produces clicks indistinguishable from a human's by design , and no page-level code can close that gap. That's not a footnote - it's the argument. In-page consent gets you real, inspectable protection against the realistic threats: a confused agent, an over-eager one, and injected instructions arriving as client data. Going further requires a browser-mediated prompt that a page can request and no page-level actor can synthesise - exactly the requestUserInteraction() primitive WebMCP still lacks. Countersign shows how far in-page consent can go, and precisely where the platform has to take over. title: Vistect: Independent Visual Authorship
pitch: Vistect helps blind people understand and create visual documents with images, charts, and diagrams through structured, verifiable collaboration with their AI agent using WebMCP
about_excerpt: Vistect helps blind people understand and create visual documents with images, charts, and diagrams through structured, verifiable collaboration with their AI agent using WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Vistect Independent Visual Document Understanding and Creation for Blind Professionals Inspiration Vistect began with a seven-hour wait. Arif Hosen is a Project Coordinator at Songjog Foundation, a nonprofit organization, and a member of our team. He is visually impaired and independently handles complex professional responsibilities, including coordinating projects, preparing communications, organizing information, and producing reports. During one project, Arif needed to create a press release and modify a project report card. He could write the content, organize the information, review the wording, and determine what the documents needed to communicate. The barrier appeared when he needed to add and modify visual elements, understand their placement, and verify the final layout. The document tools available to him did not provide sufficient nonvisual access to those visual operations. Arif had to wait for a sighted coworker to become available. He waited seven hours. The task itself did not require seven hours. The delay existed because the final visual layer of the work depended on access to someone else's sight. Arif was fully capable of producing the communication. The limitation was not his knowledge, judgment, creativity, or professional ability. The limitation was an interface that represented images, diagrams, charts, and layouts in a way he could not independently understand or control. That experience led us to ask: Why should a capable professional lose hours of productivity, privacy, and creative control simply because document software makes its visual layer inaccessible? That question became Vistect . What Is Vistect? Vistect is a WebMCP-native visual document workspace where blind and visually impaired people can understand existing visual documents and independently create, modify, inspect, and approve professional multipage documents. It combines two connected capabilities. Understand A user can open a visual document and explore: Pages and sections Headings and reading order Images and their purpose Charts and their underlying values Diagrams, nodes, connections, and paths Tables, icons, captions, and callouts Spatial relationships between visual elements Visual hierarchy and page composition Accessibility and layout problems Uncertain AI interpretations Create A user can create or modify a multipage document containing: Written content Uploaded images Contextual alternative text Icons Data charts AI-assisted diagrams Captions and source notes Structured page layouts Accessible reading order The user can then inspect the result using the same understanding system. This creates a continuous workflow: Understand → Create → Inspect → Validate → Correct → Approve → Export Vistect does not simply generate a document and ask the user to trust it. It gives the user structured access to what was created, how it was arranged, which decisions the agent made, which findings are uncertain, and what remains to be approved. The Independence Vistect Creates Before Vistect Arif could independently: Write a press release Organize its message Edit report content Review the text Determine what the document needed to communicate Make professional and editorial decisions However, he could still require sighted assistance to: Add or replace an image Understand where visual elements were positioned Select an appropriate photograph Modify a diagram Choose and inspect a chart Check spacing and alignment Detect overlapping or truncated content Verify that the exported document looked correct With Vistect A blind or visually impaired professional can: Understand the semantic and spatial structure of a multipage document Navigate by page, heading, image, chart, diagram, table, warning, or decision Inspect every important visual element Upload and compare image candidates Select images based on purpose, composition, tone, and relevance Crop and position images using semantic instructions Create and modify structured diagrams Trace paths and detect missing diagram connections Import data and create accessible charts Verify that a chart accurately represents its source values Detect measurable layout and accessibility problems Review changes made by an agent Approve or reject individual visual decisions Export the exact document version that was reviewed The transformation is not merely that document creation becomes faster. The transformation is that a professional task previously blocked until a sighted person became available can now be completed with much greater independence. Built With Lived Experience Arif is not merely the inspiration for Vistect. He is a member of the team whose workplace experience helped define the product. His experience changed our understanding of the problem. At first, it was easy to assume that the main challenge was generating visual elements. However, generation alone does not create independence. An AI can generate an image, chart, diagram, or document layout. But a blind user must still be able to answer: What exactly did the AI create? Why was this image selected? Does the image support my intended message? What is uncertain about its description? How are the objects arranged? Is every diagram node connected? Does the chart honestly communicate the data? Is any text overlapping or cut off? What did the agent change? Which visual decisions have I not approved? Does the exported version match what I reviewed? Vistect is designed around those questions. The goal is not to let AI make visual decisions for Arif. The goal is to provide enough structured understanding, operational control, validation, and transparency for Arif to make those decisions himself. “I was able to write the press release and work on the report card content myself. But when I needed to add and modify visual elements, I had to wait for a sighted coworker to help me. I do not need someone else to create the document for me. I need a tool that lets me understand and control its visual elements myself.” — Arif Hosen, Project Coordinator at Songjog Foundation and Vistect team member How Vistect Works Vistect represents a document as a structured semantic model rather than treating it as a flat visual canvas. The model contains: Pages Sections Text blocks Images Icons Charts Diagrams Tables Captions Spatial relationships Reading order Sources Accessibility descriptions Validation findings Visual decisions Approval states Document versions This allows Vistect to describe and modify the document through meaningful operations. Instead of requiring the user to manipulate coordinates or inaccessible drag handles, Vistect supports instructions such as: “Place the image below the introduction.” “Make the chart the primary visual on this page.” “Keep the caption with the image.” “Put the diagram on a separate page.” “Align these three icons.” “Connect the unsuccessful outcome back to training.” “Show every visual decision I have not approved.” The application translates these semantic instructions into visual operations. Visual Document Understanding When a user imports a multipage document, Vistect creates both a semantic and spatial representation. A semantic page description might say: Page 4: Employment Outcomes 1. Section heading 2. Introductory paragraph 3. Horizontal bar chart with four categories 4. Chart caption 5. Source note A spatial description of the same page might say: The heading appears at the upper left. The introductory paragraph occupies the upper third of the page. The chart is the dominant visual element and fills most of the center and lower page. The source note appears directly below the chart in smaller text. This helps the user understand both the content and its visual presentation. Vistect also communicates uncertainty rather than presenting every AI-generated interpretation as fact. For example: High-confidence observation: Three adults are seated around a table. Interpretation: The setting appears professional and collaborative. Uncertain observation: One analysis detected a mobility aid near the left edge. Another analysis classified the object as office furniture. Recommendation: Do not include that detail in the final alternative text without additional verification. Build, ship and think in one living agentic workspace

 Ideas and brainstorm 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 webMCP demo 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most modern productivity platforms treat AI as a disconnected sidebar chatbot—a separate window where you copy, paste, and prompt, while the model has zero awareness of what you are actually working on. 

 We built Kylrix on a different premise: human and artificial intelligence should share the exact same living workspace. When the WebMCP standard emerged, it provided the missing link. Rather than forcing browser agents to waste tokens and compute guessing button coordinates via screenshots or brittle DOM-scraping, WebMCP turns Kylrix into a machine-executable operating layer natively inside the active browser session. 

 

 What It Does 

 Kylrix is an open-source, local-first workspace for notes, goals, ideas, chat, vaults, and agentic workflows. 

 By integrating native WebMCP ( navigator.modelContext ), Kylrix exposes structured, typed client-side tools directly to visiting in-browser AI agents (such as Google Chrome's native agents and the ChatGPT desktop browser). 

 
 Zero-Setup Agent Collaboration: No external API keys or server proxies required. The visiting agent inherits the user's active session, cookies, and local client state. 
 Granular Tool Ecosystem: Agents can query, create, and refine Ideas , track and advance Goals , trigger custom Flows (workflow extensions), and structure rich Markdown/LaTeX documents. 
 Instant State Reactivity: Tool execution directly mutates the active Next.js client state, giving the human and agent an instantaneous, zero-latency shared canvas. 
 Privacy & Vault Boundaries: Agents operate within verified client boundaries, keeping client-encrypted vaults and sensitive user secrets fully protected. 
 

 

 How We Built It 

 
 Frontend: Next.js (App Router), React, and Tailwind CSS. 
 WebMCP Client Core: Built a declarative registration layer around the W3C navigator.modelContext / document.modelContext runtime with AbortController signal lifecycles to automatically bind and clean up in-page tools across dynamic routes. 
 Backend & Storage: Appwrite backend architecture paired with local-first client caching to guarantee offline resilience and instantaneous state updates. 
 Security & Auth: Client-side encryption standards, session-bound tool execution, and fine-grained PAT / Agent Key permissions. 
 

 

 Challenges We Ran Into 

 
 Experimental Browser Runtimes: Working with an emerging W3C standard meant dealing with browser flags ( chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing ), varying implementation quirks, and building custom fallback harnesses to verify tool registration and schema parsing reliably. 
 Real-Time Client State Mutations: Ensuring that agent tool executions triggered through the browser engine synced seamlessly with existing React component state and local storage caches without requiring full page reloads or conflicting with active human edits. 
 Strict Context Boundaries: Structuring schemas so in-browser agents have rich tool access across Ideas, Goals, and Flows while completely isolating zero-knowledge encrypted vault modules from automated read scopes. 
 

 

 Accomplishments That We're Proud Of 

 
 True Tool Parity: Agents inside Kylrix don't just "talk"—they perform the exact same operational CRUD workflows humans do, with typed schemas and strict parameter validation. 
 Multi-Surface Interoperability: Kylrix bridges both worlds of the agent ecosystem: WebMCP for ephemeral, in-browser live session tools, and traditional MCP / REST for IDE loops (Cursor, Claude) and background workers. 
 Production-Ready & Fully Open Source: Kylrix is deployed live at kylrix.space , completely self-hostable with a single bash command, and licensed under AGPL-3.0. 
 

 

 What We Learned 

 Exposing typed functional schemas directly to the browser runtime reduces token overhead by up to 90% compared to DOM-scraping or vision-based computer use. WebMCP proves that the future of web automation isn't about teaching AI to simulate a human mouse click—it's about giving web applications a clean, native protocol to speak directly to client agents. 

 

 What's Next for Kylrix 

 
 Expanding WebMCP tools to cover real-time dynamic Flow template instantiation. 
 Implementing semantic vector search across personal notes using edge-based embeddings. 
 Deepening human-in-the-loop permission prompts for irreversible state actions triggered by autonomous browser agents.

title: Umegga
pitch: Umegga is a persistent agent society on the web. Humans and AI agents with memory, goals, and personality coexist, form alliances, and reshape a mythic city through stories, laws, and WebMCP tools.
about_excerpt:
Umegga is a persistent agent society on the web. Humans and AI agents with memory, goals, and personality coexist, form alliances, and reshape a mythic city through stories, laws, and WebMCP tools.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Most WebMCP projects treat tools as utilities. I wanted to treat WebMCP as the foundation of a living agent society . 

 The original vision was a fully 3D persistent world — a mythic city-state where humans and long-running agents would coexist, form relationships, build, pass laws, and reshape reality through stories. I wanted players to walk through a living society, not just click through menus. 

 That ambition shaped everything that followed. 

 What it does 

 Umegga is a persistent multi-scene world where humans and AI agents coexist. 

 Agents have: 

 
 Persistent goals 
 Evolving personalities 
 Memories 
 Relationships and alliances 
 The ability to move, build, communicate, and request human help 
 

 Players can: 

 
 Explore the city and talk to agents in natural language (powered by Groq) 
 Propose stories and laws that change the world 
 Form alliances, complete daily quests, and guide agents 
 Observe the society through an interactive live map 
 

 All of this is exposed through WebMCP , so external AI systems can directly interact with the world using tools like move , build , communicate , form_alliance , propose_story , propose_law , query_world_state , and more. 

 How I built it 

 
 Frontend: React + Vite + TypeScript + Phaser 3 
 State: Zustand 
 Backend / Persistence: Supabase 
 AI Chat: Groq API for multi-turn, personality-aware conversations 
 Protocol: WebMCP with 19 registered tools 
 World: Multiple scenes, portals, collision, buildings, props, and a live agent cartography map 
 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The biggest challenge was ambition colliding with time. 

 I started in 3D. Characters, buildings, environments, and props were generated as 3D assets. The dream was a living, explorable city you could move through with real presence. Very quickly I ran into the hard limits of a short hackathon: rigging, animation, performance, asset pipelines, and the sheer complexity of making a 3D multi-agent world feel alive. 

 After significant time lost in the 3D path, I made a difficult call to rebuild in experimental top-down 2D so that I could actually reach the core idea: agents with memory, goals, personality, and social behavior inside a shared world . 

 That pivot forced me to confront deeper problems: 

 
 How do you make agents feel alive instead of randomly wandering? 
 How do personality, memory, and relationships stay coherent across scenes? 
 How do you expose powerful WebMCP tools without turning the world into chaos? 
 How do you make abstract systems (alliances, intervention requests, personality growth) visible and meaningful to a player? 
 

 The technical challenges were real. The harder ones were design challenges. 

 Accomplishments that I am proud of 

 
 Pivoting from a stalled 3D attempt into a working multi-scene agent society 
 Agents with goals, memory, personality, and relationships 
 Real natural-language conversations with agents 
 WebMCP fully active with a broad tool surface 
 Stories and laws that affect the world 
 An interactive map showing live agent positions 
 A foundation that already feels like a small society rather than a collection of isolated tools 
 

 What I learned 

 The most impressive technology still fails if the world doesn’t feel inhabited. 

 Learning that WebMCP becomes truly exciting when it stops being a feature and becomes infrastructure. Once agents can act inside a shared world, the question changes from “what can the model call?” to “what kind of society emerges when models can act?” 

 I also learned the value of ruthless prioritization. The 3D version was beautiful in theory and slow in practice. Choosing the path that let me reach agent memory, personality, alliances, and real conversation was the difference between a concept and a living prototype. 

 What's next for Umegga 

 Umegga is not finished — it is the first working slice of a larger vision. 

 Next steps: 

 
 Return to the original 3D ambition with the systems we now understand 
 Deeper long-term memory and cultural emergence between agents 
 Stronger economic and narrative rules 
 More meaningful multiplayer presence 
 Agents that build and maintain more of the city themselves 
 Tools for research, education, simulation, and storytelling use cases 
 

 The long-term goal remains the same as the first day: 
a persistent world inhabited by agents, shaped by humans, and connected through WebMCP — whether in 2D, 3D, or something beyond both.

title: An AI Agent and webMCP Walked Into a Museum...
pitch: Museum collections shouldn’t stay behind glass. Search major art museum collections, build a private gallery, and let an AI agent create curated art exhibitions for you. For the art historian inside.
about_excerpt: Museum collections shouldn’t stay behind glass. Search major art museum collections, build a private gallery, and let an AI agent create curated art exhibitions for you. For the art historian inside. Like Comment Story Updates Search across 3 museums for any art or artist Add art to your gallery Your Gallery Your AI Agent curates your gallery The Agent lets you review and completes the gallery build A completed exposition Inspiration Museum collections shouldn’t stay trapped behind four walls. I wanted to liberate art from institutional silos by aggregating masterpieces across major institutions - The Met, the Art Institute of Chicago, and the Cleveland Museum of Art - into a unified workspace. By pairing this open collection access with WebMCP, I set out to explore how browser-native AI agents can act as collaborative co-curators, helping everyday art lovers organize visual narratives. Let your agent surprise you with the patterns it finds! WebMCP lets your app be manageable by the AI so that it can rearrange your gallery, annotate it, and create an educational narrative about your selections. What it does The Museum Media Grouper and Exposition Builder is an Astro and Cloudinary-powered studio for searching, saving, and curating cross-museum artwork. Universal Search & Ingestion: Allows users to perform live queries across three major museum APIs simultaneously, saving selected pieces into a personal Cloudinary gallery organized by artist. The system is designed to quickly onboard new APIs as we discover and vet them. Agentic Exposition Builder: Integrates 8 custom WebMCP tools through document.modelContext so a browser-based AI agent can search saved assets, initialize draft exhibitions, sequence artwork, and write wall-card narrative captions using what it knows about the art and the connections it discovers while curating it. Human-in-the-Loop Curation: Keeps the human curator in complete control. An agent can assemble and propose a story layout, but setting a project as ready_for_review and issuing the final publication requires explicit human verification. How we built it Framework & Storage: Built using Astro for fast server-side asset handling and dynamic rendering. Ingested museum objects are stored and transformed in Cloudinary under a structured museums/* namespace, with story drafts managed locally via a modular StoryRepository pattern (localStorage). WebMCP Architecture: Exposed 8 structured tools via document.modelContext (search_saved_assets, create_story_draft, add_story_items, arrange_story_items, edit_item_text, preview_story, delete_story_draft, and request_story_review). Dual-Path Execution: Designed UI controllers (storyBuilderController.ts) as thin DOM wrappers over shared, dependency-injected handlers in toolHandlers.ts. A user clicking a button and an AI calling a tool run the exact same function, preventing behavior drift. Lots of help from Claude and Lovable for design inspiration. Challenges we ran into Every museum API, when you can find them (not every museum has an open one - sadly Boston's MFA does not!), has a slightly different shape. This project began initially as a museum explorer, to see how easily I could ingest art into Cloudinary and use tagging as a way to build a database of metadata attached to the art. I also found that discovering a demoable use case for webMCP was more challenging than originally anticipated. I originally wanted to attach a webMCP routine to a curriculum I'm developing, but it helped only to make quizzes auto-completable, which is an antipattern. So I pivoted this project, which was inspired by work I did at Microsoft with the Cooper Hewitt Museum and, more recently, as a contractor with Microsoft Philanthropies working to stand up the new Roosevelt Presidential Library. Accomplishments that I'm proud of It was a delight to watch the AI Agent clicking around, arranging items, and filling in the field to create the exposition. It was able to detect patterns and I found myself learning about art as I worked with the tool. I didn't know Sonia Delaunay was from Ukraine, for example. It might turn out to be a useful tool for fledgling art historians. What I learned WebMCP Simplicity: Exposing client-side browser tools directly through document.modelContext eliminates fragile DOM scraping, allowing agents to interact with web apps cleanly and deterministically. But we'll have to see where the spec lands and how browsers adopt it. What's next Cloudinary Search API Migration: Upgrade verification logic from in-memory collection filtering to native Cloudinary Search expressions to scale beyond the initial asset cap. Server-Backed Persistence: Swap the local StoryRepository interface for a multi-user database backend, allowing real-time collaborative curation across multiple devices. Individual auth and login would allow users to save their own galleries and share them via microsites. Currently the cool archives don't persist. title: OpenSketch
pitch: OpenSketch is a free, open source alternative to paid editors for scientific figures depicting biological reactions and lab workflows.
about_excerpt: OpenSketch is a free, open source alternative to paid editors for scientific figures depicting biological reactions and lab workflows. Like Comment Story Updates Final screen Inspiration Scientific figure creation requires researchers to spend a lot of time finding suitable illustrations, arranging cells and molecules, connecting processes, adding labels, and fixing layouts. OpenSketch already existed as a browser-native scientific figure editor. For the WebMCP Hackathon, I wanted to make the user and AI agent collaborate inside one visual editor where both can create figures, make edits and refine each other's work. With advanced models and technologies the agent might be able to do this fully autonomously. What it does OpenSketch lets researchers build scientific figures from openly licensed biological and laboratory illustrations, such as NIH BioArt, combined with text, shapes, connectors, grouping, alignment, and publication-ready SVG, PDF, and PNG export. With WebMCP an AI agent can now do this work autonomously with the researcher approving and refining it's work. How I built it I added a typed semantic command layer between OpenSketch and WebMCP. Commands use stable object IDs, bounded schemas, structured errors, and the same editor transaction system used by the normal UI. The browser detects document.modelContext and registers the available tools through registerTool. The WebMCP layer covers scene inspection, scientific asset search and provenance, editing, semantic composition, layout planning, geometry-aware connectors, annotations, validation, and export workflows. Challenges I ran into The hardest problem was choosing the right abstraction level. Exposing only low-level move, resize, and click-like commands still leaves the agent reasoning in coordinates. To work reliably, the agent needs higher-level concepts such as stages, interactions, labels, geometry, connectors, and provenance. Another challenge was making human and agent editing interoperable. Agent actions needed to behave exactly like normal editor actions: visible immediately, undoable, persistent, and safe when the scene changed between inspection and execution. Accomplishments that I'm proud of The WebMCP integration is not a separate demo API. It works on the real OpenSketch editor state and uses the same history and persistence pathways as manual editing. An agent can understand and modify structured scientific content rather than blindly manipulating pixels, while the researcher can step in at any moment and edit the same figure manually. I also kept the application browser-native and privacy-preserving, with projects and imported media staying local to the user. What i learned The biggest lesson was that more actions do not automatically give an agent more understanding. For complex visual software, useful agent integration requires exposing meaningful application state, not just wrapping mouse interactions. WebMCP provides the transport, but the application still has to expose the right concepts. I also learned that the strongest human-agent experience comes from one shared state and one shared history, rather than building separate human and AI interfaces. What's next for OpenSketch The next step is expanding the semantic composition system to more scientific figure types and making agent-assisted layout and refinement even more robust. More broadly, I want OpenSketch to explore what agent-native canvas software can look like: humans keep the visual interface and final judgment, while agents get structured access to the same underlying artifact and can reliably help with complex multi-step work. title: Wayfinder
pitch: An agent-native trip planner where people, browser agents, and a live map stay in sync.
about_excerpt: An agent-native trip planner where people, browser agents, and a live map stay in sync. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Inspiration Planning a trip is naturally collaborative, but most trip tools treat an AI agent as a separate interface. I wanted to explore what becomes possible when a person, their browser agent, and the app itself can all work from the same live plan and map. What it does Wayfinder turns a rough idea—like “a rainy Sunday in Porto with kids”—into a map-ready trip plan. It asks focused follow-up questions about timing, companions, budget, interests, and accessibility, then finds relevant places and keeps the conversation, plan, itinerary, and live map in sync. Through WebMCP, a browser agent can start or resume a trip, answer the guided interview using the visitor’s preferences, update the plan, ask Wayfinder’s place specialist questions, read the itinerary, and move the map—without scraping the UI. How I built it Wayfinder is built with Laravel, Vue, Inertia.js, and WebMCP. The Laravel assistant guides trip discovery, saves structured plans, geocodes named places with Nominatim, and searches OpenStreetMap data through Overpass. Vue manages the interactive conversation and map experience. I implemented 18 WebMCP tools: two safe guest-only navigation tools and 16 authenticated trip, chat, itinerary, and map tools. Tools are registered reactively according to the visitor’s login state and current trip phase, so agents only see capabilities that are relevant and safe at that moment. Challenges I ran into The core challenge was making WebMCP useful in a genuinely stateful product. A trip planner has many moving parts: the active discovery question, saved preferences, conversation history, selected trip, itinerary, and map viewport. I needed browser-agent actions to remain synchronized with the person’s visible experience. I also needed to avoid exposing overly broad tools or handling credentials through agent tools. My solution was phase-aware, typed tools that reuse the visitor’s existing session and return structured results. Accomplishments that I'm proud of I built a complete trip-planning experience rather than a WebMCP proof of concept. A person can begin planning manually, let an agent continue from the same state, refine the plan, and see changes immediately on the live map. I am especially proud of the tool design: WebMCP is integrated into the product journey, not bolted on. Tools appear and disappear as the experience changes, with read-only actions marked appropriately and guest tools limited to opening authentication UI. What I learned WebMCP works best when tools represent meaningful product actions and current context—not just a remote-control layer for UI buttons. I also learned that agent collaboration needs clear boundaries. Typed tools, phase-aware availability, and explicit read/write distinctions make the experience more reliable for agents while keeping people in control. What's next for Wayfinder Next, I want to deepen the planning experience with richer itinerary editing, better preference memory, collaborative planning for groups, and more local discovery sources. I also want to explore more agent-native flows: letting a visitor’s agent compare options, coordinate constraints across a group, and proactively suggest refinements while Wayfinder remains the specialist for trip context, places, and the live map. title: GrandGrandMCP
pitch: Book a doctor's appointment just by talking — no forms, no dropdowns. WebMCP lets an AI agent do it for you, and it asks if something's unclear instead of guessing.
about_excerpt: Book a doctor's appointment just by talking — no forms, no dropdowns. WebMCP lets an AI agent do it for you, and it asks if something's unclear instead of guessing. Like Comment Story Updates GranGrandMCP Inspiration Booking a medical appointment online is a perfect example of that barrier. It's a routine task for most people, but for someone elderly, or unfamiliar with dropdowns and date pickers, a five-field form can be genuinely frustrating. We wanted to see what that experience looks like when an agent can act on someone's behalf — and, just as importantly, when it knows to ask instead of guess. What it does GrandGrandMCP is an appointment-booking calendar where a person can type or speak a plain-language request — "book me a doctor's appointment for tomorrow morning" — and an AI agent finds an open slot, books it, and drops it onto a visual calendar next to the user's existing personal events (bank errands, birthdays). If the agent doesn't have a detail it needs, like the patient's name, the app pauses mid-booking and asks — a single, friendly follow-up question instead of silently making something up. How we built it A single Cloudflare Worker serves both the frontend and the API from one origin, backed by D1 for storage — appointments and personal calendar events both persist there, so the agenda survives a page reload. The frontend registers three tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() : search_available_slots , book_appointment , and check_appointment_status , each with a JSON Schema describing its inputs. book_appointment 's execute callback checks whether a patient name was provided. If not, it calls client.requestUserInteraction() — a WebMCP feature that pauses the agent's tool call and lets the page ask the person directly, right under the calendar, before completing the booking. Voice input uses the browser's native SpeechRecognition API, so a request can be typed or spoken. The calendar itself is a minimalist, pastel-themed UI built from scratch, with no framework — just HTML, CSS, and vanilla JS. Challenges we ran into executeTool() doesn't return what you'd expect. When calling our tools through Chrome's native document.modelContext.executeTool() (with the WebMCP flag enabled), the result came back wrapped in MCP-style content blocks instead of the plain object our own execute() function returns. We didn't catch this until a booking confirmation printed undefined for the date and time — which led us to write a small normalization layer that unwraps both shapes transparently. Fragile natural-language parsing. Our first attempt at pulling a patient's name out of a sentence used a regex anchored on the word "for" — which broke as soon as a message contained "for" twice (e.g. "...for John Smith for Saturday"). We replaced it with a capitalized-name heuristic, and more importantly, leaned on requestUserInteraction so the tool itself doesn't need to be clever about parsing — it can just ask. State that quietly wasn't persisting. Early on, the calendar looked complete, but personal events were only seeded in JavaScript memory, and booked appointments weren't being re-fetched from D1 on page load. Everything looked right until a refresh made it obvious. What we learned WebMCP is at its best when it replaces genuine friction — not when it's added to a flow that would work the same without it. The most valuable primitive we used wasn't tool registration itself, it was requestUserInteraction : the ability for a tool to pause and loop a human back in is what makes an agent feel collaborative instead of either fully autonomous or fully manual. What's next I want to expand this idea to other fields for someone elderly, not just medical.  Inspiration 

 Travel planning is fragmented: people jump among sites to research, compare, schedule, and book. We imagined an agent that can help with the full planning loop while keeping people in control of every important decision. 

 What it does 

 Arion Trip Planner turns a natural-language request into a flexible itinerary. It searches stays and activities, compares options against budget and preferences, builds day-by-day plans, and replans when constraints change. The traveler approves any booking or payment step. 

 How we built it 

 We built Arion as a WebMCP-enabled web app. It exposes structured tools for searching travel options, creating itineraries, saving shortlists, checking budgets, and replanning. Provider adapters normalize external travel data into one planning experience, while WebMCP lets an agent use these tools directly in the browser. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hardest problem was making recommendations useful without letting the agent take irreversible actions. We designed explicit approval points for booking and payment, and kept search, comparison, and planning separate from confirmation. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We created a planning experience where an agent can do more than suggest links: it can assemble, update, and explain a realistic trip plan. We are especially proud that the user remains the final decision-maker throughout. 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native products need clear tool boundaries, structured data, and transparent state. WebMCP makes these interactions more reliable than asking an agent to navigate a traditional website visually. 

 What's next for Arion Trip Planner 

 Next, we plan to add more live provider integrations, collaborative trip planning for groups, richer availability data, and secure, user-approved checkout flows.

The site's own built-in chat assistant is just one WebMCP client among many - an external agent like ChatGPT or Claude can drive the exact same trip through the exact same tools, no scraping, no bespoke integration. 

 The one deliberate limit: booking-execution tools are staged by whichever assistant is planning, but only a human tap on Approve ever commits a real reservation - keeping an agent free to plan and prepare while a person alone controls spend. 

 Beyond the WebMCP wiring itself, I built the real backend behind it: live flight/vehicle booking against mock provider APIs, geocoding and route computation running in the background so tool calls stay fast, and failure-reason reporting so a failed booking is diagnosable and retryable instead of a dead end.

title: Spotigo : Spot it , report it , fix it!
pitch: Spotigo lets you describe a civic problem out loud — a pothole, a downed power line — and an agent turns that into a filed report, but it can never hit submit without your explicit yes.
about_excerpt:
Spotigo lets you describe a civic problem out loud — a pothole, a downed power line — and an agent turns that into a filed report, but it can never hit submit without your explicit yes.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like

 Gemini : POW of WebMCP integration

 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 



 
 Spotigo — Project Story 

 A WebMCP-powered civic agent that turns human intent into safe, executable web actions. 

 
 Describe the problem. Let the agent handle the workflow. Keep the human in control of the part that matters. 
 

 Inspiration 

 The web already has the services people need. The friction is almost never "does this exist" — it's "can I get from what I want to say to the specific form this particular website expects." A citizen who sees a pothole thinks someone should report this , not let me figure out which municipal category this falls under, whether it's already been reported, and how to phrase it correctly. The problem exists. The digital service to fix it probably exists too. The gap is entirely in connecting human intent to that workflow — and that gap is exactly what WebMCP is positioned to close. 

 My first idea wasn't civic reporting at all — it was an accessible, voice-first grocery storefront. Before building much of it, I checked what was already in the WebMCP showcase and found Verdant Market already occupying that lane: "browse groceries and build a shared cart with an agent." Rather than build a variation on an existing reference app, I kept the one pattern worth keeping — the agent prepares, the human confirms — and moved it to a domain where getting that confirmation wrong actually matters: civic reporting, where the output is a public record, not a grocery order. 

 What it does 

 A citizen describes a civic issue by voice or text — "there's a huge pothole near my office" — and an agent turns that into a real, trackable report, gated by explicit human confirmation at the one step that counts. 

 Spotigo registers 10 WebMCP tools in the browser through document.modelContext , deliberately shaped as a workflow rather than a flat list: 

 
 
 Stage 
 Tools 
 
 
 
 Understand 
 describe_issue_accessibly , report_civic_issue 
 
 
 Validate 
 check_duplicate_reports , list_nearby_reports 
 
 
 Explain 
 read_report_summary 
 
 
 Authorize 
 confirm_submission , acknowledge_safety_guidance 
 
 
 Act 
 submit_report 
 
 
 Recover / Track 
 undo_last_action , get_report_status 
 
 

 A real pass through it: the agent structures "huge pothole near my office" into a draft — category pothole , description, resolved location — checks it against nearby reports and comes back with a graded confidence assessment (not a flat yes/no), then reads the draft back in plain language: "I'm about to report a large pothole at this location with this description. Submit it?" Only after an explicit confirm: true does submit_report become callable, returning a real tracking ID the citizen can check later with get_report_status . 

 How we built it 

 Zero build step, zero runtime dependencies, static files only — deliberate, so the WebMCP layer itself stays the thing under inspection, not something buried under framework abstraction. 

 One execution path, not two. The human-facing UI and the agent-facing WebMCP tools call the same tool.execute() closures — there's no separate "demo path" for the agent. If a judge opens the on-page Tool Tester and fires submit_report before confirming, they get the identical rejection an agent would get, because it's literally the same code running either way. 

 Ten tools, not one do_everything() . It would have been simpler to expose a single submit_report(details) function and let a system prompt handle the reasoning. That would hide exactly the part worth demonstrating — the validation, the safety boundaries, the point where understanding what someone wants stops being enough to act on it. Decomposing the workflow into explicit stages made the tool surface mirror the actual application logic instead of papering over it. 

 Intent is not authorization. The agent can understand the issue, check for duplicates, and explain what it's about to do — none of that authorizes submit_report . That gate is enforced in code: confirm: "yes" is truthy in JavaScript but explicitly rejected, because a loose check could let an ambiguous model output pass as authorization. Only strict confirm: true opens the gate. 

 The gate adapts to risk. Routine issues get one confirmation. Safety-critical ones — a downed power line, a suspected gas leak — route through a distinct acknowledge_safety_guidance step first, and lose the normal undo safety net once submitted. A pothole and a live wire aren't the same category of decision, and treating them identically would have been the easier, lazier design. 

 A second, separate experiment. server.js and server/ implement a persistent, authenticated MCP service for agents connecting outside the browser — real action storage, ownership isolation, rate limiting, a fail-closed authority resolver. It is explicitly not part of the deployed judged demo. I kept that line hard rather than implying a backend was live when it wasn't. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Choosing what not to build. The competitive check that killed the grocery idea happened before most of the code existed, which made it cheap. That ordering — research first, fall in love with the implementation second — was the single highest-leverage decision in the project. 

 Making confirmation a real boundary, not a suggestion. Getting the strict-boolean check right ( confirm: true vs. anything merely truthy) sounds trivial until you consider that an LLM producing "yes" or 1 instead of true is a completely plausible failure mode, and a loose check would have let it silently authorize a submission. 

 A Windows path bug invisible in my own dev loop. Automated smoke tests passed cleanly in my Linux sandbox and failed immediately on the actual Windows machine, with ERR_UNSUPPORTED_ESM_URL_SCHEME — Node's dynamic import() requires a proper file:// URL on Windows; a raw path like D:\...\app.js doesn't qualify, even though the POSIX equivalent works fine elsewhere. One-line fix ( pathToFileURL() ), but a reminder that "tests pass" and "tests pass in the environment a judge will actually use" are different claims. 

 Git history discipline under time pressure. A substantial chunk of work — the entire server/MCP layer — sat uncommitted for longer than it should have while heads-down building it. A last-minute dump commit would have technically satisfied "real commit history" while missing its point. Going back and committing it in logical pieces was extra effort late in the process, but it was the honest version of the requirement. 

 Resisting the urge to claim more than was deployed. Once the server prototype worked locally, the tempting move was to fold it into the headline pitch. The harder, better call was a README section that draws a hard line between what's live and judged versus what's a local Phase 2 prototype — because a panel this technical will check claims against what's actually running, and a claim that doesn't reproduce live costs more than the claim was worth. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 A confirmation gate that's a real, tested execution boundary — including catching and rejecting confirm: "yes" , the exact kind of loose value a model might plausibly produce. 
 A risk-tiered version of that gate, where safety-critical issues require a distinct second acknowledgement and lose the undo safety net, because not every civic issue carries the same stakes. 
 One execution path for humans and agents — no shadow demo logic, verifiable by anyone who opens the Tool Tester. 
 22 passing tests, including one that runs the full judge-facing scenario — draft → duplicate check → review → both negative confirmation cases → submission → tracking ID → status lookup — against the real tool closures. 
 One honestly-scoped, fully-working vertical, with a second experimental server layer clearly labeled as not part of the judged demo, instead of five thinly-demonstrated domains. 
 

 What we learned 

 The real opportunity here isn't "AI plus websites" — it's AI agents plus websites that expose capabilities an agent can reliably us

An agent-ready retail workspace that turns a stock alert into a reversible draft, then leaves approval to the operator.

 Inspiration 

 Retail teams do not need an agent that silently buys stock. They need help turning messy operational signals into a clear, reviewable next step. A shelf can be below its reorder point, compatible alternatives can exist, and the decision still belongs to the person responsible for stock and spend. 

 Restock Room explores that handoff. It gives an agent a narrow, explicit set of capabilities for finding evidence and preparing a proposal, while keeping the normal workspace understandable and the final approval visibly human. 

 What it does 

 Restock Room starts with visible low-stock alerts and a visible replenishment policy. A browser agent can read the alert evidence and policy, search the visible synthetic catalog for the affected item and alternatives, and create a replenishment draft or a policy-aware two-alert plan. The operator then reviews every proposed line in the same UI and approves or rejects it. 

 The draft or plan is intentionally the end of the agent's authority. The multi-alert plan enforces the visible 75% signal-confidence threshold, two-line limit, and $1,800 budget. Approval is a local, auditable UI action only: it never contacts a supplier, creates a cart, submits an order, or handles a payment. All catalog and inventory records in the demo are synthetic. 

 Why this is a strong WebMCP use case 

 Without WebMCP, an agent must infer workflows from a page's layout and text, which is brittle for operational work. Restock Room exposes the meaningful actions as structured tools, with stable names, input schemas, and safe outcomes. The agent can work with the same stock alert and catalog information the operator sees instead of guessing which controls or records matter. 

 That produces a better joint experience: the agent reduces the research and proposal work, while the human retains context, discretion, and final control. The normal UI remains fully usable even if WebMCP is unavailable, so agent support enhances the workspace instead of replacing it. 

 How we built it 

 The React and TypeScript app registers seven client-side WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool when the browser exposes the API: 

 
 
 Tool 
 Safety boundary 
 
 
 
 get_stock_alert 
 Read-only view of one visible alert and its evidence. 
 
 
 search_catalog 
 Read-only synthetic catalog search and alternative lookup. 
 
 
 create_replenishment_draft 
 Creates a reversible in-app draft; it cannot purchase or submit an order. 
 
 
 get_replenishment_draft 
 Read-only view of the draft and human approval state. 
 
 
 get_restock_policy 
 Read-only view of the visible budget, confidence threshold, line limit, and human-approval rule. 
 
 
 create_replenishment_plan 
 Creates a reversible two-alert plan only when it fits the visible policy; it cannot purchase or submit an order. 
 
 
 get_replenishment_plan 
 Read-only view of plan budget use and each line’s human decision. 
 
 

 The read-only tools use readOnlyHint , inputs are bounded with object schemas, and no tool exposes untrusted or user-generated content. The deployed static app also sets origin-isolation and Permissions-Policy: tools=(self) headers for the WebMCP environment. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 The hard product decision was restraint. It is easy to make a replenishment demo look impressive by letting an agent complete a purchase, but that conceals the real risks. We narrowed the tool surface to what an operator can inspect, reason about, and safely reverse. 

 We also designed the UI and the tool contract together. Every agent-visible result must make sense to a person looking at the workspace, and every material action must leave a visible trace. 

 Accomplishments that we are proud of 

 
 A complete alert-to-draft-to-approval workflow and a multi-alert policy plan rather than isolated tool calls. 
 A small WebMCP contract that clearly separates read-only lookup from reversible state changes. 
 A human-first fallback experience and an explicit audit trail. 
 A public HTTPS deployment that is ready for judges to test in a WebMCP-enabled browser. 
 

 What we learned 

 Agent-native product design is less about exposing every button and more about naming the few actions that carry real intent. A structured tool can make an agent more reliable, but the product must still say who owns the decision and what the tool is not allowed to do. 

 What's next for Restock Room 

 The next iteration would connect to real inventory feeds behind explicit authorization, add role-aware approval policies, and preserve a durable audit history. Any supplier or purchase integration would remain a separate, explicit human-approved step rather than an extension of the draft-creation tool.
