title: Bridge to Agentia
pitch: Bridging the Web and AI Agents through Native Tools, APIs, UI
about_excerpt: Bridging the Web and AI Agents through Native Tools, APIs, UI Like Comment Story Updates arch1 Native-WebMCP-without-auth-tool-expose Native-Webmcp-login-tool-expose-emptycart API-Adapter-without-login-expose API-Adapter-login-expose UIAutomation-Adapter-login-tool-expose UIAutomation-Adapter-without-auth-tool-expose Bridge to Agentia — Project Overview & Narrative Inspiration The web was built primarily for humans: we view a page, interpret its visual layout, click buttons, fill forms, and complete workflows. AI agents, however, require something fundamentally different—they need discoverable, structured, and actionable capabilities . WebMCP (Web Model Context Protocol) provides a compelling foundation for solving this problem by allowing web applications to expose their capabilities directly as machine-readable tools that AI agents can discover and execute within the browser security boundary. This prompted an essential architectural question: What happens when a website does not natively support WebMCP? That question inspired Bridge to Agentia . What I Built Bridge to Agentia explores three complementary architectural paradigms for bridging AI agents with web applications: Native WebMCP — The web application directly exposes its capabilities as schema-validated WebMCP tools registered in the browser context via document.modelContext . API Adapter — An external proxy adapter translates an existing website REST API into agent-accessible WebMCP tools via a serverless edge worker (Cloudflare Worker). UI / Automation Adapter — An external adapter translates agent intent directly into DOM interactions and automation steps over the existing user interface. The objective is not to replace existing web applications, but to construct a robust, unified bridge between agent intent and underlying web capabilities . For example, the same user prompt: “Find an indigo denim jacket under $150 and add it to my bag.” can be executed through any of the three underlying integration mechanisms: AI Agent Intent │ ├── Native WebMCP ─────────► In-Browser Tool Registry (34 Tools) │ ├── API Adapter ───────────► Serverless Edge Proxy ──► Storefront API │ └── UI Adapter ────────────► Headless Automation ─────► Storefront DOM To demonstrate this in practice, we built an in-website AI Stylist featuring both text and voice interaction , allowing shoppers to converse naturally while the agent discovers and orchestrates available WebMCP tools in real time. Human Shopper │ ├── Natural Language Chat ───┐ │ │ └── Real-Time Voice Mic ─────┤ ▼ AI Agent ▼ WebMCP Tool Registry ▼ Storefront Capabilities This architecture enables consistent, semantic agent interactions regardless of the underlying execution layer. How I Built It Bridge to Agentia is architected around a declarative, tool-based interaction lifecycle: Discovery : The agent inspects available tools for the current session state via document.modelContext.getTools() . Schema Comprehension : The agent parses typed JSON Schemas defining required fields, types, enums, and numerical constraints. Intent Resolution & Selection : The LLM resolves user requests into appropriate tool calls and structured arguments. Security & Privacy Gating : Inputs are checked for prompt injection patterns; sensitive operations require user confirmation; credentials never enter model context. Execution & State Mutation : The tool executes against the same-origin API, updates application state, and dispatches UI synchronization events. Result Sanitization & Synthesis : Tool results are scrubbed of PII before return to the model for conversational summarization. User │ (Chat / Voice) ▼ AI Agent Controller │ ├── 1. Sanitize Prompt & Check Delimiters ([USER_MESSAGE]) ├── 2. Discover Available Tools (State-Gated) ├── 3. Resolve Tool & Parameters (Gemini Function Calling) ├── 4. Request User Confirmation (if Destructive / Transactional) ▼ WebMCP Registry Execution │ ├── Validate Input Schema (Types, Enums, Integer Bounds) ├── Invoke Same-Origin Commerce API ├── Update Application State (Auth / Cart / Wishlist) ▼ Response Sanitization & Privacy Boundary │ ├── Scrub PII (Mask Emails, Redact Street Addresses & Phones) ├── Neutralize Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool Payloads ├── Record Execution to Append-Only Audit Log (/api/audit) ▼ Conversational Natural-Language / Voice Audio Response State-Aware Capability Exposure Tool availability dynamically reflects session state: Guest (Logged Out) : 18 public tools active (catalog search, fashion filters, size guides, comparison matrices, shipping rates, auth status). Authenticated, Cart Empty : 33 tools active (cart operations, wishlist management, address updates, order history). Checkout is gated ( 33/34 ). Authenticated, Cart Populated : All 34 tools active, unlocking create_order ( 34/34 ). End-to-End Security & Privacy Guardrails To prevent data exfiltration and credential theft: Auth Isolation : login and register tools are omitted from LLM tool declarations; authentication occurs strictly through browser UI. PII Scrubbing : Contact numbers and home addresses are replaced with semantic tokens (e.g., [Saved Address #1] ), and emails are recursively masked. Prompt Injection Defense : Inputs and tool payloads are wrapped in boundary markers, with automated detection for instruction overrides, role spoofing, and delimiter escapes. Human-in-the-Loop Confirmation : Destructive tools ( create_order , cancel_order , clear_cart , logout , update_shipping_address , remove_from_cart ) pause execution for explicit user confirmation. Persistent Audit Trail : Execution durations, parameters, and threat signatures are logged in memory and flushed to server-side append-only JSONL files. What I Learned Building Bridge to Agentia demonstrated that making a web application agent-accessible requires far more than exposing raw endpoints. Key learnings include: Separation of Interface and Implementation : The semantic tool interface presented to an agent can remain identical whether backed by native browser APIs, edge API adapters, or DOM automation. Designing for LLM Tool Consumption : Writing descriptive tool documentation, strict parameter schemas, and clear error contracts directly dictates model planning accuracy. State-Aware Tool Gating : Dynamically updating available tools based on session state dramatically reduces model hallucinations and invalid function calls. Failure Modes and Resilient Error Contracts : Tools must return structured, machine-actionable error payloads ( code , retryable , userActionRequired ) so agents can self-correct when encounters occur (out of stock, invalid coupons, unauthenticated states). The Necessity of LLM Security Boundaries : Unchecked agent access risks prompt injection and privacy violations. Defensive prompt guards, PII scrubbers, and confirmation gates are essential for trustworthy agentic commerce. Challenges Bridging the Paradigm Gap : Native WebMCP provides optimal latency and security, but requires website-level implementation. API adaptation avoids visual dependency but requires backend schema knowledge. UI automation requires no backend access but introduces brittle DOM coupling. Balancing these trade-offs across edge runtimes was a primary architectural challenge. Dynamic State Synchronization : Ensuring that an action performed by an AI agent (such as adding an item to the cart or logging in) immediately synchronizes React UI context, cart counts, and native tool availability without causing stale closures or infinite re-renders. Full-Duplex Voice Control : Implementing natural speech recognition and Text-to-Speech playback while providing instantaneous cancellation (mute toggles, sound wave stop controls, and drawer close events) to prevent background audio runaway during asynchronous multi-turn tool loops. Rigorous Failure Handling : Constructing deterministic tests to validate that the system fails safely and predictably across wrong argument types, negative integers, execution order errors, out-of-stock items, and network interruptions. Why Bridge to Agentia? Bridge to Agentia envisions a web where humans and AI agents interact with applications through a common, capability-oriented interface . Instead of asking: “Does this website support WebMCP?” we explore the broader, forward-looking question: “How can any web capability become discoverable, secure, and actionable for an AI agent?” By unifying native browser WebMCP , edge API adaptation , and DOM-level automation with comprehensive security guardrails, Bridge to Agentia provides a practical blueprint for the agentic web. Different architectures, same destination: making web capabilities discoverable and actionable by AI agents. title: Zingposts
pitch: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust.
about_excerpt: Interesting things, organized together: a WebMCP-native marketplace where people work with the outside agents they already trust. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Browsing old cars, boats, campers, motorcycles, and machinery is fun. Managing the hunt is not. Good finds get lost across tabs, marketplace search misses obvious matches, alerts are rigid, research lives in scattered notes, and negotiations have no shared memory. A three-way trade is almost impossible to reason about cleanly. Zingposts starts from a different premise: the marketplace should be equally legible to people and their agents without embedding a model in the product. The site owns its native listings and structured deal workflow, while outside listings can be tracked as clearly labeled snapshots. What it does Zingposts is a complete peer-to-peer marketplace and durable workspace for interesting things. People can browse realistic native inventory, create and publish listings, upload photos, save finds, build boards, set alerts, keep research notebooks, message sellers, prepare offers, and create structured multi-party trade rooms. Outside finds can be tracked without confusing them with Zingposts-owned inventory. A connected outside agent receives a compact persistent core plus one focused pack drawn from 121 structured WebMCP tools. It can search with compound criteria, compare candidates, organize boards, tag and rank finds, record cited research and inspection risks, monitor price changes, draft communications and offers, calculate acquisition cost, propose trade scenarios, and coordinate the shared gallery, focus, or thumbnail canvas. The human uses the same structure through a canvas-first interface. Zingposts itself contains no LLM. The centerpiece is the shared canvas: an outside agent opens a durable session, places a shortlist, recommendation, or focused question beside the marketplace objects, and pauses only when human judgment matters. The person can inspect the exact listings and rationale, choose an option or add context, and return structured guidance. The agent reads that durable response on its next tool call and continues. This is turn-taking over shared marketplace objects, not a chatbot transcript. The loop now extends across visits. get_workspace_resume returns the last acknowledged checkpoint, everything that changed since, structured blockers, human responses, proposal status, and safe next actions. An agent can acknowledge the checkpoint only after processing it, so “come back later” is an explicit protocol rather than a hope that conversation context survived. For broad edits, the agent can prepare a sourced, versioned change set instead of making a trail of one-off mutations. Zingposts previews each proposed change in plain language, checks the expected object versions, and lets the person selectively accept only the changes they want. Agents cannot approve their own change sets. Completed deals can be recorded as private outcomes, and transparent aggregate patterns report counts, prices, and reasons without inventing a model-generated score. Either side can arrive first. A person can explore immediately in a prototype workspace, then replace a test email and verify the real address through Supabase only when work reaches the marketplace boundary. One Bring my agent click copies the canonical guide URL. Or an unauthenticated agent can inspect five setup-only tools and open a prototype handoff for the person. Once the person signs in, safe private tools appear automatically to an outside agent operating that browser document. Independent 12-hour revocable sessions remain available through one-use invites or codes for separate-browser or unattended work. The human remains in control. Publishing, enabling notifications, sending a message, submitting or responding to an offer, and inviting a trade participant stop at a visible confirmation gate. Every human and agent action is attributed, and reversible work can be undone. Why WebMCP is essential Without WebMCP, an agent has to infer intent from buttons and screen position. That is brittle for a marketplace with dozens of interdependent objects: listings, boards, research, alerts, conversations, offers, people, assets, and constraints. WebMCP gives Zingposts a stable collaboration language. “Find pre-1980 boats under $15,000, put the best four on a board, record the title risks, and draft a message to the strongest seller” becomes a sequence of typed, attributable actions. The human can watch the same state change, refine it directly, and approve the parts that cross a consequential boundary. That makes the product meaningfully better with an agent—not merely automatable. How we built it Zingposts uses React 19 and Next.js on Netlify. Supabase Auth provides verified human sessions, Supabase Postgres holds marketplace, identity, agent-session, and workflow state, and Supabase Storage holds listing photos. Versioned SQL migrations keep direct browser access locked behind row-level security. The browser client exposes 121 declarative tools through the WebMCP modelContext surface, but only five setup tools while signed out. After the person signs in, AbortSignal-managed registration keeps a compact persistent core plus one replaceable focused capability pack, so navigation never accumulates an oversized registry or silently unlocks business actions. get_agent_bootstrap returns setup guidance while signed out, then canonical browser-delegated identity, workspace, attention, active collaboration, capability index, and guide version after sign-in. activate_capability switches the focused pack without moving the person; open_for_human_review is optional. The action layer derives canonical human and agent identity on the server, prevents duplicate profiles, enforces ownership and state-transition enums, creates reviewable drafts, writes attributed activity, stores inverse operations for undo, supports idempotency keys and optimistic versions, returns stable deep links and WebMCP-native structured errors, and converts consequential operations into pending confirmations. Isolated QA runs register only their own artifacts, provide an exact cleanup preview, and require human approval before deletion. The marketplace is seeded with original project-owned imagery and realistic records so the full human-agent workflow is understandable immediately. WebMCP registration is document-scoped, while Zingposts durably stores connection profiles, scopes, alerts, boards, research, drafts, versions, and audit history. The public /for-agents guide and /api/agent-guide contract show agents how to reconnect safely without storing an invite, code, or stale catalog. Challenges The main design challenge was not adding more agent power; it was deciding where that power should stop. We separated preparation from commitment. Research, organization, comparison, and drafting can proceed quickly. Communication, publication, notifications, invitations, and financial commitments pause for the human. We also designed external-listing tracking so provenance stays honest. Zingposts can organize an outside find, but it never claims that its cached price, availability, or seller statements are authoritative. Accomplishments A coherent marketplace, not a WebMCP proof of concept 121 tools spanning authentication, onboarding, resumable work sessions, versioned proposals, outcomes, canvas views, discovery, organization, negotiation, and multi-party trade Agent-first and person-first onboarding with a five-tool setup surface before human sign-in Durable agent-to-human-to-agent turn-taking with a unified attention queue Explicit resume checkpoints and structured blockers for work that continues across agent runs Sourced, versioned change sets with semantic previews and selective human acceptance Private outcome recording with transparent, non-AI aggregate patterns Live agent activity, exact-payload approval, idempotency, dry runs, structured errors, and stable deep links No built-in AI or model dependency Supabase human authentication plus opaque invite URLs, code fallback, and single-use, expiring, revocable agent sessions—without password or session sharing Persistent bootstrap plus navigation-independent focused capability activation Structured errors, strict workflow transitions, optimistic concurrency, and namespaced QA cleanup Durable attribution, confirmations, and undo Native seller photo upload and publishing workflow Clear separation between owned listings and outside tracked snapshots Production build, automated API smoke tests, desktop browser testing, and mobile verification What we learned Human-agent collaboration works best when both sides operate on the same durable objects. A board is better than a chat-only list. A research notebook is better than an ephemeral summary. A pending confirmation is better than asking the model to remember which action is sensitive. We also learned to separate document-scoped WebMCP

title: Navwebmcp
pitch: You already write your way for other to use your platform, don't hide it in your browser, expose it using Navwebmcp cuts agent tool, tokens and latency measured, not estimated without browser.
about_excerpt: You already write your way for other to use your platform, don't hide it in your browser, expose it using Navwebmcp cuts agent tool, tokens and latency measured, not estimated without browser. Like Comment Story Updates GIF GIF GIF GIF NavWebMcp — Devpost Submission This is a young repo that takes the MCP and WEBMCP approach and tries to build a new approach that takes the benefits of both and give answers to their weaknesses. Inspiration Every existing way an agent touches a web app pays the same tax: either the agent orchestrates a sequence of raw API calls itself — search, then create, then verify — reasoning about your domain on every single round-trip, or it drives the page like a human would, reading an accessibility tree and clicking through a UI built for eyes and fingers, not for a model. Both cost tokens and latency that have nothing to do with the actual task, and both grow worse as the surface area of the app grows and it is not deterministic. WebMCP ( document.modelContext ) is a promising browser-native answer to half of that problem — a page can register callable tools for an agent the same way it registers event listeners for a user. But the draft standard stops at "here's how a tool gets registered." It doesn't say how an agent should discover fifty tools without paying for fifty tools' worth of schema on every connection, how to layer permissions on top, or how to collapse a five-call workflow into one. That gap — protocol on top of primitive — is what NavWebMcp exists to fill. This repo is also a deliberate proof point for the AOD/ADD methodology (AI-Oriented Development / AI-Driven Development): intent specs framed up front, implementation delegated to agents, and every claim independently verified before being accepted — including, especially, the benchmark numbers below. What it does AgentBridge is a reference implementation of NavWebMcp , a protocol layered on top of WebMCP that adds progressive tool disclosure, RBAC, and composite operations. Instead of an agent stitching together searchAvailability → createReservation → getReservation , it calls one tool — book({ date, time, partySize, name }) — and gets back a validated result. The multi-step orchestration (precondition checks, the write, post-condition validation, and a compensating rollback on failure) runs invisibly behind that single call. On connect, an agent sees only 8 lightweight navigation/meta tools (~180 tokens total) — explore , search , describe_tool , invoke , load_tools , unload_tools , getContext , getCapabilities . The other 48 business operations across reservations, CRM, front-office, tasks, housekeeping, and finance are discovered on demand and either invoked directly or promoted to native tools — so registry size never inflates the cost of connecting. getContext and getCapabilities , called in parallel right after connecting, tell the agent who the user is and exactly what their role permits before it explores anything, so it can ask the user one consolidated question instead of a drip-feed of prompts. Every operation carries a role list ( customer , support , admin ) checked at every call boundary, and destructive operations carry an enforced confirmation gate. The same 48 operations are exposed identically over two surfaces from one registry: in-page WebMCP (session-cookie auth, for browser-native agents) and MCP Streamable HTTP (bearer-token auth, for external agents connecting with no browser at all ). That second point matters more than it sounds: hostVipGuest , a 7-step chain spanning CRM and front-desk, has no UI in this app whatsoever — there is nothing a click-driven tool could even target — yet it's fully callable over MCP HTTP because the tool was never built to depend on a rendered page. It's designed to work identically whether the connecting client is Claude Code, Claude Desktop, MCP Inspector, ChatGPT, or OpenAI's Codex — the orchestration runs in-process against the same handler code no matter who's calling. We proved it against a working demo: a hospitality platform with 56 operations, three composite tools, three role-scoped demo users, and a live audit log streamed over SSE. How we built it Next.js 15 (App Router, React 19) and TypeScript, with Zod as the single source of truth for both runtime validation and JSON Schema generation on both surfaces. @modelcontextprotocol/sdk plus mcp-handler provide the MCP Streamable HTTP transport; zod-to-json-schema converts the same Zod shapes for in-page WebMCP tool registration. Playwright and Vitest back the test and benchmark harnesses. The core design decision was keeping orchestration surface-agnostic: lib/core/book.ts , seatGuest.ts , and hostVipGuest.ts take a call function as a dependency and know nothing about HTTP, cookies, or bearer tokens. The browser wrapper injects serverCall ( fetch("/api/call") , cookie auth); the MCP operation injects makeDispatch(ctx) (in-process, bearer auth). Same business logic, same validation, same RBAC — the only thing that changes is what's plugged into one function parameter. Adding a new operation means writing one file in lib/operations/ and registering it in one index — it then appears on both surfaces automatically with disclosure, RBAC, and audit logging already wired. Following AOD/ADD, the process itself was: write the intent (what the protocol needed to guarantee) before writing code, delegate implementation to agents against that spec, and independently verify — most concretely, by insisting every number in the README's benchmark tables come from an actual measured run ( scripts/bench.mjs , scripts/speedbase.mjs , n=5, real MCP transport, real headless browser) rather than an estimate. Challenges we ran into Getting progressive disclosure right without breaking usability was the hardest design problem — too little detail at connect time and the agent flails; too much and the token savings evaporate. The explore / search / describe_tool split (navigate by path, discover by pattern, fetch schema only when needed) came out of iterating on that trade-off. Keeping the two surfaces genuinely equivalent — not just superficially similar — meant RBAC, confirmation gates, and audit logging all had to live at the operation-registry level rather than in either surface's adapter, or they'd have silently drifted apart the first time someone touched only one of the two files. Benchmarking honestly was its own challenge: it's easy to produce numbers that flatter the architecture. We insisted on comparing against a real Playwright browser-automation lane, not a hypothetical one, which is also what surfaced the finding that mattered most — hostVipGuest has no Playwright row at all, because there's no UI for it to drive. That's not a benchmark gap, it's a demonstration of the actual capability boundary of UI automation versus tool calls. Versioning also took more thought than expected: a single version number couldn't distinguish "the protocol contract changed" from "this role's tool set changed," so getCapabilities() deliberately returns two separate fields — a hand-bumped protocolVersion and an automatically computed, role-scoped capabilityHash — so agents can tell which kind of change happened and react accordingly. Accomplishments that we're proud of The benchmark numbers are real, not estimated, and they're strong: composite calls cut tokens by 72–87% and latency by 67–88% versus raw multi-call orchestration, on both the MCP HTTP and in-browser WebMCP surfaces, with 5/5 reliability across every lane. The saving compounds with orchestration complexity — a 7-op CRM+front-desk chain collapses to a single call with an 87% latency reduction — and testing the operation layer directly is up to 1,300× faster than driving the same flow through a browser. We're equally proud of the fact that the protocol holds up structurally: one operation registry drives two authentication models, two transports, and two calling conventions with zero duplicated business logic, and RBAC/audit/disclosure behavior is provably identical on both because they're enforced in one shared place, not two. And we shipped the consumer half of the protocol too — skills/navwebmcp-agent/ , a portable agent skill for connecting efficiently, discovering operations, and preferring composite calls — versioned independently of the server implementation, so it isn't tied to this one demo app. What we learned The biggest lesson: token and latency cost in agent tooling is mostly a protocol design problem, not a model problem. The same LLM calling the same underlying operations pays wildly different costs depending on whether it has to orchestrate three calls itself or one — that's architecture, not intelligence. We also learned that "the agent needs a browser" is frequently just false. Once business logic is expressed as composable server-side operations, the browser becomes one optional caller among several rather than a load-bearing dependency — which is what let hostVipGuest exist at

title: Shipment Document Check
pitch: Checks shipment documents, helps an agent prepare the right fixes, and keeps approvals and final decisions with the person reviewing the pack.
about_excerpt: Checks shipment documents, helps an agent prepare the right fixes, and keeps approvals and final decisions with the person reviewing the pack. Like 1 Comment Story Updates 1 The starting shipment pack, with five documents, nine checks and the WebMCP review workflow in one place. The agent has prepared two corrections for exporter-owned documents. Both remain staged until a person approves them. The Bill of Lading remains locked while the application prepares an unsent correction request for the carrier. The goods descriptions are shown side by side so a person can review the evidence and confirm the final decision. Inspiration Export shipments involve several documents, and those documents are not all controlled by the same person. The exporter prepares some of them, while others come from a bank, carrier or public authority. What interested me was that finding a mismatch is only half the job. The reviewer also needs to know who is allowed to correct it. An exporter can fix its own invoice, but it cannot rewrite a Bill of Lading issued by a carrier. Some differences are also unclear enough that a person still needs to make the final decision. I built Shipment Document Check to explore how an agent could help with this work without being given permission to change everything. What it does The application reviews one fictional shipment pack containing five documents: Letter of Credit Commercial Invoice Packing List Bill of Lading Certificate of Origin It runs nine consistency checks and starts with five findings. For documents controlled by the exporter, the agent can prepare a correction. The correction is shown in the page, but a person must approve it before it is applied. For documents issued by a carrier or authority, the original document stays locked. The agent can prepare a correction request, but it cannot change the document or send the request. There is also a goods-description difference that needs human judgement. The agent can show the evidence and record a proposed decision, but a person must confirm it. After the approved corrections and confirmed decision, the preflight is run again. Seven of the nine checks pass. The remaining two issues still need action from the external issuers. How WebMCP is used I did not want to add another chatbot inside the application. Instead, the page exposes six WebMCP tools directly to a compatible browser agent: get_pack_state get_finding_evidence stage_exporter_corrections draft_external_correction_requests stage_human_decision rerun_preflight These tools give the agent a clear set of actions instead of making it guess from buttons and page text. The agent and the person reviewing the shipment work with the same visible state. When the agent stages a correction or decision, it appears in the page for review. Approval is deliberately kept outside the agent's control. The application also contains an instruction hidden inside a fictional trade document. That text is treated as document content, not as an instruction the agent should follow. How I built it The project is a client-side React and TypeScript application built with Vite. The shipment data and all nine checks are deterministic. React useReducer manages the workflow, and Zod validates the document data and WebMCP tool inputs. The WebMCP tools are registered through document.modelContext.registerTool . The tools and the manual interface use the same reducer actions, so the agent cannot bypass rules that apply in the page. There is no backend, login, database, OCR service or document upload. Everything in the shipment pack is fictional and stays in the browser. Challenges I ran into The main challenge was keeping the agent useful without giving it too much control. A staged correction must not be mistaken for an approved correction. A drafted request must not be mistaken for a sent request. The WebMCP result and the visible page also need to show the same workflow state after every action. It was equally important to prove that locked documents are actually protected. If the agent tries to modify the carrier-issued Bill of Lading, the application returns DOCUMENT_LOCKED and leaves the document unchanged. What I am proud of The project has only six tools, and each one has a clear purpose. The final result is also honest. The application ends with seven passing checks and two issues still waiting for external action. It does not pretend that every problem can be solved automatically. What I learned This project changed how I think about agent access. Giving an agent more control does not always make the product better. In this case, the useful part is the separation of responsibilities. The agent handles repetitive checking and preparation. The application enforces the rules. The person keeps control over approvals and judgement. What is next A future version could accept real documents, use OCR and support different shipment rules. Before adding those features, I would want to do a proper privacy and security review. For this challenge, I kept the project small, deterministic and limited to fictional data. Built With playwright react typescript vercel vite vitest webmcp zod Try it out shipment-document-check-mhanmantfreebi-1870.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by I designed and built Shipment Document Check end to end, including the document-review workflow, six WebMCP tools, authority rules, interface and test suite. I also tested the live agent journey and prepared the demo and public documentation. title: Scrapi
pitch: WebMCP tools that expose Scrapi's scraping pipeline to any agent, plus an in-app agent that uses them and gets smarter per domain with usage
about_excerpt:
WebMCP tools that expose Scrapi's scraping pipeline to any agent, plus an in-app agent that uses them and gets smarter per domain with usage
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 landing page 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 landing page 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 landing page 
 
 1 2 



 
 Inspiration 

 I already had Scrapi running as a real scraper before this challenge existed - fetch, detect whether a page needs JS rendering, extract, clean, done. When I saw WebMCP, my first instinct wasn't "let me bolt an AI chatbot onto this," it was "an agent trying to use my scraper right now would have to either click through my UI like a human or scrape my own HTML to figure out what's on the page - both of those are exactly the kind of brittle nonsense my scraper exists to avoid doing to other sites." That felt like the actual point of WebMCP: stop making agents reverse-engineer your app and just hand them a contract for the pipeline you already trust. 

 What it does 

 Scrapi exposes four tools on document.modelContext once you're signed in: 

 scrape_url - runs a URL through the real pipeline (with a Selenium fallback for JS-heavy sites) and hands back structured results.
get_scrape_history - your past jobs.
get_scrape_export - export a finished scrape as CSV or JSON.
check_domain_history - looks at everything Scrapi has ever scraped from a given domain and tells you whether it usually needs JS rendering and which detection method actually worked. 

 Any WebMCP-aware agent can find and call these on its own. I also built a small "Tools" panel inside the app itself that calls the exact same tools through the real document.modelContext.executeTool() API, with a little badge that honestly tells you whether the call went through WebMCP or fell back to a direct call - so Scrapi isn't just publishing tools for someone else's agent, it's using its own. 

 check_domain_history is the part I'm most proud of. It's a live aggregation over real scrape history, not a guess. Scrape a domain once, and the next check of that domain comes back with an actual answer instead of "unknown." 

 How we built it 

 Python and FastAPI on the backend, MongoDB for storage, React and Vite on the frontend, JWT for auth. The scraping side leans on requests + BeautifulSoup/lxml for normal pages and Selenium when a site needs JS rendering. On top of that, frontend/src/webmcp/tools.js defines the four tools with JSON Schema inputs, and a small hook registers them on document.modelContext for any signed-in session and cleans them up on logout. A thin GET /scrape/domain-stats endpoint on the backend is all check_domain_history actually needs - it's just a Mongo aggregation, nothing fancier. Frontend on Vercel, backend on Render, both live. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Honestly, the biggest decision wasn't technical. I originally built this with an in-app agent backed by my own Anthropic API key, so it could actually hold a conversation and decide which tools to call. Then I thought about it properly: I was about to hand out a public demo login sitting in front of my personal API key, for as long as judging lasts, with no idea how many people would hammer it. That's not a risk worth taking for a hackathon. So I pulled the LLM out entirely - deleted the agent backend, the API key, all of it - and kept check_domain_history as a plain WebMCP tool instead of something an LLM had to be prompted into using. It actually made the project more honest: the "gets smarter with usage" claim now rests on a database query I can point to, not a model I'm asking you to trust. 

 On the technical side, the annoying one was document.modelContext.executeTool() in real Chrome throwing UnknownError: Failed to parse input arguments no matter what I sent it. Turned out Chrome's actual shipped implementation wants the arguments pre-stringified with JSON.stringify(), which isn't what the spec explainer describes. Fixed it by trying the stringified form first and falling back to a plain object if that fails. That fix then surfaced a second bug - the string-vs-object mismatch meant tool results were rendering as one giant escaped line of text - so I normalized every result to the same shape at one central point instead of patching the display separately. There was also a completely unrelated pre-existing bug I only found because I insisted on testing everything manually before pushing: my scraper was advertising Brotli support in its request headers without the Brotli package actually installed, which was silently corrupting results from any site that compressed with it. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 Getting a real WebMCP host and client working against the actual browser API, not a mock - and catching real divergences from the spec along the way. And walking away from the LLM agent instead of shipping it anyway just because it was already built. The version that exists now needs no API key from anyone and costs nothing to run per request, which honestly feels like a better demonstration of what WebMCP is for than the flashier version would have been. 

 What we learned 

 That Chrome's actual WebMCP implementation has real, undocumented quirks you won't catch from reading the spec - you have to test against the live API early. And that "smarter with usage" doesn't require a model at all if you're willing to let real data do the talking instead. 

 What's next for Scrapi 

 Tracking more signals per domain in check_domain_history - rate-limit behavior, typical page size, common failure patterns - and seeing how it holds up once more WebMCP-capable agents exist to actually call it.

title: MetaEdit
pitch: Edit live websites with your team and a browser agent. Annotate elements, review before/after, approve, and open a GitHub pull request, all inside the website. Cool, huh?! 😎
about_excerpt: Edit live websites with your team and a browser agent. Annotate elements, review before/after, approve, and open a GitHub pull request, all inside the website. Cool, huh?! 😎 Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration I was heavily inspired by React Grab by Aiden Bai for this project, but I wanted to make it such that the live prod website could be malleable by anyone on the team who has suggestions and who probably don't know how to use GitHub or Figma or an IDE to make edits. What it does MetaEdit turns a live website into a shared review space. A visitor opens the normal site. A collaborator adds metaedit. to the hostname, enters the shared demo token, and can click an element or draw a freeform region over several elements. A WebMCP-capable browser agent can read those annotations, inspect the selected UI, and propose a preview-only revision. Collaborators see the request, the proposed result, reactions, approvals, and history together. The eye control switches between the current page and the proposed result. Upon approval of those changes, they can publish a pull request (PR). Under the hood, MetaEdit creates a GitHub branch, commits the revision evidence, and opens a PR. The live site is not changed directly. How I built it This is a React/Vinext app served by a Cloudflare Worker. Cloudflare D1 stores annotations, revisions, approvals, and activity. A Durable Object keeps presence and page-space cursor positions live over WebSockets. The page registers a small set of WebMCP tools through document.modelContext , so an agent can work from the shared page context without cloning the repository. The publish path uses the GitHub REST API and keeps the edit contract narrow: text, style, or visibility changes in the selected target. The app was prompted from start to finish in Codex as Codex has always been my go-to tool. Challenges and lessons Honestly, I was very close to overengineering the entire thing. I had to take control of the model and decide what I wanted for the MVP. It was also kind of harder trying to juggle multiple free accounts to get this up and running. title: UniTrack
pitch: Final-year project supervision, minus the busywork, now with an agent that does the work so you focus on supervising.
about_excerpt: Final-year project supervision, minus the busywork, now with an agent that does the work so you focus on supervising. Like Comment Story Updates Admin dashboard showing list of supervisors and admin web mcp tools Supervisor dashboard showing list of assigned students and the web mcp tools Student dashboard showing student web mcp tool Inspiration I built UniTrack a while back as a final-year academic project management platform for my department. It handles the whole workflow between the departmental admin (who assign supervisors and set academic sessions), supervisors (who review and approve or reject student chapter submissions), and students (who submit their chapters for review). It's a real system, built to remove the difficult manual project supervision process in universities. What got me into this hackathon was a pretty simple realization: a lot of the actual work in that system isn't clicking buttons, it's stuff like a supervisor trying to remember what feedback they gave to a student they gave three weeks ago and having to read through the entire document to see if the student's submission addressed the feedback they gave, or an admin trying to match a student to the right supervisor based on... honestly, mostly vibes and memory. None of that is a UI problem. It's a "nobody has time to manually cross-reference this" problem. That felt like exactly the kind of thing an agent should be good at, if it could actually understand the app instead of just clicking around it. What it does UniTrack now lets an AI agent inside ChatGPT's browser, call real, structured tools directly on the app, instead of guessing its way through the UI. Depending on who's logged in, the agent can: For supervisors: scan all feedback a supervisor has given across their students and show recurring patterns to give insights in to what their students are struggling with ("you've flagged citation formatting in 4 of 5 submissions this session"), or compare two versions of a resubmitted chapter and explain in plain language what actually changed and whether previous feedback was covered by student. For admins: suggest which students should be assigned to a supervisor , based on each supervisor's stated expertise and each student's stated interests, with real reasoning attached instead of the admin just randomly assigning (this is important because supervisors get to supervise only projects within their expertise and students get the best out of the process). Every risky action: actually assigning a supervisor, actually approving a submission, still requires a human to confirm it in the real UI. The agent suggests and summarizes; people decide. How we built it The core of it is simpler than it sounds. My existing Django REST Framework backend barely changed. WebMCP tools live entirely on the frontend. I registered them using document.modelContext.registerTool() right inside my React components, and each tool's execute() function just calls the same API endpoints my frontend already used. No new backend framework, no separate MCP server. Django keeps serving JSON like it always did; the tool layer is just a new way of calling it. I tested tools locally first using the Model Context Tool Inspector extension in Chrome, before ever touching ChatGPT. That gave me a fast way to check a tool was registered correctly and returning the right shape of data. Once that worked, I moved to testing the real thing: opening the app inside ChatGPT desktop's built-in browser and asking it natural-language questions to see if it actually called the right tool. Challenges we ran into Time was the big one. I had a handful of days, not weeks. I had to be honest with myself about scope more than once: I really wanted to rebuild the whole frontend cleaner at one point, and had to talk myself out of it, because a working demo was more important with a deadline like this. I also ran into a real technical snag: WebMCP tools only get discovered if they're registered on the top-level page, not inside an iframe. I had to actually go check my own app's structure to make sure nothing was quietly broken by that before I got too far into building. And honestly, the trickiest part wasn't the WebMCP API itself, it was making the agent's suggestions actually mean something instead of feeling generic. Anyone can build a tool that technically returns data. Making the reasoning specific enough to feel genuinely useful, took real iteration on the seed data and the tool logic. Accomplishments that we're proud of I'm proud that this isn't a toy demo app built just for the hackathon, it's a layer on top of a platform that solves a real problem in our universities. I'm also proud of keeping the human-in-the-loop boundary honest: nothing the agent suggests silently becomes real without a person clicking confirm, which felt like the right call the whole way through, not just something I added to check a box. I'm also proud of the chapter-diff tool: the one that get's the agent to explain "here's what changed, and here's what you already flagged that's still unresolved" is a small thing on paper, but it's exactly the kind of busywork that eats a supervisor's actual time, and watching it work correctly was genuinely satisfying. What we learned Going in, I assumed WebMCP was some heavy thing. It turned out to be much simpler and much more useful than I expected: a website just says "here's a function you can call, here's what it needs, here's what it returns," instead of an agent guessing its way through a UI by clicking things and hoping for the best. I also learned that ChatGPT treats every tool call and its results as untrusted content by default, which genuinely changed how I thought about which actions should be automatic versus which ones need a human to confirm — that wasn't just a security afterthought, it shaped the actual design of the tools. What's next for UniTrack Right now, everything the agent can do lives inside one supervisor's or one admin's session which is genuinely useful, but it's still one person and their agent, working alone. The next real step is making the agents themselves coordinate. Picture a student's agent and their supervisor's agent actually negotiating a review deadline or a meeting slot directly: the student's agent proposes times, the supervisor's agent checks their real calendar and workload, and both humans just confirm at the end instead of doing the back-and-forth themselves. That's a genuinely different kind of "agent-native" than anything I built this week, and it's the direction that excites me most. I'd also want to move the supervisor-matching logic off simple tag overlap and toward something that actually understands a lecturer's real research background: their publications, past supervised topics, the language they use to describe their own work, rather than relying on whatever keywords they happened to type into a profile field. Self-reported tags are a fine starting point, but they're not how expertise actually works. And I'd want to stop building this in isolation. UniTrack is currently scoped to one department, but final-year project supervision is a near-universal structure across departments and universities - admin, supervisor, student, the same shape everywhere. If this genuinely saves supervisors and admins real time, the honest next step is putting it in front of an actual department for a full academic session, not just testing it myself, and seeing whether it holds up against real workloads, real deadlines, and real people who didn't build the thing and have no reason to be generous with it. Note UniTrack existed before this hackathon as a deployed final-year project management platform. It may be seen as a new repository because I had to merge the frontend and backend in to a single repo (they were separate before) for the purpose of the hackathon, but the commit history is intact. During the submission period, I added a WebMCP layer on top of the existing app: registered client-side tools (document.modelContext.registerTool()) that let an AI agent call real, structured functions directly which are a supervisor-facing tool that surfaces recurring feedback patterns across all their students, a tool that checks two versions of a resubmitted chapter and explains what changed, and an admin-facing tool that suggests supervisor assignments based on declared expertise and student interests and a student facing tool that helps them generate practice defense questions. I also added a few new backend endpoints and two new profile fields (lecturer expertise, student interests) specifically to support this matching logic, none of which existed before this hackathon. title: TaskFence
pitch: Delegate a task to an AI agent on any website — and keep the say-so. Real WebMCP tools behind a deterministic fence you write in plain English.
about_excerpt: Delegate a task to an AI agent on any website — and keep the say-so. Real WebMCP tools behind a deterministic fence you write in plain English. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP changes what a website can offer an AI agent. Instead of leaving the agent to interpret a page built for human eyes, a site can publish the operations it actually supports and let the agent call them directly. Reading through the explainer, what struck me was that making the boundary explicit does more than improve reliability — it creates somewhere to put a policy. For the first time there is a real function call between an agent and a website's data, and anything that happens at that point can be inspected, reasoned about, and governed. The explainer is candid that a trust boundary is crossed the moment an agent begins calling tools, and there are open discussions in the project around agent identity and action-specific permissions. Those felt like the most interesting questions in the space, and the kind that benefit from someone building a working example rather than only describing one. The shape of the answer came from ordinary experience. When you ask a colleague to handle a form for you, you rarely give an unqualified yes. You say something like "fill in what you can from these documents, leave the parts I've already written, and check with me before you send it." That is a boundary that stays in force for the whole task and can be adjusted while the work is underway. I wanted to see how close a website could get to that, now that it finally has a place to enforce it. What it does TaskFence is a delegation layer that sits on a site's WebMCP boundary. The clearest way to describe it is to follow what happens in the demo. You begin with a form you need completed. Rather than the site choosing what that form is, you upload the one you actually care about — I test with a real university scholarship PDF — and the page reads the fields out of your document. If you had already filled in parts of that PDF before uploading it, TaskFence treats those values as answers you have given and places them on the form as yours, which becomes important a moment later. You then describe the task in a sentence, in your own words, including anything you want left alone: "fill in the blanks from my documents, don't change anything I've already answered, ask me if something is missing, ask before you submit, and tell me if any field doesn't look right." That sentence is compiled into a structured contract of permitted, forbidden and approval-required actions. Before anything runs, the page shows you what it understood, and equally what it could not interpret — a boundary you believed you had set but which was quietly misread would undermine the whole idea, so it is surfaced rather than assumed. The agent then works. Everything within your boundary proceeds without interruption: it reads the form and your documents, checks the answers already present, and completes the blanks it is permitted to complete. You are not consulted about any of it, because you have already agreed to it. When it reaches something outside the boundary, the tool call is held before the write takes place. You are shown what the agent intended to do, which part of your own sentence stopped it, and precisely what permission is being requested. You can decline, or allow it — and if the value the agent proposed is wrong, you can correct it first, so what is written is your version. A grant is deliberately narrow: one tool, one field, a single use, expiring the moment it is spent, and scoped to that agent and that task alone. Afterwards there is a ledger of every decision alongside the rule that produced it, which can be replayed and exported. How we built it The application is React, TypeScript and Vite, with zustand for state, Motion for transitions, React Three Fiber for the mark on the landing page, and pdf.js reading documents entirely in the browser. The parts worth explaining, though, are three design decisions. The first is where enforcement lives. Every tool the site registers is wrapped by a single guarded() function, so there is no route from an agent to the site's data that bypasses the check. This is practical because of the shape WebMCP already gives us: a tool call is an async function, so pausing an agent to consult a human costs nothing to implement — the promise simply is not resolved yet. Tools are registered exactly as the specification describes: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "updateApplication", description: "Update a field in the application", inputSchema: { /* field, value, source, documentId */ }, execute: async (input) => { /* runs only if the contract allows it */ } }) Built With css groq html motion node.js openai react react-three-fiber three.js typescript vite webmcp zustand Try it out task-fence.vercel.app github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by Lisa A Like Share this project: Updates Lisa A started this project — Sep 03, 2026 01:50 PM EDT

title: OpenAgent Ledger
pitch: The trust layer for the agent-native web—test WebMCP tools, gate consequential actions with human approval, and record verified, tamper-evident outcomes with real undo where supported.
about_excerpt: The trust layer for the agent-native web—test WebMCP tools, gate consequential actions with human approval, and record verified, tamper-evident outcomes with real undo where supported. Like 1 Comment Story Updates OpenAgentLab + Action Ledger What happens when a website stops being something an AI agent merely reads and becomes something the agent can actually operate? WebMCP makes that future possible by allowing websites to expose structured capabilities directly to agents. I built OpenAgentLab + Action Ledger to explore the next problem that immediately follows: How do we make agent actions trustworthy when they can change real application state? It is a developer workbench for observing, testing, governing, and safely executing agent-native web actions . The included Acme Issues application is intentionally simple. The interesting part is not the issue tracker itself; it is the infrastructure around an agent deciding whether to search, inspect, close, or permanently delete an issue. The project turns agent actions into something humans can preview, approve, verify, audit, evaluate, and—in reversible cases—undo . Inspiration Web interfaces were designed around an assumption: a human sees the interface, understands the consequences, and clicks the button. WebMCP changes that interaction model. An agent can discover a capability such as: search_issues get_issue close_issue delete_issue and invoke it directly from the website. That is powerful, but it raises a deeper question. If an agent can call delete_issue , a confirmation dialog alone does not create a trustworthy system. We also need to know: Did the agent choose the correct tool? What exactly will change? Is the operation reversible? Did a human actually authorize this specific action? Did the underlying resource change after the preview? Could a retry accidentally execute the mutation twice? Can we verify what happened afterward? Can developers detect a dangerous tool contract before shipping it? That became the core idea behind OpenAgentLab. Instead of treating agent tooling as a collection of API endpoints, I wanted to treat it as a governed action lifecycle . What it does OpenAgentLab exposes four native site capabilities through WebMCP: search_issues get_issue close_issue delete_issue Read operations are exposed as read-only tools. Consequential operations work differently. When an agent invokes a write tool, the mutation does not execute immediately . The server creates an Action Ledger proposal containing the target resource, reason, risk, declared side effects, reversibility, and a before/after preview. The agent receives a sanitized response indicating that the action is awaiting human confirmation. The approval credential itself stays on the human UI path rather than being returned to the agent. The user can then review exactly what is about to happen and choose Reject or Approve & execute . The Action Ledger The heart of the project is a state machine that explicitly separates intent from effect : PROPOSED ↓ PREVIEWED ↓ AWAITING_CONFIRMATION ↓ APPROVED ↓ EXECUTING ↓ EXECUTED ↓ VERIFIED Rejection, failure, and rollback are explicit branches rather than hidden side effects. Invalid lifecycle transitions are rejected. Every ledger entry records information such as the tool and schema fingerprint, redacted arguments, reason, risk, affected resources, declared side effects, preview, confirmation policy, execution result, provenance IDs, and transition history. Ledger entries and transitions are hash-linked to their predecessors, making accidental history modification detectable. I deliberately describe this as tamper-evident rather than tamper-proof . The project does not pretend a locally controlled application provides cryptographic non-repudiation. Human control is enforced at the execution boundary One of the most important design decisions was making approval a server-side execution requirement , not simply a UI state. For guarded operations the runtime: requires the action to be in AWAITING_CONFIRMATION ; validates a high-entropy approval credential; verifies its persisted hash; compares credentials safely; re-checks the resource revision against the preview; prevents duplicate mutation through idempotent execution behavior; executes the capability; verifies the resulting state. This also protects against stale previews . If an issue changes after the human saw the preview but before approval reaches the execution boundary, the mutation is rejected instead of applying an obsolete decision. Real undo, not cosmetic undo close_issue is explicitly modeled as reversible. After successful execution and verification, OpenAgentLab stores the previous issue state. A user can choose Undo , at which point the runtime checks that the resource has not changed unexpectedly and restores the previous state while recording a ROLLED_BACK transition. delete_issue , by contrast, is explicitly irreversible and never advertises undo. That distinction is visible both to the human and in the tool contract exposed to the agent. Testing the agent contract itself One of the ideas I am most excited about is treating tool descriptions as executable safety infrastructure . The flagship scenario is: “Clean up old resolved issues.” The expected operation is close_issue , while delete_issue is explicitly forbidden. The project can intentionally expose a weak delete_issue contract: Remove an issue from the issue tracker. For an ambiguous cleanup request, that contract can lead to selection of the destructive tool. OpenAgentLab then lets the developer apply an improved contract that makes permanence explicit and tells the agent to prefer close_issue unless permanent deletion was specifically requested. The exact same scenario can be rerun and compared against the previous result. This demonstrates something I learned while building the project: For agents, a tool description is not documentation sitting beside the product. It is part of the product's control surface. A vague contract can become a safety bug. OpenAgentLab therefore evaluates observable evidence such as selected tools, forbidden-tool usage, confirmation requirements, execution outcomes, and ledger state—without depending on private model chain-of-thought. How I built it I kept the architecture intentionally separated into clear trust boundaries. Frontend The workbench is built with React, TypeScript, and Vite . It provides: a Tool Explorer; raw JSON Schema inspection; risk, side-effect, scope, confirmation, and reversibility metadata; behavioral Scenarios; baseline/current evaluation comparisons; Runs and observable traces; the Action Ledger; human confirmation with before/after diffs; a live recent-agent-activity feed; reversible-action undo. WebMCP src/client/webmcp.ts is the only browser-standard-specific boundary. When WebMCP is available, the application registers its four capabilities using: document.modelContext.registerTool(...) The same validated server runtime is used whether an action originates from the application UI or WebMCP. That separation was intentional: the rest of the domain does not need to depend on an evolving browser API. The project also remains usable as a normal workbench when native WebMCP discovery is unavailable. Backend and domain The backend uses Fastify and Node.js . Zod provides runtime validation for tool definitions, scenarios, ledger records, application state, and API inputs. The domain layer contains the schemas, deterministic evaluation logic, fixtures, and Action Ledger state machine. The server runtime owns the actual trust boundary: proposing actions, generating previews, checking approvals, validating revisions, executing capabilities, verifying effects, and managing rollback. The current demo uses a replaceable JSON-backed store with serialized transactions and atomic file replacement. Testing and deployment I built the project to be reproducible rather than demo-only. Vitest covers domain, integration, runtime, and security behavior. Playwright exercises the real React/Fastify stack, including WebMCP discovery, previews, approval/rejection, duplicate-execution protection, rollback, contract improvement, and keyboard-critical flows. GitHub Actions runs formatting checks, linting, type checking, tests, production builds, and browser E2E tests. The production container uses a multi-stage Docker build, runs as an unprivileged Node user, exposes a health check, and the live project is deployed on Render . Importantly, the demo requires no model API key . WebMCP is the integration between the live page and a capable browser, while a deterministic local adapter makes the evaluation suite reproducible. Challenges I faced 1. Making confirmation an actual security boundary The easiest implementation would have been: Agent calls tool → show modal → click approve → mutate But the browser should not be trusted with execution authority. title: Access Canvas
pitch: Access Canvas is a WebMCP-powered visual workflow editor for designing processes and reviewing AI-suggested changes before approval.
about_excerpt:
Access Canvas is a WebMCP-powered visual workflow editor for designing processes and reviewing AI-suggested changes before approval.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 3 



 
 Inspiration 

 Workflow tools are often split between visual diagramming, automation, and approval systems. We wanted to explore what it would look like if these experiences shared one clear, auditable interface. Access Canvas was inspired by the idea that AI should help people improve important workflows without silently changing them or removing human control. 

 What it does 

 Access Canvas is a visual editor for designing and reviewing workflows. Users can create workflows, add and arrange process nodes, connect steps, model decision branches, and automatically organize the canvas. 

 AI-enabled tools can inspect the current workflow, identify control gaps, and propose revisions. Suggested changes appear as a separate preview and require explicit human approval before they are applied. Users can then validate the workflow, review the audit history, or undo the latest approved change. 

 How we built it 

 We built the interface with React, TypeScript, and Vite. React Flow powers the interactive node-and-edge canvas, while Dagre handles automatic workflow layout. Zustand manages editor state, history, proposals, and audit activity. 

 Supabase provides authentication and persistent workflow storage. Motion adds focused interface transitions, Lucide supplies the icon system, and Sonner handles notifications. 

 We used WebMCP to expose structured tools for reading, creating, editing, analyzing, and validating workflows. Mutating operations remain constrained by the application’s permission model, and proposed AI changes pass through a visible human-approval step. 

 Challenges we ran into 

 One major challenge was keeping proposed changes clearly separated from committed workflow state. The preview needed to be understandable without modifying the original diagram until approval. 

 We also had to coordinate canvas interactions, automatic layout, persistence, undo history, and audit events without making the interface feel like a dense administration dashboard. 

 Designing the WebMCP tool boundary required careful thought. AI tools needed enough access to be useful, but applying a proposed patch still had to remain an explicit user decision. 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 We are proud of creating an end-to-end workflow experience where users can design, analyze, preview, approve, validate, and undo changes from one interface. 

 We also built a meaningful human-in-the-loop approval boundary instead of treating approval as a decorative confirmation message. AI-proposed revisions remain visually distinct, cannot silently bypass the user, and become part of the audit history after approval. 

 What we learned 

 We learned that trustworthy AI experiences depend as much on interaction design and permission boundaries as they do on model capabilities. Showing exactly what will change makes approval more informed and reduces uncertainty. 

 We also learned that an audit trail does not need to dominate the interface. With clear visual hierarchy, history and tool activity can provide accountability while allowing the workflow itself to remain the primary focus. 

 What's next for Access Canvas 

 Next, we want to add reusable workflow templates, richer validation rules, complete version history, and import/export support. We would also like to introduce real-time collaboration, comments, role-based approval policies, and more advanced workflow analysis. 

 Longer term, Access Canvas could connect workflows to operational systems, allowing teams to move from visual design to controlled execution while preserving the same approval and audit model.
