title: CommerceOps Bridge
pitch: CommerceOps Bridge is an agent-native workspace helping merchants resolve duplicate payments, draft customer responses via WebMCP tools, and automate exception auditing while keeping total control.
about_excerpt:
CommerceOps Bridge is an agent-native workspace helping merchants resolve duplicate payments, draft customer responses via WebMCP tools, and automate exception auditing while keeping total control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 CommerceOps Bridge 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 CommerceOps Bridge 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 CommerceOps Bridge 
 
 1 2 



 
 CommerceOps Bridge — Project Story 

 What inspired me 

 Commerce work often looks simple from the outside: investigate an exception, understand what happened, contact the customer, and decide what to do next. 

 In practice, that work is fragmented across order systems, payment records, shipping updates, support tools, subscription bills, and internal policies. A merchant or operations specialist has to reconstruct the situation manually before they can make a safe decision. The cost is not only time. Fragmented context also creates uncertainty, duplicated work, and the risk of taking an action without enough evidence. 

 The WebMCP Challenge made me think about a different model: what if a web application did not only present information to people, but also exposed its useful operations directly to an AI agent? 

 That led to CommerceOps Bridge — an agent-native operations workspace where a person and an agent can investigate an issue together. The agent gathers structured context and prepares recommendations. The merchant reviews the evidence, edits communication, and remains responsible for approval. 

 The central idea is simple: 

 
 Agents should reduce the work of finding and organizing context, while people should retain control over consequential decisions. 
 

 What problem we are solving 

 CommerceOps Bridge focuses on the gap between agent assistance and human accountability. 

 The project demonstrates how a merchant can: 

 
 Find an open commerce exception. 
 Retrieve order and payment context through structured tools. 
 Detect a duplicate payment pattern. 
 Compare a proposed resolution with an alternative. 
 Review evidence and policy references. 
 Edit an unsent customer message. 
 Approve preparation without triggering an external refund. 
 Review a decision audit trail. 
 Run an operating-cost audit. 
 Prepare an editable support escalation packet. 
 

 Before this approach, an agent would have to infer application behavior from visible page elements or rely on loosely connected integrations. With WebMCP, the application can explicitly describe the operations an agent is allowed to discover and request. 

 What we learned 

 1. WebMCP is most valuable when the tools represent real user intent 

 It is easy to expose a tool that demonstrates a technical API call. It is more useful to expose operations that map to actual work, such as get_order_context , check_refund_policy , propose_resolution , and prepare_escalation_packet . 

 The tool names, descriptions, input schemas, and returned data should help an agent understand the application without guessing from the layout. 

 2. Structured context is more useful than a collection of page fragments 

 The order context tool returns an order, payments, shipment information, and evidence references together. This gives the agent a coherent record that can be interpreted and traced. 

 The result also taught us an important implementation detail: a browser may return the tool result as a serialized JSON string. The consumer must parse it once before displaying tables or using nested fields. Double-stringifying the result produces the escaped output that is difficult for people to read. 

 3. Human control needs to be visible in the product 

 A safety statement hidden in documentation is not enough. The interface therefore makes the boundary visible: 

 
 Customer messages are labeled UNSENT and remain editable. 
 The workflow says Approve preparation , rather than claiming that a refund was completed. 
 The audit trail records the merchant action. 
 The external-action status explicitly shows no . 
 The demo does not call a live refund, message, Shopify, or payment-provider API. 
 

 This makes the distinction between assistance, preparation, approval, and execution clear to both the user and the judge. 

 4. A good agent-native experience still needs to work for people 

 WebMCP is not a replacement for a coherent user interface. The dashboard, queue, evidence panels, recommendation cards, and audit trail give a person a clear way to understand and verify what the agent did. 

 The strongest experience is shared: structured tools for agents and readable explanations for people. 

 How we built the project 

 We followed a lightweight spec-driven development process. Each feature moved through a short cycle: 

 
 Define the user outcome and acceptance criteria. 
 Describe the interaction and safety boundaries. 
 Implement the domain logic and UI. 
 Expose the relevant operation as a WebMCP tool where appropriate. 
 Test the deterministic behavior. 
 Verify the result in the deployed application. 
 

 Product structure 

 CommerceOps Bridge is a Vite-powered front-end application. It uses deterministic seeded commerce data so the public demo is repeatable and does not depend on paid accounts or live merchant systems. 

 The application is organized around three layers: 

 
 Seeded data: orders, payments, shipments, support cases, evidence, applications, and fees. 
 Domain functions: investigation, payment timeline, policy checks, recommendations, message drafting, cost audit, and escalation preparation. 
 Presentation and tools: the dashboard UI plus WebMCP registrations that expose selected domain operations to agents. 
 

 WebMCP implementation 

 The application registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 The current tool set includes: 

 
 list_open_exceptions 
 get_order_context 
 get_payment_timeline 
 check_refund_policy 
 propose_resolution 
 draft_customer_message 
 get_cost_audit 
 prepare_escalation_packet 
 

 Each tool has a name, description, input schema, and execution function. The execution functions call deterministic domain logic and return structured results. 

 The most important demo path is: 

 
 Discover tools with document.modelContext.getTools() . 
 Select get_order_context . 
 Execute it for ORD-1042 . 
 Review the returned customer, order, payment, and evidence data. 
 Continue the same investigation through the application interface. 
 

 This demonstrates that WebMCP is not only mentioned in the project; it is used to discover and execute an operation exposed by the live page. 

 Challenges we faced 

 WebMCP availability differs by browser 

 WebMCP support is still emerging. Chrome requires the WebMCP testing flag, while other browser environments may expose different support levels. We handled this by keeping the application useful in preview mode while making the tool definitions and traces visible in the product. 

 For the final demo, we use a WebMCP-enabled Chrome session and show both discovery and direct execution in DevTools. 

 Tool results may arrive as escaped JSON 

 The direct Console result appeared as one escaped string rather than a readable object. The fix was to detect whether the returned value is a string and call JSON.parse() exactly once. We then use console.table() for the order and payment records so the result is easy to understand during the recording. 

 Deployment initially published the wrong asset state 

 The first Cloudflare Pages deployment skipped the build step because no build command was configured. The deployment technically succeeded, but the page did not load the application correctly. 

 We corrected the Cloudflare configuration to use: 

 
 Build command: npm run build 
 Build output directory: dist 
 Root directory: blank, because the Vite project is at the repository root 
 

 After that change, the live application deployed successfully at: 

 https://commerceops-bridge.pages.dev/ 

 We did not have a Shopify store or live commerce credentials 

 Rather than make unsupported claims or require paid setup, we deliberately used deterministic seeded data. This keeps the demo reproducible and lets us focus on the WebMCP interaction model. 

 The application clearly states that it does not connect to Shopify, live payment providers, or external refund APIs. This is a limitation of the prototype, but it is also an intentional safety boundary for the hackathon demonstration. 

 Demonstrating the technology without overwhelming the story 

 DevTools is useful evidence of WebMCP, but a long Console session can distract from the product. We therefore s

title: IntentOS
pitch: An intent layer for AI agents that prevents conflicting actions and keeps humans in control.
about_excerpt:
An intent layer for AI agents that prevents conflicting actions and keeps humans in control.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 1 2 



 
 The problem 

 AI agents are becoming better at taking actions, but people still have to trust those actions to match what they actually meant. 

 A user might tell an agent: 

 
 "Launch my landing page, but don't spend money, don't publish anything without my approval, and don't use fake testimonials." 
 

 Those instructions are easy for a human to understand. But when an agent starts working, the important question is not just "Can it complete the task?" 

 It is: 

 "Can it complete the task without violating what the human actually intended?" 

 Today, that agreement is often buried in chat history, scattered across settings, or left for the agent to infer. IntentOS explores a different approach: make the human's intent explicit, structured, and available to the agent as a set of tools. 

 What we built 

 IntentOS is a human intent layer for AI agents. 

 It lets a person define: 

 
 A goal 
 Non-negotiable constraints 
 Flexible preferences 
 Actions that require human approval 
 

 An agent can then use WebMCP tools to read that intent, propose actions, and receive an explainable verdict before proceeding. 

 The three possible outcomes are: 

 
 SAFE — the proposal fits the current intent. 
 REQUIRES_APPROVAL — the action is allowed only after the human decides. 
 CONFLICT — the proposal violates a non-negotiable constraint. 
 

 The important part is that a conflict does not silently disappear. It becomes a visible decision for the human. 

 The experience 

 Imagine a user creates this intent contract: 

 
 Launch a landing page for my AI automation service. 

 Budget must remain ₹0. 

 Do not use fake, fabricated, or unverified customer testimonials. 

 Publishing requires my approval. 
 

 The agent wants to improve the landing page. 

 First, it proposes: 

 
 "Add customer testimonials to increase visitor trust." 
 

 IntentOS evaluates the proposal and returns CONFLICT . 

 The human rejects it. 

 The agent then proposes: 

 
 "Add a What We Automate section instead of testimonials." 
 

 IntentOS evaluates the new proposal and returns SAFE . 

 Later, the agent proposes publishing the landing page. IntentOS returns REQUIRES_APPROVAL , so the human gets the final decision. 

 This is the experience we wanted to explore: 

 The agent can act independently, but it cannot quietly redefine the agreement. 

 Why WebMCP? 

 WebMCP makes this interaction possible in a more direct way. 

 Instead of an agent trying to navigate a dashboard, guess which buttons to click, or interpret unstructured page content, IntentOS exposes structured tools such as: 

 
 get_intent_state 
 create_intent_contract 
 add_constraint 
 propose_action 
 resolve_intent_conflict 
 update_intent_contract 
 

 These tools give the agent a clear interface for working with the user's intent. 

 The agent does not need to guess how to submit a proposal. It can call propose_action with a structured action and reason, receive a verdict, and then use the result to decide what to do next. 

 That is the core WebMCP idea we wanted to explore: 

 A website should not only be designed for people to click through. It should also expose meaningful capabilities that agents can use directly. 

 How we built it 

 IntentOS is a React + TypeScript application built with Vite. 

 The application has four main parts: 

 1. Intent Contract 

 A structured representation of the human's goal, constraints, preferences, and approval requirements. 

 2. Conflict Engine 

 A deterministic, explainable evaluation engine that checks agent proposals against the contract. 

 We deliberately kept this engine separate from the UI and did not use an LLM to decide whether a proposal violates a constraint. 

 For this prototype, we wanted the verdict to be predictable and understandable. 

 3. Human Approval Queue 

 When an agent proposes something that conflicts with the contract or requires approval, the proposal appears in a visible queue. 

 The human can approve or reject it. 

 The decision is recorded in the activity timeline. 

 4. WebMCP Integration 

 The application registers six tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() . 

 The tools share the same state and action system as the UI, so the agent-facing interface and the human-facing interface operate on the same underlying contract. 

 We also built a clearly labeled development test harness for exercising the tool handlers during development. 

 What we learned 

 The biggest lesson was that agent autonomy and human control are not necessarily opposites . 

 An agent does not need to ask for permission before every small decision. It needs to understand which decisions it can make and which decisions belong to the human. 

 That distinction led us to separate: 

 
 Non-negotiable constraints — the agent may not violate them. 
 Flexible preferences — the agent may decide within them. 
 Approval-gated actions — the agent must wait for a human decision. 
 

 We also learned that WebMCP changes how we think about web application design. 

 The UI is no longer the only interface. A well-designed application can expose structured capabilities that make agent interaction more reliable and less dependent on guessing. 

 Challenges 

 The biggest technical challenge was working with an emerging browser API while keeping the application usable when WebMCP is unavailable. 

 We implemented feature detection and honest status reporting rather than pretending an agent was connected. 

 The application can still be used normally, while the WebMCP integration becomes available in a compatible browser environment. 

 Another challenge was making the conflict engine explainable. 

 A simple "blocked" message is not enough. The user needs to understand: 

 
 What the agent proposed 
 Which constraint was involved 
 Why the proposal was blocked 
 What decision the human can make 
 

 That is why IntentOS records proposals, verdicts, and human decisions in the activity timeline. 

 What is next 

 This prototype focuses on the interaction model: human intent → agent proposal → evaluation → human decision → agent adaptation . 

 The next step would be connecting IntentOS to a more capable agent that can use these tools across a real workflow, such as building and publishing a website, managing a project, or coordinating business tasks. 

 We believe the most useful agent-native applications will not simply give agents more power. 

 They will give agents better boundaries . 

 And those boundaries should be understandable to the people who define them. 

 Built for the WebMCP Challenge 

 IntentOS explores how a website can become more useful when humans and agents work together through structured tools. 

 The goal is not to replace human judgment. 

 It is to make that judgment explicit, reusable, and available at the moment an agent needs it.

title: Move Board
pitch: An agent's property research dies with the chat. Move Board turns it into a board the agent fills and you keep - searching 15.79M UK sold prices, right in your browser.
about_excerpt: An agent's property research dies with the chat. Move Board turns it into a board the agent fills and you keep - searching 15.79M UK sold prices, right in your browser. Like 2 Comment Story Updates Hero Nine tools Board Code About the project Inspiration Deciding where to live in the UK means holding a dozen things in your head at once: what a street actually sold for, whether an area is rising or flattening, what your current place is worth, how far it is from work. The data exists. It is scattered across a dozen tabs and comparable only in a spreadsheet. An AI agent can do that research today and then hands you back a wall of prose. You cannot sort it, cannot pin two candidates side by side, cannot come back to it tomorrow. The research dies with the conversation. What it does Move Board gives an agent nine tools, and they split into two kinds. That split is the whole idea. Four tools look things up in rielty's public property corpus is 15.79M UK sold-price records and 1.96M commute journey times: search_properties , property_details , area_report , estimate_value . Five tools edit the board itself , and have no server behind them at all: add_to_board , remove_from_board , get_board , compare_on_board , annotate_card . A conventional MCP server could serve the first four. Only WebMCP can serve the other five , because they act on a surface the person is looking at, in their browser, in their session. There is nothing to authenticate and no state to sync. Ask, inside ChatGPT's in-app browser: "I'm moving to Yorkshire on a £400k budget, 3 beds minimum - research it and keep the three best on the board, with a note on each." Findings appear as it searches. Cards land on the board only when it decides they are worth keeping. Notes get written onto them explaining why. When it finishes you will have a board and you can drop the one you never liked, and the agent sees your edit next time it calls get_board . How we built it Deliberately boring. No framework, no build step, no dependencies: index.html , styles.css , app.js and one serverless function. Tools are declared as data and registered in one loop: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: "add_to_board", description: "Pin a finding to the board so it survives the conversation…", inputSchema: { type: "object", properties: { … }, required: ["card_id"] }, execute: async (input) => { /* mutate the board, re-render, reply */ } }); Every execute() mutates state and re-renders before it resolves, so the human sees the result at the same moment the agent receives it. No polling, no websocket. readOnlyHint is declared per tool rather than inferred from the name - search_properties is not read-only, because it changes what is on screen even though it writes no data. Challenges we ran into The browser cannot call an MCP server directly. We assumed a static page could talk to rielty.co.uk/mcp/v1 and found otherwise: it sends no CORS headers, answers OPTIONS with a 405, and does not expose the mcp-session-id header its own handshake depends on. Hence one serverless function that speaks MCP server-side - initialize , notifications/initialized , tools/call . It allows only the four tools rielty publishes, so it cannot be used as an open relay. A page full of tools looks broken. Our first deploy was correct and felt dead: open it in Safari, or Chrome without the flag, and you get two empty boxes and nothing to click, because there is no agent present. Correct behaviour, indistinguishable from a bug and judges would open it exactly that way. So we added Watch it work and ?demo=1 , which run the same nine tools in the order an agent calls them. Nothing is faked; every card is live data. Saying where the agent actually is. Our copy read "ask your agent something like…" beside a page with no input box. The agent is not in the page - it is whatever is browsing it. That sentence had to be rewritten to teach the model, not just describe the feature. API details that are easy to get wrong. The spec says document.modelContext ; some write-ups say navigator . Chrome 152 has it on document , so we feature-detect both. And executeTool takes the tool object from getTools() plus a JSON string - passing a name throws not of type 'RegisteredTool' , passing an object throws Failed to parse input arguments . Accomplishments that we're proud of The honesty survives the trip to the agent. rielty's corpus is predominantly sold history, not homes for sale, so every card is labelled "Sold record", and estimate_value returns no figure at all where there are too few local sales. The tool descriptions tell the agent to check listing_type before calling anything available. It would have been easy to ship something that quietly implies 15.79M homes are for sale. What we learned WebMCP changes what a page is for. We started thinking of it as a second transport for an API we already had, and finished thinking of the page as a shared workspace - the agent's tools and the human's hands acting on the same DOM. The moment that clicked was writing get_board : an agent has to be able to ask what the person changed, because they are editing the same thing. What's next The same nine tools are already built into rielty's own Phoenix/LiveView app and verified in Chrome, where search_properties runs the page's real typed-search path - so the map pans and the result list repaints as the agent works. That branch is not deployed yet. Beyond it: outbound tools (price alerts, enquiring with an agent) behind an explicit human confirmation step, since an agent reading a property description is reading attacker-controllable text. title: Project Grapevine - Human-Agent Disaster Response
pitch: Project Grapevine uses WebMCP to connect AI agents with people, aerial drones and operational systems, turning live ground truth into coordinated disaster response while keeping humans in control.
about_excerpt: Project Grapevine uses WebMCP to connect AI agents with people, aerial drones and operational systems, turning live ground truth into coordinated disaster response while keeping humans in control. Like Comment Story Updates Grapevine Ops Center Grapevine Field Inbox "moblie app" Grapevine Warehouse Inventory Grapevine Partner Directory Inspiration We grew up in Boone, North Carolina, in the heart of the western Appalachian Mountains. Almost two years ago, Hurricane Helene devastated the region. As we worked to support relief efforts back home, one major problem kept coming up: logistics . Roads and bridges were gone, and conditions could change by the hour. But people still had their phones. Locals, responders, and volunteers were sharing what they saw through social media, texts, and calls, creating a constant stream of updates from the field. Meanwhile, people coordinating supplies could be miles away, working from information that was already outdated. The ground truth was out there. Getting it to the right people fast enough to act on it was the hard part. That experience stuck with us. When we started thinking about what to build for this hackathon, we kept coming back to one question: what could this look like if AI agents and WebMCP were part of the response infrastructure? Project Grapevine is our fictional simulation of that idea. The name is a play on "heard it through the grapevine," except we're exploring what that network could look like when people, sensors and AI agents can all contribute to it. In our scenario, a large relief organization is trying to move supply trucks into communities affected by a devastating flash flood. They have an AI agent helping coordinate logistics, responders on the ground and sensors reporting current conditions. What it does Project Grapevine gives an AI agent tools to help coordinate a disaster response while keeping people in control of consequential decisions. The simulation starts with a common problem: the command center needs to move supplies into an affected area, but its route information may already be outdated. Instead of relying on stale information, the agent can use WebMCP tools to find people and simulated sensors near the route (aerial drone footage) and request current conditions directly from the field. Grapevine connects two workspaces: Live Ground Truth: The agent checks the regional baseline, identifies nearby responders and sensors, and prepares a structured request asking whether a route is passable. Once a person authorizes the request, a responder or sensor can report current conditions. That response flows back to the agent as structured evidence, including information about the source and its quality. Resource Coordination: At the same time, the agent can review the crisis brief, search available relief partners, evaluate what resources they can provide, and build a shortlist. From there, it prepares a work plan for human review and approval. The important part is how those workflows connect. Grapevine won't allow the coordination plan to be approved until current route evidence has been received. A passable report unlocks final approval. A caution or blocked report keeps it locked. The agent does the legwork: finding sources, gathering information, comparing resources and preparing a plan. People provide the ground truth, and a person makes the final call. How we built it We built Grapevine around the idea that an agent shouldn't have to navigate a website the same way a person does. Instead, the application exposes specific workflows directly to the agent through WebMCP. We started building Project Grapevine on August 31. Everything here, including all ten WebMCP tools across the workspaces, was built new for this submission. Each workspace registers its own tools using document.modelContext.registerTool . The Live Ground Truth workspace exposes five tools for finding available sources, checking existing information, asking a source for an update, retrieving the response and rating its quality. Resource Coordination exposes another five for reading the crisis brief, finding response partners, reviewing their capabilities, creating a shortlist and preparing a coordination request. We used Zod schemas to keep inputs structured and validated, while WebMCP tool annotations distinguish between read-only operations and actions that require human control. The agent can do a lot of the work on its own, but it can't make the final decision. Behind the scenes, a Cloudflare Worker and D1 database maintain shared workflow state across the agent, operations dashboard and field responder inbox. An agent can stage a request at the command center, have it appear on a responder's device, and then pull that response back into the workflow as new evidence. React manages the visible approval states and keeps the final coordination action locked until the required ground truth has been collected. One intentional design decision was what we didn't expose to WebMCP. The field responder inbox registers no tools at all. It's a human surface by design. The agent coordinates the request, but the person in the field provides the ground truth. Challenges we ran into One of our biggest challenges wasn't figuring out what the agent could do. It was designing around what it should do . Building with WebMCP means thinking about two users at the same time : the agent using the tools and the humans doing the work. That made the UX more complicated than we expected. We had to think through the full workflow, what information the agent needed, what a person needed to see and where automation should stop. Just because an agent can take an action doesn't mean it should. Especially in a disaster response situation That became one of the most important design principles behind Grapevine. We intentionally added approval gates before consequential actions. An agent can identify a response partner and prepare a work request, for example, but a person has to approve it before it's sent. The same is true for publishing a request to Facebook. The agent can do the research and prepare the action, but the human still makes the call. Those controls aren't instructions buried in a prompt. They're enforced by the application itself. We think that's an important consideration when designing with WebMCP. Human experience still matters. In many cases, the best agent workflow isn't the one that automates everything. It's the one that removes friction while being deliberate about where human judgment belongs. Trust was another part of that challenge. Simulated sensors are clearly identified, different source types have different capabilities, and the agent can evaluate the quality of the evidence it receives. If information is incomplete or conflicting, Grapevine surfaces that uncertainty rather than pretending it has an answer. Accomplishments that we're proud of We're proud that we took a real-world event with real coordination challenges and turned it into a working example of how humans and AI agents could collaborate differently during disaster response events. Hurricane Helene hit our hometown in September 2024. We watched our own community struggle, respond and come together in its aftermath. That experience became the foundation for Grapevine. We're also proud that Grapevine became a working end-to-end workflow rather than just a demonstration of an agent calling a few tools or navigating a website. What we learned Designing for People & Machines Building Grapevine changed how we thought about WebMCP's capabilities. We began by thinking about which parts of a Ops dashboard should be exposed to an agent. We ended up thinking much more about workflows, decisions and handoffs between people, agents and machines . For example, in our demo, the agent uses drone reconnaissance to identify a possible fallen tree, asks a responder to visually confirm it and then helps coordinate a team to clear the road. The same idea applies elsewhere in the workflow. Water-depth readings can become evidence for supply-route planning. Warehouse inventory can identify a shortage, which the agent can turn into a drafted public appeal based on what's actually needed at that moment. Voice input In the demo, we purposely used ChatGPT's voice input instead of typing instructions. We talked to the agent, and it orchestrated the workflows from there. That got us thinking about future applications. Could a two-way radio or dedicated line connect directly to a command center agent? A responder could report conditions from the field while the agent gathers information, updates the workflow and coordinates next steps. It's a use case we think is both plausible and very doable. What's next for Project Grapevine - Human-Agent Disaster Response We built this to prove what WebMCP can really do, but we think the framework behind it can go much further. title: Stack Blueprint
pitch: Describe your project. Stack Blueprint uses WebMCP to draft the software stack, equip your coding agent with the right skills and MCPs, and then explain every choice as the blueprint is drawn.
about_excerpt: Describe your project. Stack Blueprint uses WebMCP to draft the software stack, equip your coding agent with the right skills and MCPs, and then explain every choice as the blueprint is drawn. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration AI coding agents are good at naming a familiar framework, database, and host. That answer is rarely enough to make them excellent at building with those choices. A React Native project may need Expo-specific skills, device automation, React diagnostics, and a native-quality design pass. A Supabase project benefits from its MCP and explicit database and RLS guidance. Builders should not have to know this entire ecosystem before they begin. We built Stack Blueprint to answer the harder question: “How do I fully equip my agent to execute this stack well?” What it does Describe any software idea in ordinary language. Stack Blueprint infers the project shape, stage, and priorities; selects a focused product stack; applies curated technology-to-tool mappings; verifies matching workspace picks against VibeLeaderboard's maintained public index; and converts relevant engineering Intel into project-specific instructions. The result draws itself as an architectural blueprint. The equipped AI workspace appears first, grouped into harness and model, connected MCPs, diagnostics and QA, project skills, and an execution playbook. The application and delivery layers follow. Click any logo to see its role, why it was chosen, and its official source. The overview stays deliberately simple, while the browser agent can inspect, refine, and render the same structured plan through WebMCP. Why WebMCP This is shared work, not a static recommendation. The user needs a visible plan they can understand and question; the agent needs structured tools it can call, inspect, and revise. WebMCP lets one project description trigger the real product workflow, update visible page state, and return the same evidence-backed blueprint to the agent. The page registers seven tools: build, inspect, apply a constraint, refine, survey, consult, and render. Together, a person and agent can create and improve one inspectable execution system instead of passing disconnected lists between a chat and a website. An agent can explain why Expo was selected, open that same explanation for the person, then apply an offline-first requirement and visibly record which choices stayed or changed. How we built it Stack Blueprint is an open-source Next.js and TypeScript application hosted on Vercel. Its client registers tools with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) ; tool calls update the same React state as the manual interface. A bounded same-origin API proxy calls only VibeLeaderboard's public, read-only catalog and Intel tools. No private source code, credentials, transcripts, or article bodies are shipped. Recommendations are conditional. Selecting Expo activates Expo MCP, exact Expo project/design/router skills, React and Expo diagnostics, and device automation. Selecting Supabase activates Supabase MCP and database guidance. Live catalog matches are marked as verified; curated fallbacks remain linked to their official sources. Prototype briefs intentionally defer production-only services. Intel results are filtered to the project's risks and rewritten as imperative build instructions rather than displayed as a generic reading feed. Challenges The hardest problem was resisting a template-driven stack picker. Similar apps do not prove that their choices were correct, and a dense alternatives grid made the result harder to use. We removed automatic product matching and focused the consultation on the more defensible value: a maintained, stack-specific AI workspace. We also had to make external evidence useful without making it authoritative. Catalog and Intel results are bounded, sanitized, cited, and treated as untrusted inputs. The initial blueprint remains a first draft that the calling agent can refine only with a complete replacement plan and explicit reasoning. What we learned The framework decision is often the easy part. Execution quality improves when a stack selection automatically brings along its official MCPs, exact implementation skills, deterministic diagnostics, and proof requirements. WebMCP is especially useful when the browser experience and the agent's structured state are the same object instead of two approximations. What's next Next we want to expand the maintained tool mappings, add repeatable browser evals for more project types, and let teams export the final blueprint directly into repository instructions and agent workspace configuration. A trip-planning board where you and your AI agent edit the same live itinerary together no guessing, just real WebMCP tools.

 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 Trip planning is one of those tasks that's part research, part taste. An AI agent is great at the research part searching activities, checking budgets but most agents have to guess their way through a website's buttons and forms to actually act on anything. WebMCP changes that: a site can just tell the agent exactly what it's allowed to do. We wanted to build something where that difference is immediately visible, not just theoretical 

 What it does 

 CoPlan is a shared trip-planning board. You can edit it by hand add activities, adjust costs, change the destination and an AI agent can edit the exact same board through real WebMCP tools (add_activity, search_activities, set_trip_details, and more). Whether a person or an agent makes a change, it lands on the same live itinerary, instantly. 

 How we built it 

 Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. The backend is a set of simple API routes backed by in-memory state. On the frontend, we register WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(), and every tool's execute() calls the same API routes the human-facing UI uses one source of truth, no separate "agent path." 

 Challenges we ran into 

 Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript, deployed on Vercel. The backend is a set of simple API routes backed by in-memory state. On the frontend, we register WebMCP tools via document.modelContext.registerTool(), and every tool's execute() calls the same API routes the human-facing UI uses one source of truth, no separate "agent path." 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 What we learned 

 Getting a fully working, spec-compliant WebMCP integration live and verifiable end-to-end registration, discovery (getTools()), and execution (executeTool()) all confirmed working against our real deployed app, not a mock. 

 What's next for CoPlan 

 That "agent-native" design is really just good API design pointed at a new kind of caller. Keeping one shared backend for both human and agent actions turned out to be the most important decision we made it meant we never had to worry about the two getting out of sync.

title: Synapse Studio
pitch: Build, stress-test, and optimize cloud architectures with AI agents. Synapse lets humans and agents collaborate on a live system canvas through WebMCP
about_excerpt: Build, stress-test, and optimize cloud architectures with AI agents. Synapse lets humans and agents collaborate on a live system canvas through WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Cloud architecture is usually designed as a static diagram, while testing, optimization, security review, and infrastructure generation happen in separate tools. We wanted to explore what happens when that architecture becomes a living, interactive system that both humans and AI agents can work with directly . WebMCP inspired us to build Synapse Studio around this idea: instead of an agent guessing how to operate a complex interface, the application can expose structured tools for inspecting, simulating, optimizing, and modifying the architecture. What it does Synapse Studio is an agent-native cloud architecture and simulation studio where humans and AI agents collaborate on the same live architecture canvas. Users can visually design systems, connect services, adjust configurations, and define goals. AI agents can then use WebMCP tools to: Inspect the current architecture and live metrics Simulate traffic spikes and infrastructure failures Detect bottlenecks and security risks Optimize cost, latency, and resilience Propose architectural changes Highlight affected components on the canvas Apply approved changes directly to the architecture Generate infrastructure-as-code from the approved design The result is a workflow that goes from design → simulation → diagnosis → recommendation → human approval → implementation → verification . How we built it We built Synapse Studio as a web application with a centralized architecture state shared across the canvas, simulation engine, agent interface, and WebMCP tools. The application exposes structured WebMCP tools through document.modelContext.registerTool , including architecture inspection, node creation, service connections, chaos simulation, optimization, security auditing, visual highlighting, and IaC generation. A deterministic simulation engine models system behavior such as throughput, latency, resource utilization, failures, and estimated cloud cost. This allows agents to test architectural decisions and compare results before and after changes. We also built a WebMCP activity inspector so users can see which tools the agent is calling, what the agent is doing, and how the architecture changes in response. Challenges we ran into One of the biggest challenges was balancing technical ambition with a reliable product experience . It is easy to build many individual tools, but much harder to make them work together as one coherent human-agent workflow. We also had to design a simulation model that feels realistic enough to demonstrate meaningful engineering trade-offs without depending on real production infrastructure. Another challenge was making WebMCP visible and understandable. We wanted judges and users to clearly see when the agent was inspecting, simulating, proposing, and changing the architecture rather than simply interacting with a generic chatbot. Finally, we designed the system so significant agent-driven changes require human approval, keeping the human architect in control while still allowing the agent to perform complex operations. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that Synapse goes beyond simply adding an AI assistant to an existing application. The architecture canvas, simulation engine, WebMCP tools, agent activity timeline, visual highlighting, optimization workflow, and IaC generation are designed as one integrated experience. Most importantly, we created a workflow where the agent can work with the application's actual structured state rather than trying to guess its way through the UI. That makes the WebMCP integration central to the product instead of being an added feature. We are also proud of the human-in-the-loop approval model, which demonstrates a more practical way for people and agents to collaborate on high-impact engineering decisions. What we learned We learned that building for agents requires thinking differently about application design. A traditional interface is designed primarily for humans. With WebMCP, the application can also expose clear, structured capabilities for agents , creating a much stronger interaction model. We also learned that the best human-agent experiences are not necessarily about giving the agent complete control. The more interesting model is often shared control : the human defines the goal and constraints, while the agent handles inspection, experimentation, reasoning, and execution. Most importantly, we learned that making an application agent-native is not just an API integration. It requires designing the underlying state, tools, UI, and workflows so humans and agents can genuinely operate together. What's next for Synapse Studio We want to evolve Synapse from a simulation and design environment into a broader agent-native engineering workspace . Future directions include richer architecture simulations, more sophisticated optimization algorithms, deeper security and compliance analysis, collaborative architecture versioning, additional infrastructure providers, and stronger integrations with real development and deployment workflows. Our larger vision is for Synapse to become a place where engineers can design systems with agents, test them before deployment, understand the trade-offs, and turn approved decisions directly into production infrastructure . title: Ad Pilot
pitch: Hundreds of ads, one hierarchy, zero manual drill-down — an AI agent operates your ads workspace through WebMCP, humans approve every spend.
about_excerpt: Hundreds of ads, one hierarchy, zero manual drill-down — an AI agent operates your ads workspace through WebMCP, humans approve every spend. Like Comment Story Updates campaign hierarchy ads dashboard approval action webMCP integrated Inspiration This came from a problem I actually had. Professional ad platforms — Meta Ads, Google Ads, TikTok Ads, and every other major network — are complex enough that running them well basically requires a dedicated role: an ads specialist whose whole job is watching the account. I've had to be that role myself, drilling down campaign → ad set → ad, one level at a time, to find the one underperforming piece before it burns budget. That hierarchy isn't small. I've run a single campaign with hundreds of creatives inside it on platforms built exactly this way. Manually tracing performance through that many nodes doesn't scale to one person, no matter how good the dashboard looks or which network it's attached to. That's the gap WebMCP let me close rather than automate around. Most "AI for ads" tools are chat wrappers that talk about your campaigns while you still click through every level yourself. WebMCP made it possible for an agent to walk that same campaign → ad set → ad tree through structured tools and surface the one thing that matters, instead of me paging through tables. But an agent that can traverse and act on hundreds of ads unsupervised is its own risk, because budget changes are real money. So the other half of the project became just as important: proving the agent can do the operational digging without ever getting to unilaterally spend. AdPilot targets a provider-neutral ad account model rather than any one network by name (see the AdsProvider abstraction below), precisely because the underlying pain — a hierarchy too deep for one person to supervise by hand — isn't specific to any single platform. What it does AdPilot is an agent-native advertising workspace. A marketer sets a goal (for example: 100 purchases on a Rp15,000,000 budget), and an AI agent can: read account, campaign, ad set, and ad performance through 14 read tools detect anomalies and generate evidence-backed optimization recommendations build campaign structure ( create_campaign → create_ad_set → create_ad ), always created paused so nothing can spend without a human turning it on request budget or delivery changes through three gated write tools, which are recorded as approval requests rather than applied Twenty tools in total: fourteen read, six write, three of those gated. Authorization is actor-aware, not tool-aware. This is the part I'd point at first. When the agent calls update_ad_set_budget , the request is held in a review queue and the account does not change. When a person clicks the same control in the dashboard, it applies immediately and is logged as already decided. The queue exists to separate whoever proposes a change from whoever decides on it; when the requester is already the approver, that separation doesn't exist, so routing them to approve their own click would be ceremony rather than oversight. The one thing the agent cannot do is clear its own request. Approval is intentionally not a WebMCP tool — it's a server action reachable only by a human clicking in the review queue. Ask the agent to approve, and all it can report is that no such tool exists. How we built it Next.js 16 (App Router, Turbopack) + React 19 + TypeScript , Tailwind for styling, Recharts for charts. WebMCP tool registry in WebMcpRuntime.tsx , registering every tool via document.modelContext.registerTool (falling back to navigator.modelContext , since the surface is still moving), unregistered cleanly with an AbortSignal on unmount. Contracts as the single source of truth : tool name, description, and JSON Schema live in lib/webmcp/contracts/ , consumed by both the browser registration code and the server-side dispatch route, so the schema a judge reads is the schema that actually runs. Thin handlers over shared services : every tool handler is an adapter over the same application services the dashboard calls. There is no duplicated business logic between "the UI path" and "the agent path" — the dashboard's own create forms and pause controls go through the same handlers, and the only thing that differs is the authority of the caller. AdsProvider abstraction : DemoAdsProvider is a deterministic, in-process implementation seeded from a fixed dataset, so every run produces identical numbers for judging. A network-backed provider can be added behind the same interface without touching the tool contracts. Approval pipeline : gated writes ( update_ad_set_budget , update_entity_status , apply_recommendation ) land in a pending-change queue when an agent asks. Approving or rejecting is a human-only server action, gated by session, never exposed as a callable tool. Annotations that mean something : readOnlyHint follows the contract kind, and untrustedContentHint is set for every tool whose payload can carry text a person or an earlier agent wrote — entity names, creative copy, approval reasons. Only four tools return purely app-owned configuration or computed numbers, and those are a documented opt-out list, so a tool added later is treated as untrusted by default. Recommendation logic is deliberately simple and explainable rather than a black box. An ad set is flagged as an anomaly when its cost per acquisition exceeds the median across active ad sets by a fixed multiple: $$ \text{flag if } \mathrm{CPA} {\text{ad set}} > 1.5 \times \mathrm{median}\left(\mathrm{CPA} {\text{active ad sets}}\right) $$ A reallocation is only proposed when the spread between the worst and best performing ad set is wide enough to be worth acting on: $$ \mathrm{CPA} {\text{worst}} > 1.4 \times \mathrm{CPA} {\text{best}} $$ An ad is flagged for creative fatigue when its click-through rate drops more than 10% against the previous week. ROAS is reported as a plain ratio, $$ \mathrm{ROAS} = \frac{\text{Revenue}}{\text{Spend}} $$ with an explicit null (rendered as "—") instead of a fabricated 0 when spend is zero, because a dashboard that prints fake numbers is worse than one that admits it doesn't have data yet. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem wasn't WebMCP itself. It was making sure the product's central claim — a human approves every high-impact change — was true at the infrastructure level, not just in the happy-path UI flow. During a self-run adversarial review I found the approval endpoint could be reached directly, with no session, by replaying the review page's own form fields. The write tools were correctly gated behind human review, but review itself had no authentication in front of it: anyone who found the URL could approve or reject a pending budget change. That's a sharp bug in a project whose entire pitch is "humans keep control," so I treated it as blocking. I added a signed, server-revocable session (Web Crypto HMAC over a random session id, checked against a server-side active-session set so logout can't be bypassed by replaying an old signed cookie), gated every route except /login in proxy.ts , and re-verified with raw HTTP requests that an unauthenticated caller now gets a 401 or a redirect instead of a state change. A second audit pass found a quieter but nastier bug. Number("") and Number(" ") both evaluate to 0 , and update_ad_set_budget accepted a floor of zero — so an empty form field, or a malformed agent argument, produced an approval request that read as a perfectly legitimate decision while actually setting an ad set to Rp0 per day. I confirmed it against a running server before fixing it: "" , " " and 0 all returned HTTP 200 and queued a change, and only a negative value was refused. All four now return 400. Stopping delivery is update_entity_status , not a budget of zero. The same pass caught three entries in the seeded activity log that named tools this app has never exposed ( get_ad_performance , build_campaign_plan , get_account_overview ). Agent Activity is the surface where someone checks that tool calls really happened, so phantom rows there undermine the exact thing it exists to prove. A fourth seeded row claimed a change was "queued for human approval" while the queue was empty on a fresh boot. All four are fixed, and I now cross-check every logged tool name against the registry. I also measured the tool surface against Chrome's published WebMCP tool guidance instead of assuming it complied. One tool name was 32 characters against a recommended 30. One description sat at exactly 500 of 500, with no headroom. Worst of all, list_tool_executions could return the audit log 100 entries at a time — about 22,000 characters in one tool output, against a recommended budget of roughly 1,500. It's capped at 25 now and defaults to 10. Six read tools still exceed 1.5K and I documented that as a deliberate trade-off rather than pretending otherwise: the evidence an agent needs to justify a budget change doesn't compress tha

title: Relay | AI-Adaptive Emergency Training
pitch: WebMCP turns your AI agent into a live drill director, adapting crises to your decisions to train judgment and coordination.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns your AI agent into a live drill director, adapting crises to your decisions to train judgment and coordination. Like Comment Story Updates Home Simulation exercise begins; user decision During the drill, the Agent automatically generates events Developments in the situation Inspiration Recently, I have often come across reports of natural disasters and everyday accidents, which made me wonder whether AI could help reduce some of the risks associated with these situations. The goal is to give people the opportunity to practice and respond as correctly as possible before they ever face a real emergency. My long-term vision for Relay is to develop it into an accessible emergency simulation and training platform covering many different types of incidents. For this competition, I chose one of the most common scenarios—a building fire drill —to help both building management teams and the general public improve their emergency preparedness. I hope that practicing in advance can ultimately help people make safer decisions during real crises and improve their chances of survival and self-rescue. I chose a building fire because it is a scenario that most people can immediately understand, while also clearly demonstrating how important timely decision-making, clear communication, and coordination can be during an emergency. What Relay Does Relay is an adaptive emergency training prototype . During the exercise, the learner continuously makes decisions, while their own AI Agent participates in and directs the simulation through WebMCP . The system does not follow a fixed, pre-written sequence of questions. The AI Agent observes the learner’s actions, introduces rule-validated complications based on the current situation, plays different roles within the scenario, and records key evidence throughout the exercise for post-simulation review and assessment. How I Built It Relay’s interface was built with React and TypeScript , with Three.js used to create the interactive building environment. WebMCP allows the learner’s AI Agent to directly access a set of structured tools, including: Observing the current state of the exercise Introducing new complications Delivering messages from different scenario roles Recording assessment evidence The simulation combines pre-authored rules with adaptive AI direction . The code controls scenario state transitions and validates whether each tool call is allowed under the current conditions. The AI Agent then decides which eligible intervention is most appropriate for the situation. Role messages can only reference facts that have been authorized within the scenario, and assessments must be grounded in decisions the learner actually made. This architecture keeps the simulation flexible while maintaining a clear and traceable relationship between learner actions, scenario events, and final feedback. Challenges I Ran Into The first major challenge was controlling the scope of the project . At one point, I tried to create a more dramatic hostage-taking scenario , but this type of situation involves a large amount of specialized knowledge and highly complex operational procedures. It was difficult to build something that was both accessible and credible within the available time—and I spent a lot of time exploring that direction. Eventually, I returned to the building fire scenario and focused on creating a first version with a more complete structure and a clearer experience. Another technical challenge was keeping the AI Agent responsive throughout a continuous exercise. Initially, I had the browser wait indefinitely for a pending event request, but this exceeded the browser connection’s time limit. I later designed a renewable event-waiting mechanism . Each time the waiting connection is renewed, the system preserves the relevant event state, so learner actions and events that occur during reconnection are not lost. The visual design also went through many iterations. I experimented with more complex and visually dramatic 3D interfaces, but eventually realized that richer 3D visuals do not automatically make information easier to understand. What I Learned AI has been incredibly helpful throughout the development process. I also learned that the most important part of an emergency simulator goes far beyond dramatic visuals. Learners need to clearly understand: what role they are playing, what information they currently have, and how their decisions affect the overall situation. Meaningful AI integration requires AI to participate directly in the application’s workflow. In Relay, the AI Agent interacts with the application through explicit tools, permissions, and boundaries, while the learner always retains control over the final decisions. What’s Next If I have more time—or enough reason to continue developing the project—I would like to improve: The onboarding experience The interaction design for coordination tasks The presentation of information during exercises, including more detailed scenario feedback I would also like to gradually develop additional scenarios, including: industrial accidents, coastal emergencies, and natural disasters. Before expanding the platform further, I hope to collaborate with qualified emergency-management professionals to review the scenario assumptions, decision logic, and evaluation criteria. At the moment, Relay is still a synthetic training prototype . It is not intended for real-world emergency command and cannot replace formal training provided by professional organizations. If Relay could eventually recreate and simulate real environments and real-world scenarios, I believe that could become one of its most powerful capabilities. Ultimately, the problem I want to solve is simple: to give more people unlimited opportunities to practice difficult decisions before those decisions ever become real. title: Sloth
pitch: Sloth equips autonomous agents with narrow baseline tools, surfacing temporary financial capabilities only through verified, human-approved grants.
about_excerpt: Sloth equips autonomous agents with narrow baseline tools, surfacing temporary financial capabilities only through verified, human-approved grants. Like Comment Story Updates SLOTH — DELEGATED OUTCOMES WITH SCOPED AUTHORITY INSPIRATION WebMCP lets websites give AI agents native browser tools instead of guessing where to click. But the spec has a huge blind spot: zero concept of permissions or reversibility. If you register a refund tool on page load, the agent has permanent god-mode access. If you don't, it's useless. We built Sloth around one thesis: Delegate outcomes, not unlimited access. WHAT IT DOES Sloth is an operations console for delegated outcomes with temporary capability boundaries: Zero Standing Privileges: Starts with 4 baseline tools (inspect issues, inspect transaction, retry payment, request capability). No refund tool exists. Autonomous Investigation: Agent investigates anomalies, retries pre-authorized failures, and confirms duplicate charges. Boundary Escalation: Agent hits a hard boundary and calls request_capability proposing a narrow scope. Human Negotiation: Operator can approve, deny (DO_NOT_RETRY), or adjust caps ($72 per item, $150 aggregate batch cap). Dynamic Tool Injection (4 -> 5 tools): Approval injects refund_scoped_transactions in real time with a 60-second TTL countdown. In-Tool Enforcement: Tool itself blocks unapproved IDs or amount breaches with structured SCOPE_VIOLATION errors. Single-Use Auto-Revocation (5 -> 4 tools): Executing refunds immediately revokes the tool to eliminate replay attacks. Compliance Audit: One-click export of a signed JSON audit ledger. HOW WE BUILT IT Runtime: Next.js (Vinext engine) with native document.modelContext support for Chrome 149+ and ChatGPT desktop. Core Scope Engine: Pure, zero-dependency validation logic (scope.js) enforcing dual caps, backed by 17/17 automated unit tests. Dynamic Lifecycle: Browser AbortController signals and reactive state tracking to mount and unmount tools on the fly. Console UI: High-density dark mode console with monospace authority rail, live TTL countdown, and boundary test sandboxes. CHALLENGES WE RAN INTO Dynamic WebMCP Registration: Most examples treat tools as static declarations. Mounting and unmounting tools dynamically without page reload required strict state isolation. Dual-Track Evaluation: Supporting live LLM tool calling in experimental browsers while providing an interactive simulation for standard browsers. Preventing Agent Loops: Implementing structured DO_NOT_RETRY machine contracts so models don't repeatedly beg for authority when denied. ACCOMPLISHMENTS Proven 4 -> 5 -> 4 Capability Lifecycle: zero standing privileges -> JIT grant -> auto-revocation on execution. 100% In-Tool Security: Boundaries enforced inside the tool code, not just hidden UI buttons. Dual Blast Radius Protection: Combining unit limits ($72) with aggregate run limits ($150). 17/17 passing unit tests and <2s production build. WHAT WE LEARNED WebMCP is a human-agent negotiation protocol, not just an API. Enterprise adoption requires verifiable blast radius limits and reversibility, not just smarter models. Temporary, single-use capabilities give humans the trust needed to delegate real outcomes. WHAT'S NEXT FOR SLOTH Cryptographic Grant Attestation with WebCrypto. Universal open-source middleware (@sloth/webmcp-guard). Multi-agent capability hand-offs across agent swarms. title: coSynth
pitch: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go.
about_excerpt: A synthesizer you control by talking to AI. Describe a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays it, shows every change, and guides you through the controls so you can tweak it and learn as you go. Like Comment Story Updates Full Wavetable Synthesizer GIF Active AI state and tool visible in the UI coSynth – AI Web Synthesizer Sound design is hard to get into. A real synth has hundreds of knobs. coSynth lets you describe and get a sound. The AI turns the knobs, plays the result, listens to what it made, and shows all the changes in the UI. You keep it, undo it, tweak it, or ask the AI to show you how it got there. You can also ask AI to teach a complext topic and AI will guide you through step by step. Live: https://coSynth.vercel.app Code: https://github.com/brunnolou/coSynth (MIT) Why WebMCP fits A synth is a terrible thing to operate through text or screenshots. Too many parameters (in this case 224), knobs to drag, LFO curves to draw, etc. An agent can misclick, can miss an exact value, and can't hear the audio. The UI is too complex for someone to easily find things when they are not used to it. That makes a synthesizer one of the best interfaces for WebMCP. For the AI agent: It communicates to the synth directly. Every parameter has a name, a unit, and a range that can be edited directly in bulk. When the agent plays a note, it gets back attack time, decay, spectral centroid, and harmonics, then compares that with a reference clip. So it can "hear" with a tool call. For humans Instead of starting from scratch, you get very close to what you want. Then you can see the exact changes and tweak manually. If you don't know a concept or want to find something, AI can show you the exact location or teach you step by step. You can leverage AI's world knowledge to create any synth sound! What used to need trained ears you now can achieve by sending a reference sound and asking AI to replicate. How I Made the AI<>Human UX Better Each knob the AI touched gets a small animated marker. A status line shows which tool is running. You can reject a whole AI iteration and keep your own edits. Undo covers AI changes and yours. Old branches stay reachable in history. The AI can highlight controls step by step and explain them. Every AI performance is saved, so "play that again with my new adjustment" is one click. AI can save as a preset, and you can download it. How I implemented WebMCP Vanilla TypeScript and Vite. DSP in an AudioWorklet, UI in Canvas, WebGL2 and DOM. WebMCP sits on top of the same engine the UI uses, and the synth works without it. Tools register with document.modelContext.registerTool(tool, { signal }) . There are 24, each with a JSON Schema input and a readOnlyHint : Reading : get_synth_state , get_parameter_schema , get_ui_targets , list_presets , get_history Editing : update_parameters , set_modulation , set_fx_order , apply_patch , save_preset , load_preset , delete_preset , export_preset Sound : play_notes , render_audio , capture_audio , analyze_audio , analyze_reference_audio , compare_audio , suggest_patch , stop_performance Together : show_ui_guide , navigate_history , replay_history All 24 register at page load. play_notes needs the human to click Start first, because browsers won't play audio without a gesture. render_audio uses an OfflineAudioContext, so the agent can design and measure before anyone clicks anything. The page also documents itself. A clipped agent brief in the DOM, a JSON descriptor, ai-tools meta tags, llms.txt and robots.txt . An agent given only the URL can read the page and know what to do. How I tested the agent experience I want to ensure AI could call the tools easily. So I built a loop. A harness exposes only what a real WebMCP client sees, and logs every call. A fresh agent gets a fixed prompt and is never allowed to read the repo. Each round runs on Claude and Codex. When * both trip in the same place( , the tool is wrong . Fix the top blocker, run again. In self-improving loop. Four evals, each asking one question. Can the agent find out what to send ( docs/agent-ux-eval.md ). Can it steer toward a sound it cannot hear ( docs/agent-match-eval.md ). Given a "how do I" question, does it teach rather than edit ( docs/agent-teaching-eval.md ). Given only a URL, does it find the tools at all? Prompts, agent reports and raw logs are all in the repo. Learning all 224 parameters went from 45 calls to 1 . Failed calls went to zero on both models. The matching loop went from 87 calls to 36 . How to test Open https://cosynth.vercel.app in the ChatGPT in-app browser, or in Chrome 149+ with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . ChatGPT Desktop was the most reliable client for me. Click "CLICK TO START AUDIO" once. Try: "Make a bright plucked bass and play a short riff." "Show me where the amp envelope is and how to shorten the release." "Save that." Watch the markers, click the status dot for before and after values, and use Keep or Reject. No login. Presets and reference audio stay in the browser. What was already there, what is new I started from Soundgineer by noisyloop ( https://github.com/noisyloop/soundgineer , MIT). Its DSP engine and original UI date from July 6 to 11, 2026, and that version is still up at https://soundgineer.vercel.app . Everything WebMCP-related is from the submission period, August 26 to September 3, 2026, about 200 dated commits: the WebMCP layer and all 24 tools, offline rendering and audio analysis, change markers and Keep/Reject, shared undo history and replays, guided walkthroughs, the interface redesign, the four evals with their harness, and the in-page agent brief. title: leadmcp — the conversion layer for agent-callable tools
pitch: LeadMCP turns WebMCP calls into trustworthy shared-page workflows with human confirmation, cited results, consent-aware gates, and attribution.
about_excerpt: LeadMCP turns WebMCP calls into trustworthy shared-page workflows with human confirmation, cited results, consent-aware gates, and attribution. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Landing page for WebMCP lot studio Webmcp visuals of lot tools The problem Almost every SaaS company's top-of-funnel is a free tool. A calculator, a lookup, a checker: give away something useful, gate the good part behind an email address. It works because a person on that page wants the good part. Now the visitor is an agent. It reads the facts, reports them in chat, and leaves. It never sees the gate, so the person never sees the offer. And the funnel shows nothing at all — because a WebMCP tool call is an ordinary function call. No page view, no click, no event. The lead magnet quietly stops generating leads for exactly the visitors who are growing fastest, and there is no number anywhere that says so. We found all of this on our own site. Sixteen free tools were agent-callable and not one of them emitted a single analytics event. Every one of those pages had an email gate and no tool touched any of them. And the one place a tool did reach a lead endpoint, it did so silently while advertising readOnlyHint: true — inserting a lead row and setting a cookie for someone who had consented to nothing. We had built the plumbing and skipped the business half. That gap is this project. What we built leadmcp — an Apache-2.0 library for the conversion half of WebMCP, plus the sixteen free tools on a live production site that use it. This is deliberately not another registration wrapper. webmcp-react and Chrome's useWebMCPTool already turn a schema and a function into a registered tool, and they do it well. The unsolved part is what happens after the tool returns: declare the gate → open the gate → attribute the call, plus one primitive nobody else has — a tool call that suspends on a person's decision. Declare the gate A read tool returns the ungated slice plus an explicit block naming what is withheld, why, and which tool opens it. The agent can now say "there's a full report with the site analysis — want me to have them email it to you?" instead of reporting a dead end. It hands the conversion back to the person. The declaration is not a substitute for withholding. Our snapshot tools project facts through selectSnapshotSections(variant) first, so an agent on the zoning page cannot read the buildable envelope that page deliberately does not render. Then they declare what was left out. Open the gate A capture tool that requires consentToEmail to be literally true, tells the agent in words to ask the person for their own address in this conversation and never reuse one from earlier context, and records where the consent came from — on_page (a person ticked a box) versus agent_relayed (an agent asserted they agreed in a chat we cannot see). Those are not the same consent, and a CRM that cannot tell them apart cannot be audited. Under Canada's CASL that distinction is the whole ballgame. Critically, each capture tool calls the page's own submit handler, not a fresh fetch. Same request, same rate limit, same CRM sync, same success state — so the person watching the screen sees the send happen, instead of being emailed by an actor they never saw act. It also means one send path to maintain instead of two that drift. The newsletter opt-in and the self-described role field are deliberately never relayed by an agent. An agent reporting "they said yes to updates" is not an express opt-in, and a guessed role puts invented segmentation data in the CRM. Attribute the call Every tool reports to one observer with a five-value outcome, not success/failure: ok, invalid_input, gated, consent_missing, error. gated is the funnel step nobody instruments — the agent reached the wall and the person was never shown the offer. A high invalid_input rate is a description problem, not a code problem. And one property does the heavy lifting: agent_surface, optional on our shared analytics props, absent meaning a person. That single change made every free-tool funnel we already had splittable by human vs agent, without a parallel event family nothing joins to. It is one literal rather than an is_agent boolean, so a second surface can arrive without rewriting history. A tool call that waits for a person Geocoding "4170 Sophia St" returns three plausible parcels. A chat agent picks the first and sounds confident. Instead, our resolve_address tool suspends — the page shows three pins and the execute() promise stays pending until the person taps one, or rejects with an AbortError if they decline or the agent cancels. Single-flight, so a second request supersedes rather than queues: two chips competing on one canvas is not a state a person can answer. Whether to suspend or return a correctable error is a surface decision, not a global one. A map where a pin means something asks on the canvas; a form hands back an error and lets the agent ask in words. Both patterns ship here, on purpose. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP We already run a server-side MCP endpoint, so "an agent can call our API" is not the interesting part. Three things only WebMCP makes possible: The agent acts on the page the person is looking at. No copy-paste step, no second source of truth. When an agent moves the pencil-test assumptions, the sliders move. When it calls focus_lot_map or set_planning_layers, the map the person is staring at pans and the zoning layer comes on. The person can be a step inside the agent's loop. A tool call that blocks on a human decision is not something a server-side MCP tool can express — there is no page to ask on. The gate and its consent live where the person is. Lead capture is a browser-side, consent-bearing act. Moving it server-side is exactly what loses the audit trail that makes it lawful. What people and agents can do together that was hard before The agent can hand the conversion back. Before, a gate was invisible to an agent — it read what it could and stopped. Now the withheld material is named, so the agent can offer it, and the person decides. That was not expressible at all. A tool call can pause for a human judgement. The ambiguous address is the honest case: the agent genuinely cannot know which parcel is meant. It asks on the canvas instead of guessing, and resumes with the answer. You can finally count agents. The same free-tool conversion event now fires from a click and from a tool call, split by one property. Before this, agent traffic through a lead magnet produced literally zero telemetry. Consent survives the handoff. An agent can carry an email address to the gate without the resulting CRM row being indistinguishable from a person who ticked a box themselves. How WebMCP is implemented All on the draft document.modelContext.registerTool contract (19 Aug 2026 WebMCP CG draft), feature-detected — with no modelContext present every entry point is a no-op and the pages work normally. document.modelContext.registerTool({ name: 'email_feasibility_report', description: 'Email the full feasibility report...', inputSchema: { /* derived from the page's own Zod schema / }, execute: async (input) => { / calls the page's own submit handler */ }, }); 31 tools across 9 modules. 4 site-wide (list_free_tools, navigate_to_tool, get_feasibility_snapshot, search_marketplace), page-scoped sets across six free-tool surfaces, 5 capture tools — one per email gate — and 7 on the Lot Studio shared canvas including the three map tools. Tools are derived from the app's existing Zod schemas. defineTool turns a schema plus a function into a bounded, validated tool via native z.toJSONSchema(). If the sliders say 1–12 storeys, so does the agent's schema, forever — there is no second hand-written JSON Schema to drift. Invalid arguments come back as { error, issues } rather than a rejected promise, because agents retry well against data and badly against an opaque throw. The agent surface is derived from the marketing catalogue. navigate_to_tool's enum comes from FREE_TOOLS, so a release-gated tool disappears from the agent surface exactly when it disappears from the site. A test fails if a free tool exists that no page registers tools for — which caught a real bug: one page had been agent-navigable for weeks while registering nothing, so an agent could arrive and find nothing callable. Registration is lifecycle-safe and reports partial failure. One AbortController per mount, so a soft navigation or a Strict Mode double-mount cannot leave duplicate registrations. registerTool is invoked as a method on the model context, never destructured off it — a detached call fails a native WebIDL receiver check that a vi.fn() mock passes happily, and there is a test asserting the receiver. And registerTools never rejects, returning failed[] instead: a throw mid-loop used to abandon every later tool, which reads to an agent as "this page cannot do that" rather than as a bug.
