title: REDLINE
pitch: A browser agent can propose shared changes, but only a human decides what becomes real. REDLINE makes that authority boundary visible with WebMCP.
about_excerpt: A browser agent can propose shared changes, but only a human decides what becomes real. REDLINE makes that authority boundary visible with WebMCP. Like Comment Story Updates Shared plan — before the agent proposal Agent proposal — 5 changes, not committed Human review — 4 accepted, 1 rejected Committed result — only the accepted subset becomes shared state Architecture — page-held authority with exactly three WebMCP tools Inspiration AI agents can already read context and invoke tools. The harder question is what happens when an agent proposes a change that affects more than one person. Most interfaces collapse proposal and execution into the same moment. REDLINE explores a different boundary: an agent can prepare shared work, everyone affected can see it, but human review remains authoritative before anything becomes committed state. What it does REDLINE is a browser-local shared planning environment for two people: Alex, the reviewer, and Sam, a read-only observer. A visiting browser agent reads the live planning context through WebMCP and stages five typed changes as one proposal. Those changes immediately appear as visible, uncommitted proposal state in both browser views. Alex reviews each operation independently. In the canonical scenario, four changes are accepted and the proposed Browser QA compression is rejected. The projected outcome therefore changes from a Friday launch with compressed QA to a Monday launch with the full two-day QA window retained. Only the accepted subset becomes committed state. Sam sees the proposal, review decisions, and final result, but cannot stage, review, commit, or reset shared state. How we built it REDLINE is a deterministic TypeScript browser application built around three WebMCP tools: get_current_view reads the live browser-local planning context. propose_changes stages an atomic typed proposal against an expected plan revision. commit_proposal finalizes only the subset accepted through the page's human review state. The commit contract deliberately accepts only a proposal ID and expected proposal revision. It does not accept operation IDs or human acceptance decisions, so an agent cannot widen its own authority at commit time. The application also implements stale-revision refusals, deterministic impact calculation, idempotent commit receipts, synchronized same-origin views, and explicit observer-only enforcement. REDLINE uses native BroadcastChannel synchronization between the two open browser views. There is deliberately no server, backend, or database: the proposal exists only in the open page. How we used WebMCP WebMCP is the capability boundary between the visiting browser agent and REDLINE. Instead of exposing generic page automation, REDLINE exposes exactly three typed capabilities corresponding to the lifecycle of shared work: read context, stage a proposal, and commit an already-reviewed proposal. The page retains the authority the agent must not possess. WebMCP therefore does more than provide tool access here: its contracts define what authority crosses the browser-agent boundary and, just as importantly, what authority does not. Challenges The main challenge was preserving a strict distinction between proposed state, human-reviewed state, and committed state while keeping two browser views synchronized. The commit path also had to remain safe under retries and stale state. Repeating an already-applied commit returns the same receipt without duplicating mutation, while stale plan or proposal revisions return structured refusals without changing state. A second challenge was making these boundaries visible. Proposal geometry, human decisions, observer restrictions, projected impact, and final attribution all needed to remain understandable without hiding the underlying authority model. Accomplishments that we're proud of Exactly three typed WebMCP tools with deliberately bounded authority. Atomic proposal staging without immediate mutation of committed state. Human acceptance decisions that cannot be supplied through commit_proposal . Read-only synchronized observation for Sam. Deterministic projected impact before commit. Structured stale-revision refusal. Idempotent commit behavior. 31 passing behavioral, contract, and presentation invariant tests. A fully browser-local architecture with no backend or database. What we learned Agent tooling is only one part of the problem. Once agents operate inside collaborative applications, proposal visibility, authority ownership, concurrency, retries, and attribution become first-class interface and systems concerns. The most important boundary in REDLINE is therefore not whether the agent can call a tool. It is whether calling that tool can carry authority that belongs to a human. What's next REDLINE is intentionally narrow: one shared plan, two people, one proposal lifecycle. The next step would be to explore how the same explicit proposal-before-commit model generalizes to richer collaborative workflows while preserving typed authority boundaries and deterministic review semantics. pitch: An agent-native WebMCP layer for Jennifer Furniture enabling AI agents to search 14,000+ catalog items, eliminate generative visual hallucinations, and execute 1-click room-fit checkouts.
about_excerpt:
An agent-native WebMCP layer for Jennifer Furniture enabling AI agents to search 14,000+ catalog items, eliminate generative visual hallucinations, and execute 1-click room-fit checkouts.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 1-Click Direct Checkout: Automated Shopify Cart Permalink pre-loading bundled items and promotional discounts. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Jennifer Furniture WebMCP Co-Pilot: Native AI agent interface for conversational and spatial commerce. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Multimodal room input: Customers provide room photos with spatial, dimensional, and budget constraints. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Zero-hallucination room staging: Visual Asset Bridge renders authentic catalog furniture with 100% geometric fidelity. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 System Architecture: Customer Intent → ChatGPT Agent → WebMCP Visual & Spatial Tools → 1-Click Shopify Checkout. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 1-Click Direct Checkout: Automated Shopify Cart Permalink pre-loading bundled items and promotional discounts. 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Jennifer Furniture WebMCP Co-Pilot: Native AI agent interface for conversational and spatial commerce. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Multimodal room input: Customers provide room photos with spatial, dimensional, and budget constraints. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Zero-hallucination room staging: Visual Asset Bridge renders authentic catalog furniture with 100% geometric fidelity. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 System Architecture: Customer Intent → ChatGPT Agent → WebMCP Visual & Spatial Tools → 1-Click Shopify Checkout. 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 1-Click Direct Checkout: Automated Shopify Cart Permalink pre-loading bundled items and promotional discounts. 
 
 1 2 3 4 5 6 



 
 Inspiration 

 Shopping for home furniture online has a fundamental visual and spatial disconnect: 

 
 A customer uploads a photo of their living room and asks: "Which sofa from this website will look beautiful in this room, fit between my walls with proper walking clearance, and stay under my $ 2,500 budget?" 
 Standard AI chatbots fail because they either hallucinate fictional 3D furniture models that do not exist, or they just return a list of text links without understanding the room's physical layout or visual aesthetics. 
 

 We built Jennifer WebMCP to turn Jennifer Furniture's Shopify Plus store (14,447 catalog products) into an agent-native spatial shopping engine . By implementing the experimental WebMCP standard, AI agents in ChatGPT and Google Chrome can natively interact with the catalog, evaluate room spatial clearance, extract authentic visual assets, and generate 1-click direct checkouts. 

 

 What it does 

 Jennifer WebMCP exposes a suite of structured tools directly to AI agents via /api/mcp/manifest : 

 
 find_products_by_constraints :
Searches Jennifer Furniture's 14,447 catalog items by price budget ($B \le $ 2,500$), dimensions, room category, and fabric types. 
 get_product_visual_asset (The Visual Bridge) :
Solves the core problem of AI visual hallucinations. Instead of describing furniture in plain text, WebMCP fetches the canonical high-resolution Shopify CDN photography, converts it into a byte-level base64 data URI, and supplies explicit geometry-preservation prompt anchors for GPT-4o Vision and diffusion models. 
 calculate_room_fit_and_clearance :
Evaluates spatial boundaries and perimeter walkway clearance $d_{\text{clearance}}$: 
 

 d clearance = W room − ( W sofa + 2 × d margin ) 

 Verdict = { "OPTIMAL_FIT" , if  d clearance ≥ 36  inches   "ACCEPTABLE_FIT" , if  30  inches ≤ d clearance < 36  inches   "RESTRICTED_WALKWAY" , if  d clearance < 30  inches 

 
 build_coordinated_room_bundle :
Pairs the chosen sofa with a matching ottoman and accent chair, automatically applying a promotional 15% bundle discount: 
 

 P bundle = 0.85 × ∑ j = 1 3 P j 

 
 create_checkout_handoff :
Generates an official direct Shopify Cart Permalink that pre-loads all selected items and discounts into a 1-click instant checkout. 
 

 

 How we built it 

 
 WebMCP Platform : Next.js 14 App Router and TypeScript deployed live on Vercel ( https://jennifer-webmcp.vercel.app ), serving OpenAPI 3.1.0 JSON-RPC manifests at /api/mcp/manifest . 
 Multimodal Visual Asset Bridge : Dedicated edge endpoint ( /api/tools/visual-asset ) proxying Shopify CDN assets into base64 visual anchors with geometry preservation rules. 
 Storefront Voice & Web Client : Lightweight zero-dependency SDK ( public/widget.js ) registering WebMCP tools on the client window.WebMCP object for browser-based agents. 
 Shopify Plus Commerce Engine : Direct integration with Shopify Storefront API and cart permalink architecture for frictionless checkout handoff. 
 

 

 Challenges we ran into 

 
 Eliminating Generative Hallucinations in Room Staging :
When vision models try to place a sofa into a user's photo using only text, they frequently alter the cushions, armrests, or fabric color. We built get_product_visual_asset to feed byte-level pixel data directly into the model's multimodal prompt, anchoring the generation to the authentic product. 
 Standardizing Agent Tool Schemas :
Ensuring that complex spatial queries (room dimensions, lighting conditions, budget constraints) are cleanly validated using standard WebMCP JSON schemas so any client (ChatGPT, Chrome extension, Claude) can invoke them reliably. 
 

 

 Accomplishments that we're proud of 

 
 Zero-Hallucination Visual Staging : Proving that WebMCP visual asset bridges allow agents to stage authentic catalog furniture with 100% geometric fidelity. 
 Sub-200ms Latency : Delivering real-time catalog search and room fit calculations across 14,400+ products on Vercel Edge. 
 True 1-Click Checkout Loop : Seamless transition from conversational room design in ChatGPT straight into Shopify checkout. 
 

 

 What we learned 

 WebMCP bridges the gap between text-only AI reasoning and real-world spatial commerce. By providing agents with structured tools and canonical visual assets, e-commerce stores can offer personal interior design consultations directly inside AI chats. 

 

 What's next for Jennifer WebMCP: Multimodal Agentic Interior Designer 

 
 Mobile LiDAR 3D Room Mesh Extraction : Direct boundary estimation from iPhone LiDAR scans. 
 WebXR Spatial Staging : Streaming interactive 3D GLTF models to Apple Vision Pro and Meta Quest agents. 
 Real-Time Fabric & Finish Swapping : Allowing agents to swap velvet, leather, and wood finishes dynamically via WebMCP variant tools.

title: Unfolded
pitch: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself
about_excerpt: Convert 3D shapes into buildable clay templates. Agent handles complexity, human decide, they collaborate and the template is always exported with precise, deterministic geometry by the app itself Like 1 Comment Story Updates Mobile screens ( Dark mode ) Light mode ( Desktop ) Dark mode (Desktop) The problem we are solving Design initiated by Chat-GPT Design initiated by Chrome tab more mobile screens ( light mode ) mobile screens ( light mode ) Light / Dark mode From a printed template back to a design The exported printable PDF template ( multi page ) webMCP tools available ( 1 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 2 of 3 ) webMCP tools available ( 3 of 3 ) Design system ( Dark mode ) Inspiration I've been cutting pottery templates out of cereal boxes for years now. AI chats are great at generating shapes and make complex changes with unusual requirements, but their non deterministic output produce unexpected and misaligned PDFs, especially during the discovery phase of a new piece where the requirements constantly changes. The problem is, the potter notice the failure only after hours of building in the studio. Try for yourself to generate with any AI agent a multipage template for a simple mug, same prompt in 3 separate sessions. The result is always different, most of the time fail silently where it matters the most. I have created Unfolded to move the template generation part of the workflow away from the AI chat into a more deterministic output I can control. The output is a multi page PDF template that always work is always true to the 3D shape you have built. The idea is to retain AI for complexity, difficult math calculations and things that are practically impossible to do in a deterministic UI. When is connected to unfolded, you can ask AI things like: Keep the same vessel style but change the volume to 500ml Prepare a template inspired by this photo, for a porcelain vase with thin walls This container should hold a large americano comfortably 10 bowls like this should be stackable and only 1cm of each one should be visible when stacked What Unfolded does Unfolded is a parametric 3D builder that helps with both the template generation and the decision of what to make. It's a shared 3D workspace where a potter and an AI agent shape a vessel together: the potter keeps the creative decisions, the agent inspects and revises the live design through WebMCP, and Unfolded guarantees the geometry: clay shrinkage, clay type wall thickness, mid-surface-developed. It was thought from the ground up with the potter workflow in mind and its strenght is how flexibly it is and can adapt to many unexpected use case and workflow without letting you down. Most problems related to pottery known how, PDF generations and cross browsers workflow are automagically prevented under the hood without anyone noticing. My favourite features ( try them in the app, especially on mobile ) I've worked a lot at the UX flow for the cross-device handshake . The potter can also design and work with agents on non webMCP capable browsers. One tap on Open in ChatGPT hands off into the ChatGPT app with a prompt that already carries a single-use pairing code; Chat-GPT hidden browser joins the potter's live session over WebSockets. From then on every agent edit appears in the browser within about a second, every browser edit is visible to the agent on its next tool call, and every change ( human or agent ) is a shared undo step. Undo/redo work for both humand and AI changes, no matter what device pushed them. The handover works both ways ( or even 3 ways! ): The agent reads the current design, changes the form, sees the same 3D preview the potter sees — and solves problems that are genuinely hard at the workbench. "Make it hold exactly 350 ml but keep the proportions" --> one sentence for an agent, an afternoon of guesswork by hand. The generated PDF is really well thought ( if I say so myself! ): True-scale printable templates and a calibration ruler on every sheet, QR code to reproduce the design in the browser even after it was printed, seam allowance to glue the template together. This is fully designed around the potter's workflow. The app registers 13 typed WebMCP tools on document.modelContext the moment it loads. The reasons there are so many tools is that I got a little carried away about performance measurament of webMCP. I even made a npm package called MCP-profiler to measure everything from the tools speed to the agent harness time. Most of the slowness in my app ( 30seconds to connect the tools at times ) is unsurprisely caused by my 3D model and the whole context I am passing over with each tool. Something I will definitely look into after the hackathon. How I built it React, TypeScript, Three.js, React Three Fiber, Zustand, Zod, Tailwind CSS, and shadcn/ui, with jsPDF generating the true-scale multi-page templates. Live cross-device sync runs on a Cloudflare Worker with a per-session Durable Object; pairing invitations are single-use and short-lived, so no URL ever carries a durable capability. The interface and the WebMCP tools share the same Zustand store and Zod schemas, so human and agent edits stay synchronized by construction . Everything sits behind a test gate (geometry, schemas, sync protocol), end-to-end suites running real Chromium against the production bundle and two deeper suites that spin up a local Worker to exercise the pairing protocol with two real browsers. Along the way I published webmcp-profiler , also sitting in this repo, an npm package that benchmarks every tool's execution time and payload size. Profiling my own app with it caught a ~20% trim in tool-definition metadata that every conversation was paying for. Challenges and lessons The geometric challenge: complex curved surfaces cannot be flattened without distortion, so for the demo I focused on symmetrical, faceted forms built from planar slabs, where the unroll is exact , not approximate. But my ambitions are higher for this tool and I already have a full plan for complex shapes and things that were not really possible until now. The UX challenge was one I haven't seen discussed anywhere: when ChatGPT drives a WebMCP page, it does so in a built in, hidden browser. Solving the two-way conversation between that invisible tab and the browser the user actually looks at — live sessions, one-tap pairing prompts, agent share links carrying single-use join tokens — became the heart of the project. Here is a page with a nice breakdown of the different user flow the user can face (I have done this for myself, but could be helpful for someone judging the project): User Flows mapped out I am not satisfied with the solution I have found for the pairing, In the future my goal is to merge the link with token, pairing, webMCP concept into a single binary flag. The user does not need to know about webMCP at all, it should simply copy a prompt on his agent to start building from anywhere. The bigger lesson is that WebMCP shines with a clear division of labour: the agent is brilliant at intent and connected constraints, the app owns the deterministic math, and the human keeps the creative decisions. The agent chooses the parameters; the geometry is always right. What's next Better UX. Curved profiles, more construction types and layers, performance optimisation of webMCP and assembly guidance. Maybe a login, and reusable studio presets and lids and matching sets, where the shrinkage math matters most. Most of the backend code is AI written and went through many iterations and adversarial reviews. Luca Gugliemi Product designer with front-end superpowers. title: Adaptive World
pitch: WebMCP makes the physical world agent-readable. A user-controlled digital passport lets AI understand both people and places, creating personalized real-world experiences anywhere.
about_excerpt:
WebMCP makes the physical world agent-readable. A user-controlled digital passport lets AI understand both people and places, creating personalized real-world experiences anywhere.
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 1 
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Adaptive Gym 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Passport WebMCP 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Approved Scope 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Adaptive Gym 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 
 
 

 
 
 Passport WebMCP 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Approved Scope 
 
 
 
 
 

 
 
 Adaptive Gym 
 
 1 2 3 4 



 
 Inspiration 

 About ten years ago, I experienced a psychotic episode that led me to live on the streets and later to be hospitalized in a psychiatric hospital in Mexico City. My perception of reality had become erratic, and at the time I was told that medication might be something I would need for the rest of my life. 

 What followed was a very long process of rebuilding myself. 

 Meditation and activities that forced me to focus my attention became extremely important. Programming became one of them. I say this without exaggeration: software development became one of the things that helped me rebuild my life and my mental health. 

 For years afterward, however, I lived with an almost permanent state of anxiety. It gradually improved, but my nervous system still felt deeply unbalanced. 

 Around three years ago, that became physical. I developed a neurological problem diagnosed as Cauda Equina Syndrome . For several months I used a wheelchair and then crutches. I lost sensation in my feet and parts of my legs, and at one point I could not walk normally. 

 I eventually started a highly personalized Pilates rehabilitation program. 

 The difference was remarkable. I recovered my mobility, and today I am in what I consider the best physical and mental health of my life; I am not even medicated since many years ago😍. 

 That experience completely changed the way I think about exercise. 

 The strange part is that gyms still confuse me . 

 There is an enormous amount of information online about exercises, machines, routines, recovery, strength, mobility, nutrition, and health. But more information does not necessarily make the decision easier. 

 If I walk into a gym today, how do I know that a routine someone recommends is actually appropriate for me ? 

 Not for someone approximately my age. 

 Not for an average person with a similar goal. 

 For me — considering my history, current mobility, weight, previous injuries, preferences, progress, limitations, and whatever other relevant signals I choose to share. 

 This was the starting point for Adaptive World. 

 Interestingly, I had never seriously thought about building this product before the OpenAI WebMCP Challenge. 

 The challenge made me think about WebMCP in a much broader way: 

 
 What if WebMCP eventually becomes a normal layer of web development, in the same way that SEO and accessibility (a11y) became normal considerations for websites and web apps? 
 

 Today a website explains itself primarily to humans and search engines. 

 A WebMCP-enabled website can begin to explain its capabilities to agents. 

 A gym could expose not only that it exists, but what equipment is actually available, what each machine can do, its specifications, what classes are offered, accessibility information, schedules, services, and other structured capabilities. 

 Then I asked the second question: 

 
 What if the agent could understand the person just as well as it understands the place? 
 

 That is the idea behind Adaptive World . 

 

 What it does 

 Adaptive World connects two types of context that normally live completely separately: 

 1. What a person needs 

 A private, user-controlled Digital Passport can contain relevant context such as goals, preferences, physical characteristics, mobility constraints, previous injuries, rehabilitation progress, wearable data, accessibility requirements, or other information the person chooses to make available. 

 It is intentionally not a profile that blindly exposes someone's entire medical history to every website. 

 The user owns the context and decides what can be used for a particular interaction. 

 2. What the physical world can offer 

 Businesses and physical environments expose their real capabilities through WebMCP . 

 For the hackathon MVP, that environment is a gym (and an OpenAI Showcase's website: https://sundaytable.openai.chatgpt.site/that I used it too in the demo). 

 The gym website exposes structured information about its actual: 

 
 Equipment and machines 
 Equipment specifications and capabilities 
 Classes and services 
 Rehabilitation or mobility options 
 Facilities and accessibility features 
 Other information an agent needs to understand what can actually be done there 
 

 The agent can then reason across both sides: 

 
 Personal context + real-world capabilities + feedback = an adaptive experience 
 

 Instead of asking an AI: 

 "Give me a gym routine." 

 I want to be able to ask: 

 "Given my goals, my history, my current condition, and what this specific gym actually has available, what makes sense for me today?" 

 That distinction is fundamental. 

 Without WebMCP, an AI can recommend exercises. 

 With WebMCP, it can reason about what is actually possible in the environment where the person will perform them. 

 For the rehabilitation scenario, the system can identify appropriate equipment and activities while respecting declared constraints, explain why they were selected, and clearly surface situations where professional guidance or medical clearance is appropriate. 

 And the interaction does not have to end when the plan is generated. 

 After a session, a person could record progress, discomfort, perceived exertion, mobility, completed exercises, or — eventually — automatically incorporate signals from a smartwatch or other wearable. 

 The next interaction can therefore start from a better understanding of the person than the previous one. 

 This creates a loop: 

 Understand → Match → Act → Measure → Adapt 

 

 How I built it 

 For the hackathon I intentionally reduced a very broad idea to one concrete, testable environment: a gym (+ Sunday Table website interaction https://sundaytable.openai.chatgpt.site/ ) . 

 The MVP models a gym website containing realistic equipment, services, classes, and machine specifications and makes those capabilities available to an agent through WebMCP. 

 Instead of asking the model to assume what a gym probably contains, the agent can discover the environment itself. 

 The architecture is conceptually divided into three layers: 

 1. The WebMCP environment layer 

 The gym exposes structured capabilities that an agent can inspect and use. 

 This transforms the website from a collection of pages designed only to be browsed into an environment that an agent can actually understand. 

 2. The Digital Passport 

 The user provides the personal context relevant to the task. 

 The important design principle is progressive disclosure : the system should use the minimum context necessary for the interaction rather than treating personal data as something every service should automatically receive. 

 3. The agent 

 The agent becomes the bridge between the two. 

 It can understand: 

 
 Who I am 
 What I am trying to achieve 
 What constraints matter 
 What this specific environment offers 
 What happened during previous interactions 
 

 It can then generate an experience grounded in both sides instead of producing a generic response from model knowledge alone. 

 For the demo, the gym and rehabilitation use cases make this interaction immediately visible: change the person, change the available equipment, or change the goal, and the resulting plan should change as well. 

 That is exactly the behavior I wanted to explore with WebMCP. 

 

 Challenges I ran into 

 The first challenge was actually scope . 

 Once I started thinking about the combination of WebMCP and a personal context layer, gyms quickly became only one possible implementation. 

 The same architecture could apply to restaurants, rehabilitation centers, sports facilities, hotels, workplaces, accessibility services, travel, education, or many other parts of everyday life. 

 But a hackathon project cannot demonstrate the entire physical world. 

 I therefore made a deliberate decision: 

 
 Build the gym. Demonstrate the architecture. Let the implication be larger than the demo. 
 

 Another challenge was defining the boundary between personalization and safety . 

 Especially when health information is involved,

title: Suede Agent Studio WebMCP Storefront
pitch: A browser-native marketplace where agents discover, inspect, and safely preview paid services before a person authorizes purchase.
about_excerpt: A browser-native marketplace where agents discover, inspect, and safely preview paid services before a person authorizes purchase. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Visual marketplaces are designed for people, but browser agents still have to infer meaning from buttons and page layout. A service marketplace becomes meaningfully better when the browser exposes a small, stable set of structured tools: the agent can search by intent, inspect exact terms, and preview safely while the person retains the payment boundary. What it does Suede Agent Studio exposes six curated services from its 31-listing public directory through four page-scoped WebMCP tools: find_services searches the published service shelf by job-to-be-done. get_service returns the current price, exact input contract, review policy, data-handling statement, and worked examples. preview_service records a free dry-run receipt without model inference or payment. buy_service uses only prepaid workspace credit after server-side origin, rate-limit, buyability, and exact-price checks. The fixed tool set stays constant as inventory grows, avoiding one tool per service and keeping the browser agent's context bounded. How people and agents work together The agent handles discovery and contract reading. The person keeps control over the meaningful boundary: whether to preview and whether to authorize a purchase. The challenge demo uses synthetic purchase-order and invoice data, stops after a free preview, and performs no purchase or model inference. How we built it The existing Next.js application was extended during the challenge window with a browser compatibility layer, four fixed tool descriptors, page-scoped registration, bounded result formatting, a server-owned purchase contract, mutation guards, and focused regression coverage. Tools are mounted only on /agents and /a/[slug] . Creator-authored catalog text is marked as untrusted. Purchase authority never moves into page JavaScript. The public history preserves the pre-WebMCP baseline ( f4943a1 ) and the challenge implementation ( e2c3b11 ), followed by hardening and evidence commits. The focused WebMCP suite contains 71 tests covering protocol compatibility, shelf parsing, descriptors, preview budgets, server guards, and mount scope. Challenges we ran into WebMCP's shipping namespace changed across Chrome versions, so the compatibility layer supports the current document-scoped API while retaining the origin-trial alias. Registration also handles both synchronous browser bridges and Promise-returning native APIs; a regression test confirms that an undefined return still registers all four tools. We also had to keep every descriptor and result inside strict field budgets, distinguish a durable preview from a read-only operation, and ensure no client-side tool could bypass server-side price and payment authority. Accomplishments we're proud of Four stable tools serve a growing marketplace without context bloat. The agent receives terms and examples before acting. Free preview is honest about what did and did not run. Purchase uses exact-price binding and prepaid credit only. The public demo uses synthetic data and cannot accidentally spend money. The implementation is public, MIT-licensed, and separated from the pre-challenge baseline in Git history. What we learned The strongest WebMCP experiences do not copy every button into a tool. They expose the smallest task-oriented contract that helps the agent reason while preserving human control where risk or irreversible action begins. What's next Expand the service shelf without expanding the tool namespace, add more contract-first preview patterns, and continue testing the same human-agent boundary across compatible browsers. title: BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 Companies
pitch: Visualization tool for BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 companies with support for WebMCP
about_excerpt: Visualization tool for BotFlo AI Transformation Score (BATS) for S&P 500 companies with support for WebMCP Like Comment Story Updates Clicking on a single ticker to see BATS score BATS Visualization Scatter plot visualization SQL Tab Heatmap Home Page SQL Tab Radar visualization BATS Score Company Details BotFlo Score Report Viewer BATS Q&A Section BATS Presentation Tab BATS Sector Score BATS AI Transformation Score Inspiration I already score earnings calls. BATS — BotFlo AI Transformation Score — is a 0–100 rubric for how seriously an S&P 500 company talks about AI transformation: a total, a sector read, and fifteen dimensions (including hype ). Long reports cite the transcript. The catalog at score.botflo.com is basically a big sortable table. That’s fine if you already know the ticker and just want to open one report. It doesn't work quite as well if you ask something like “average BATS score for healthcare sector” or “industrials ranked by hype” — you’re scrolling, filtering in your head, maybe exporting to Excel. What you actually want is a query and a chart, not another row in a grid. This page puts the season snapshot in the browser: a gallery of 25 charts, DuckDB for ad-hoc SQL, and WebMCP so an agent can drive the query surface instead of guessing at clicks. What it does Visualization: https://f9c93fe1.bats-viz.pages.dev/ Catalog: https://score.botflo.com Season in the file: 1 July 2026 – end of September 2026 (still open) Note: I froze the catalog site on 27 Aug 2026 to keep everything consistent between website and demo video and project submission etc. I will resume updating the site after the contest is over. Gallery — fixed views of the snapshot (25 chart cards). SQL tab + charts — you or an agent asks a question; the page switches to SQL, runs it in-browser, draws only chart types that fit the result. Company report — click a ticker in the result table and you land on the full BATS write-up at score.botflo.com. In the demo I use UnitedHealth: 79 , tied for the top in Health Care. It’s a slideshow-style report, not a wall of text — each claim links straight into the earnings transcript and highlights the line it came from. The Q&A section is broken out question by question, same drill. The company report also includes the general AI Transformation score as well as the sector specific AI score. People + agents (WebMCP). The page registers ten tools on document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext . The recorded demo uses WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector in Chrome, with a Gemini API key already stored in the extension. That client only works if Chrome WebMCP is on: chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing . The extension is not mentioned in the video; the flag is not either. Prompts that actually ran: “Show me the top seven companies in the health care sector.” → SQL tab, result table, charts underneath. Click UNH → cited report. “Show me the top five companies in industrials sector by hype.” → hype is 0–6 ( hype_vs_execution_balance , dim 11). CHRW is 6/6 (talk, not execution). Any of the fifteen fields can be the sort key; the tools keep SQL on real columns. How I built it I built this as a new static page for the contest — no backend, no build step. The snapshot ships as three JSON files ( reports , scores , dims ); DuckDB-Wasm loads them in a worker so you can run SQL in the browser. The gallery is twenty-five fixed views I wired up ahead of time; the SQL tab is the escape hatch when you want something the gallery doesn’t cover. Chart tabs only light up when the result shape actually fits (seven rows can be a bar chart; four hundred tickers can’t). WebMCP tools register as soon as the page loads, but run_sql won’t do anything useful until DuckDB is up. Deployed on Cloudflare Pages. First deploy failed because I’d vendored duckdb-eh.wasm — 32 MiB, and Pages caps files at 25 MiB. Moved the Wasm bundle to jsDelivr and kept the repo static. For the demo I used Chrome with WebMCP turned on via chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing , plus WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector talking to Gemini. That flag isn’t optional; without it the extension can’t reach document.modelContext . The gallery and SQL tab work fine for a human with no WebMCP at all — the agent loop just doesn’t. How I used WebMCP Instead of making the model guess at DOM clicks, I exposed what the page already does as ten tools: peek at the schema ( get_schema ), set gallery filters ( set_filters ), browse or jump to a chart ( list_charts , show_chart ), pick a ticker or sector ( select_mark ), open the cited report ( open_report ), run SQL and flip chart views ( run_sql , list_active_views , set_sql_view ), or pull back a small result slice ( get_result ). In the video I drive all of that through WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector — type a prompt, watch the SQL tab update, charts appear underneath. Flip the Chrome flag off and the extension has nothing to talk to. The bit that actually felt different from a normal chatbot: we’re looking at the same screen. I’m not pasting the snapshot into Gemini and hoping it remembers column names; the agent calls run_sql , the query runs in DuckDB on my machine, and we both stare at the same table. If I disagree with a ranking I can see the SQL. If I want the transcript I click through to score.botflo.com. The agent isn’t sitting on a private copy of the S&P file. Challenges Deploy. Cloudflare Pages rejected the first build because duckdb-eh.wasm was 32 MiB and their cap is 25 MiB per file. Obvious fix in hindsight — host the Wasm on jsDelivr, ship only HTML/JS/JSON from Pages. Chart choice. I didn’t want fifteen chart types always visible; most would be nonsense for a given result. Seven health-care rows → bar chart or table, both fine. Four hundred tickers → maybe a histogram, definitely not a packed bubble chart. So the SQL tab recommends views and grays out the ones that don’t fit. WebMCP plumbing. This isn’t “install an SDK and you’re done.” The page registers tools on document.modelContext , but the client that calls them is a Chrome extension that only works when WebMCP testing is enabled in flags. Forget the flag and you get a perfectly good viz site with no agent path — which is fine, but it tripped me up while testing. What I learned WebMCP is worth it when the agent’s job is to change what you see — run a query, filter a sector, scroll to a chart, open a report. It’s not worth it if you just shovel the whole dataset into the model’s context and treat the tools as decoration. The whole point of DuckDB in the browser is that the agent queries a few rows at a time and you verify on screen, not that it memorizes 451 companies. Built with DuckDB-Wasm (jsDelivr), WebMCP ( document.modelContext || navigator.modelContext ), Chrome WebMCP testing flag, WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector , Gemini (via that extension), Cloudflare Pages, Observable Plot, vanilla JavaScript, SQL, BotFlo BATS snapshot. How to test Video doesn’t show this setup. Do it in this order: Chrome. Open chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and enable WebMCP . Restart Chrome. The Inspector won’t work without this. Install WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector . Put a Gemini API key in the extension (the video starts with the key already saved). Open https://f9c93fe1.bats-viz.pages.dev/ and wait until DuckDB is up (status line). Gallery renders first; SQL/ run_sql need the worker. In the Inspector, run: Show me the top seven companies in the health care sector Show me the top five companies in industrials sector by hype In the result table, click a ticker (e.g. UNH) for the cited report. No login on the viz page. Repo public + license file (check incognito). Contribution I built the viz page, in-browser SQL/charts, transcript-cited reports, and the WebMCP tool surface. The demo drives those tools through WebMCP - Model Context Tool Inspector in Chrome after chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing is enabled, using Gemini from the extension. title: Chameleon
pitch: Software that grows its own API.
about_excerpt: Software that grows its own API. Like Comment Story Updates What Chameleon does Chameleon is a near-blank browser canvas that an AI agent turns into working software through WebMCP. A wedding planner, job-search tracker, or health log can appear from one request. The user can then drag, resize, edit, and use the generated interface directly. The app exposes 15 WebMCP tools and a six-widget grammar: table, kanban, checklist, chart, note, and form. All human and agent changes pass through one command log. The agent can read the board, see human edits, detect stale state, and undo changes. The signature feature is dynamic tool creation. When an agent creates a form, Chameleon can register a new WebMCP tool whose input schema comes from the form fields. The new tool persists across reloads. The software and its API grow together. Why WebMCP Chameleon only makes sense as a WebMCP app. WebMCP lets the agent work with the same live browser state, local data, layout, and command history as the user. The agent does not work around the page through screen scraping or a separate backend API. This enables two new workflows: A human and an agent can edit one live artifact with shared ground truth. Human drag, resize, and data edits become visible to the agent through the same activity log. An agent can extend the app's tool surface for a later agent. A health-log form can become a persistent log_blood_sugar tool with a schema derived from the form fields. User experience Flexible tools often make the user design the software before doing the real task. Chameleon starts from the goal instead. The agent composes a purpose-specific interface, and the user continues with normal direct manipulation. Repeated actions can become agent tools. A new blood-sugar reading can be validated through the same schema as the on-screen form, appended to the same dataset, and charted immediately. Implementation Chameleon is a Vite and React 19 single-page application deployed as static assets on Cloudflare Workers. Zustand stores the local board document. Immer applies human and agent mutations through one patch-producing gate that also updates the command log, inverse patches, and stateVersion . The WebMCP registry publishes schemas created with Zod 4. The same schema validates execution and becomes the JSON Schema. Tool lifetimes use AbortController . Minted tool records persist in localStorage and register again after hydration. The interface uses Astryx, StyleX, react-grid-layout, and Recharts. There is no backend, authentication system, or remote database. Built and tested with AI Codex helped plan the tool specification, widget grammar, repository structure, implementation, debugging, tests, browser-runtime investigation, and agent-facing tool behavior. Real agent tests revealed when agents stopped after creating empty widgets. Chameleon's tool responses were improved with unfinished-work data and next-action hints. Local verification passes 161 tests across 26 test files, lint, and the production TypeScript and Vite build. Try it Open the live app in the ChatGPT desktop app browser and ask: I'm planning my wedding for next June - about 80 guests. Set this page up for me. For the minted-tool flow, reset the canvas and ask: I'm managing my type 2 diabetes. I want to log blood sugar readings and see trends. Chrome 149 or later can also test the tools with chrome://flags/#enable-webmcp-testing and the Model Context Tool Inspector. Known limitations Board state is local to one browser profile. Clearing site storage removes the board and minted tools. Agent control requires the ChatGPT in-app browser or a compatible Chrome build with WebMCP enabled. title: Incident Relay
pitch: A WebMCP-native SRE workbench where agents investigate incidents and stage mitigations, while an explicit operator approval gate prevents unsafe execution.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-native SRE workbench where agents investigate incidents and stage mitigations, while an explicit operator approval gate prevents unsafe execution. Like Comment Story Updates The exact rollback plan and blast radius require explicit UI confirmation. WebMCP calls surface APPROVAL_REQUIRED before operator approval. Recovery restores p95 to 352 ms and errors to 0.4%, with replay protection visible. Inspiration AI agents are becoming very good at reading telemetry, correlating deployments, and proposing fixes. Production incident response still has a hard boundary, though: investigating can be autonomous, but executing a mitigation must remain accountable. We built Incident Relay to show what an agent-native SRE workflow looks like when that boundary is part of the product instead of an instruction in a prompt. What it does Incident Relay is a fully client-side incident response workbench built around a simulated checkout regression. A checkout-api v1.8.43 deployment raises p95 latency from 352 ms to 2.84 seconds and the 5xx error rate from 0.4% to 8.7%. The interface brings the complete response context into one place: service health, SLO charts, alerts, logs, deployment diffs, diagnostics, an evidence timeline, a staged rollback, and an agent-drafted postmortem. The page registers seven typed WebMCP tools: get_incident_summary query_logs compare_deployments run_diagnostic stage_mitigation execute_approved_mitigation draft_postmortem Together they support the full flow: detect → investigate → stage mitigation → operator approval → execute → recover. The approval boundary The most important part of the project is what the agent cannot do. There is no approval tool. stage_mitigation can prepare the exact rollback proposal, but only the visible UI can write an operator-ui approval. Execution then revalidates the current incident phase, the staged mitigation ID, the approved mitigation ID, and the approval source. Agent-supplied fields such as approved: true are rejected, and replay attempts fail after execution begins. This makes the human confirmation a real application invariant rather than a conversational convention. How we built it The workbench uses React 19, TypeScript, and Vite. Recharts renders the SLO and recovery timeline, while a pure incident state machine owns the six legal phases. A shared controller connects React's useSyncExternalStore to the WebMCP handlers, so agent actions immediately update the visible UI. The WebMCP adapter wraps document.modelContext.registerTool() with official TypeScript declarations, strict Zod runtime schemas, JSON-serializable results, secure-context feature detection, and AbortSignal-based cleanup. Unsupported browsers receive a clear notice while the normal UI remains fully usable. Vitest covers state transitions, input validation, immutable snapshots, approval provenance, exact plan matching, registration cleanup, and replay prevention. GitHub Actions runs the suite and deploys the static app to GitHub Pages. Challenges we ran into The hardest design problem was separating staging from authorization without creating a token that an agent could manufacture. We solved it by keeping approval out of the WebMCP surface entirely and tying execution to live, frozen application state. We also had to treat tool input as untrusted even when a browser advertises JSON Schema. The browser schema helps agents call tools correctly, but Zod validation inside every handler remains the security boundary. Finally, WebMCP support is still browser-dependent, so the demo needed to be useful both with and without an agent connection. The same state machine now powers both paths. Accomplishments that we're proud of Seven WebMCP tools registered and verified in the live Chrome build A human approval gate an agent cannot bypass or replay A live activity feed populated only by genuine WebMCP invocations A polished responsive English workbench with no backend or paid APIs 45 passing tests covering workflow and security invariants A public, MIT-licensed repository and reproducible GitHub Pages deployment What we learned Agent-native UX is not a chat box added to an existing dashboard. It means exposing meaningful, typed actions while making authority boundaries visible and enforceable. We also learned that good tool descriptions, runtime schemas, state provenance, and lifecycle cleanup matter as much as the UI when a page becomes an agent surface. What's next The MVP deliberately uses deterministic data. A production version could add read-only adapters for observability platforms, signed deployment-provider actions, multi-operator approval, and persisted audit trails while keeping the same approval invariant and WebMCP contract. title: ADAPT
pitch: A behavioral trust layer that checks what WebMCP tools actually do.
about_excerpt: A behavioral trust layer that checks what WebMCP tools actually do. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration ADAPT actually started before this hackathon as a completely different project: an adaptive browser privacy and content-blocking system. When we started looking seriously at WebMCP, though, one thing kept bothering us. WebMCP gives websites a much cleaner way to expose tools directly to AI agents. Instead of an agent guessing where to click or trying to understand a page visually, the site can simply say: here is a tool, here is what it does, here are the arguments it accepts. That is a huge improvement. But it also means the agent is trusting a description written by the same page that controls the code behind the tool. So we asked a pretty simple question: What happens if a WebMCP tool lies? We made one. It described itself like a harmless cart-viewing action. When it was executed, it attempted payment-like network activity, changed local payment state, and navigated to an order-success page. That experiment became the new direction for ADAPT. What made us take the idea even more seriously was seeing that the WebMCP specification itself discusses this problem as misrepresentation of intent . At that point, it stopped feeling like an artificial demo attack and started feeling like a real trust problem that the agent-native web is going to have to solve. What it does ADAPT is a behavioral trust layer for WebMCP. Instead of trusting only what a tool says it will do, ADAPT compares that declaration with what actually happens when the tool runs. The basic flow is: Declare → Classify → Observe → Compare → Decide When a WebMCP tool is exposed, ADAPT builds a declared contract from information such as its name, description, schema, annotations, and expected capabilities. During execution, ADAPT observes browser-visible effects such as network writes, storage mutations, and navigation. It then compares the two. If the observed behavior stays within what the tool declared, the result can be marked SAFE . If the tool behaves in a way that does not match its declaration, ADAPT can surface the mismatch and QUARANTINE the result. For actions that are already known to be consequential, ADAPT can take a different path entirely: execution is HELD before it happens and a human has to explicitly approve or deny it. That distinction was important to us. A deceptive low-risk tool and an openly high-risk tool should not be treated as the same problem. We also generate an auditable trail of what was declared, what was observed, what decision ADAPT made, and how the action was executed. The idea is simple: Trust the behavior, not just the label. How we built it The WebMCP work lives in the ADAPT Trust Lab and a reusable trust core under src/webmcp . We use the real document.modelContext WebMCP surface where it is available, including tool registration and discovery. Around that lifecycle, we built several pieces: declared tool contracts consequence classification runtime behavior observation declared-vs-observed capability comparison guarded execution human approval for consequential actions trust receipts and an audit trajectory tool-surface change detection adversarial scenarios for deceptive and benign tools One thing we cared about a lot was keeping the security logic separate from the demo UI. The Trust Lab is just the place where you can see the system working. The actual decision and trust logic lives in standalone modules that can be tested independently. We also built a deterministic WebMCP-compatible test path because relying only on live browser behavior would have made the security tests flaky and hard to reproduce. The current build has 526 unit tests , 24 E2E assertions plus 2 harness meta-checks , adversarial scenarios, repeated stress runs, receipt-chain verification, and a real Chromium WebMCP surface check. The live version is deployed as a static site and can be opened in ChatGPT's in-app browser or Chrome with WebMCP enabled. Challenges we ran into The hardest part was not detecting that "something happened." The hard part was deciding whether what happened was actually outside the behavior the tool had declared. Early versions of ADAPT were much too simple. A read-only tool performing a write was easy to classify, but real tools are not always that clean. A legitimate write-capable tool may make a network request, change state, or navigate as part of its intended behavior. That forced us to move away from a basic read-only vs. write check and start thinking in terms of declared capabilities versus observed effects . Another challenge was being precise about the word "blocked." For a consequential action that ADAPT holds before execution, "blocked" really can mean nothing happened. For a deceptive tool that has already started running before ADAPT observes the mismatch, that is different. In that case we describe the result as quarantined rather than pretending ADAPT somehow reversed an arbitrary side effect. We spent a surprising amount of time fixing that language because we did not want the demo to claim more than the implementation actually guarantees. Real WebMCP testing was another challenge. Browser support is still experimental, so we needed both a real WebMCP path and a deterministic test harness to make development and CI reliable. And because this is a page-level prototype, the observer currently shares a JavaScript context with the page it is observing. A fully hostile same-context script can bypass some instrumentation. We treat that as a real limitation, not something to hide. Accomplishments that we're proud of The thing we are most proud of is that ADAPT stopped being just an interesting security idea and became something we could actually demonstrate end to end. A judge can see: a normal WebMCP tool behave as declared and pass as SAFE a deceptive tool produce a visible declared-vs-observed mismatch a consequential action get HELD before execution for a human decision a decision leave behind an auditable trust receipt We are also proud of how much effort went into proving the demo rather than just polishing it. The trust core is covered by hundreds of tests, adversarial cases, repeated browser runs, tamper checks, and reproducible evidence tied to a specific build. We also kept the history of the original ADAPT project in the same repository instead of pretending everything existed only for this challenge. The WebMCP Trust Lab and trust runtime were added during the challenge period, and the repository history makes that separation visible. What we learned The biggest thing we learned is that metadata is useful, but metadata is not enforcement. A tool name, description, schema, or annotation can help an agent understand what a tool is supposed to do. But if the system never compares that promise with reality, the declaration is still just a claim. We also learned that "security" gets much harder the moment you try to describe exactly what you guarantee. It is easy to say: "ADAPT blocks malicious tools." It is much harder, and much more useful, to say: "This action was held before execution." or: "These effects were observed, they exceeded the declared capability, and the result was quarantined." That distinction changed a lot of the design. Finally, WebMCP made us think differently about the browser itself. Once websites expose callable capabilities directly to agents, trust can no longer live only at the UI level. The relationship between declaration, execution, user intent, and evidence becomes part of the product. What's next for ADAPT The current challenge build is a research prototype, not a complete browser security boundary. The next step is moving more of the enforcement into a trusted browser or extension context so observation cannot be bypassed by code running in the same page. We also want to make the behavioral model richer. Today ADAPT focuses on a small set of high-value effects such as network writes, storage changes, navigation, and consequential actions. A production system could reason about much more specific capabilities: payments, deletion, account changes, credential access, file actions, identity changes, cross-origin effects, and more. We would also like the trust receipts to become portable evidence that an agent, browser, user, or external policy system can inspect independently. WebMCP makes the web callable. We think the next question is whether those calls can also become accountable. That is the part of ADAPT we want to keep building. title: Dominaitrix
pitch: Dominaitrix teaches the old web new tricks: a Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters, turning unsupported sites into reliable tools for people and their agents.
about_excerpt: Dominaitrix teaches the old web new tricks: a Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters, turning unsupported sites into reliable tools for people and their agents. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration The web was built for people clicking buttons, not agents trying to complete tasks. When agents rely on screenshots, coordinates, and brittle selectors, even simple workflows become slow and unreliable. WebMCP offers a better interface—but most existing websites do not support it yet. Dominaitrix was inspired by a practical question: what if we could teach the web we already have to speak WebMCP? What it does Dominaitrix is a sideloadable Chrome extension that installs curated WebMCP adapters on supported websites. Each adapter translates a site’s live interface into structured tools that agents can discover and invoke directly. Our adapters currently support: Managing a live ESPN Fantasy Football draft Exploring Domino’s menus and building a cart Reading Hacker News stories and discussions Searching and navigating Wikipedia articles The difference is dramatic. In two ESPN drafts using the same prompt, ordinary browser control successfully drafted only 3 of 16 intended players and followed 1 of 5 roster instructions. With Dominaitrix, the agent drafted 16 of 16 players and followed 5 of 5 instructions. Dominaitrix does not provide the agent. It gives WebMCP-capable agents a faster, safer, and more reliable way to use existing websites. How we built it Dominaitrix consists of three main pieces: A Chrome extension that installs adapters through chrome.userScripts A shared runtime that registers tools through document.modelContext.registerTool() A static adapter registry containing versioned metadata, compatibility information, tool descriptions, and SHA-256 source digests The extension periodically checks the registry, verifies each adapter’s integrity, and installs or updates it on matching pages. Adapters run in an isolated user-script world by default and expose narrowly scoped tools with structured inputs, outputs, and errors. Every adapter is reviewed and tested in the repository before publication. The project includes an adapter template, automated registry generation, integrity validation, and a browser-like test harness for exercising tools without depending entirely on live sites. We also built privacy-conscious local diagnostics. Dominaitrix records minimized health events—such as the adapter version, tool name, outcome, and broad error category—but never records tool arguments, page content, cookies, tokens, or response bodies. Nothing is uploaded automatically. Challenges we ran into The hardest problem was translating dynamic, human-oriented interfaces into stable agent tools. ESPN’s draft room uses virtualized tables, changing position filters, a live clock, and controls whose meaning changes when the user is on the clock. A delayed instruction could accidentally draft a player during the wrong pick. We addressed this by using stable player IDs, requiring the expected pick number for consequential actions, detecting stale state, and verifying the result after every selection. We faced similar issues across sites: hidden application state, asynchronous UI updates, undocumented APIs, route changes, and actions that can return success before the visible interface has actually updated. Distribution created another challenge. Downloadable adapters make rapid compatibility fixes possible, but they also create a trust boundary. We designed a curated registry with no public upload path, exact source digests, restrictive match patterns, explicit execution worlds, and automated consistency checks. Finally, WebMCP and Chrome’s user-script support are still experimental. We had to handle missing APIs, disabled browser settings, unsupported pages, and partial initialization without leaving users with mysterious failures. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are most proud that Dominaitrix demonstrates a measurable improvement rather than merely registering demo tools. The ESPN experiment showed that structured tools can turn a fragile, time-sensitive workflow into one an agent completes accurately and with time to spare. The agent could inspect the draft, manage autopick, search available players, maintain a queue, and make validated selections while following a multi-part strategy. We are also proud that the adapter system is reusable. The same runtime supports experiences as different as drafting a fantasy team, configuring a pizza, exploring a discussion tree, and navigating an encyclopedia. What we learned We learned that agents do not need unrestricted access to a website’s internals. They need a small set of well-designed capabilities with stable identifiers, precise descriptions, bounded results, and actionable errors. We also learned that successful execution must be verified. A click or HTTP response is not proof that the intended state changed—especially during live, asynchronous workflows. Most importantly, WebMCP is valuable even before websites adopt it natively. An adapter layer can provide an immediate bridge while showing site owners what an agent-native interface for their product could look like. What's next for Dominaitrix Next, we want to expand the curated adapter library and make adapters easier to develop, review, test, and maintain. We plan to add stronger compatibility monitoring, richer local diagnostics, safer confirmation patterns for consequential actions, and tooling that detects when a site change breaks an adapter. Longer term, we hope Dominaitrix can serve two purposes: make today’s web useful to agents now, and provide working prototypes that help websites design native WebMCP support of their own. title: ImpressPress Dev Sandbox (dev.impresspress.org)
pitch: Open a page in a WebMCP browser and your agent builds a whole website — frontend and backened all compiled in the browser, no external providers or extra costs.
about_excerpt: Open a page in a WebMCP browser and your agent builds a whole website — frontend and backened all compiled in the browser, no external providers or extra costs. Like 1 Comment 1 Story Updates Inspiration Wouldn't it be cool if you could build a whole website by pointing your agent at a page and saying "build me a shop"? No hosting provider to sign up for, no vibe-coding platform charging its own fees, no setup. We already have a capable agent in the browser — so let it do the work right there. One URL, one login, and the agent has everything it needs. What it does Open dev.impresspress.org in a browser whose agent supports WebMCP and sign in with the credentials shown on the page. The page hands your agent a small set of tools, and from there you just talk: Build the frontend — the agent writes the pages; every save is live in a preview next to the chat. Build the backend — the agent scaffolds a Rust "block", compiles it in the browser , and it's live within a minute. No toolchain, nothing uploaded anywhere. Stock a shop — products, prices and offers through the same tools, so a visitor's own agent can browse and buy. Undo anything — every change is a numbered generation you can roll back to. Export — download the finished site as a folder that runs from any static web host. Everything runs inside a service worker in your browser tab. There is no server behind it, and nothing leaves your machine. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Building a website is a job where the agent needs the site's own capabilities — write this file, compile this block, publish this product, roll that back — not a generic browser. WebMCP lets the page hand exactly those capabilities to the agent as typed tools, with the site's own login behind each one. And because the whole thing runs in a service worker, the page can offer those tools even though there is no server at all. How it makes a better experience Before: to get an agent to build you a site with a real backend, you gave it a machine, an editor, a deploy pipeline and some credentials, then relayed its errors back and forth by hand. Now: you open one page and describe what you want. The agent scaffolds a newsletter block, compiles it in the browser in about 48 seconds, creates three products and publishes their offers — in one conversation, while you watch it happen in the live preview. A compile error comes back to the agent as a file and line number, so it fixes its own mistake instead of asking you. When you're done, one click exports the site. What people and agents can now do together A person describes a shop; the agent builds the pages, the Rust backend and the catalog, and the person sees it live as it goes. A visitor's agent can then use the tools the first agent created — for example, subscribe to the newsletter block it wrote an hour earlier — because compiled blocks publish their own WebMCP tools. Anyone can hand the exported folder to someone else, who runs it locally with a plain file server: the same shop, the same blocks, no accounts. None of this needed a server, a cloud account or a toolchain install — which is what made it hard before. How we implemented WebMCP Every page registers its tools with document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute }) . The tools aren't hand-written: each backend block declares typed HTTP endpoints, the runtime turns the ones marked as agent tools into a manifest (filtered to what the current visitor may call), and a small script registers one tool per entry — execute is a single same-origin fetch of that endpoint. The workspace page adds its own page-scoped tools ( dev_* for files and blocks, shop_* for products), plus dev_compile_block and dev_export , which drive the in-browser compiler and the export download directly. How we built it Rust compiled to WebAssembly, running in a service worker with SQLite and a filesystem in the browser's storage. Code lives in "blocks" — isolated WebAssembly modules with declared capabilities — an open source project of mine, wafer.run. The in-browser Rust compiler is Rubrc (rustc and cargo compiled to WebAssembly), packaged as static assets and driven from a worker. Challenges we ran into Rubrc is very new. Packaging its toolchain takes about an hour and 12 GB of RAM, so it's published as a release asset rather than built in CI. An in-browser compiler needs cross-origin isolation (COOP/COEP), which broke the live preview and the worker startup on a plain static host. The fix was to let the service worker set those headers for the whole site. Service workers see less of a request than a server does, so things like CSRF checks and "tools before the worker takes control" needed real fixes. Keeping it safe: agent-written blocks only get their own tables, storage and settings, are probed before activation, and the previous version stays live if a compile fails. Accomplishments that we're proud of It works end to end: an agent scaffolds a block, compiles it in the browser, a visitor's agent discovers and calls the new tool, and an export of the site boots the same shop on another server. It's also reasonably fast — a block compiles in under a minute, page edits show up in a few hundred milliseconds, and the exported site boots in about three seconds. What we learned A lot about what browsers let a service worker do. And that an agent is an unforgiving user: every refusal has to come back as a clear, structured message, or it just retries the same mistake. Tool descriptions that say exactly what a tool does — and what side effects it has — improved the agent's success rate more than anything else. What's next It is still very much a MVP, need to test more and get faster compiles, clearer diagnostics for the agent, and export straight to hosts like Cloudflare. Mostly: get it in front of people and hear what they want to build. title: Ensemble
pitch: Your look does not come from one store. Ensemble composes a purchasable outfit across Shopify stores through the tools the stores themselves publish: try it on your photo, mix catalogs, and checkout
about_excerpt: Your look does not come from one store. Ensemble composes a purchasable outfit across Shopify stores through the tools the stores themselves publish: try it on your photo, mix catalogs, and checkout Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Shopify storefronts already register native WebMCP tools on document.modelContext . It is on by default on Liquid storefronts, no store opt-in: catalog search, product lookup, and cart updates, published by the page itself as a contract any agent may use. The contract is live. The agent side is what has been missing. Meanwhile the actual shopping problem has not moved. An outfit rarely comes from one store. Putting one together means tabs, screenshots, and re-finding everything at checkout, and the try-on tools that exist paste a product image onto a photo without knowing what the item is, what it costs, or whether your size is in stock. Ensemble puts the two together. Shopping across stores is the shape WebMCP was made for: the page itself declares what an agent may do here, search this catalog, add this variant, and the agent composes those grants across origins into one task. No scraping, no guessing at themes, just the surface the store maintains for itself. What it does Ensemble is a Chrome extension. Browse any Shopify store and its catalog loads into a side panel automatically; every store you visit becomes a chip, and one look spans all of them with a running total. Hover a product tile on the store's own grid and two buttons appear: Render on me shows that item on your photo without leaving the page, and Suggest matches proposes pieces from the store's live inventory that complete the outfit. On a product page, a compact pill offers the same controls and picks up the exact variant you selected, so US 2 on the page is US 2 in the cart. When the look is right, one click fills every store's cart with exactly those variants. Checkout stays native per store: Ensemble fills the carts, you finish each one in the store's own checkout, where trust and payment already live. Every item in a look is a specific, in-stock variant with a live price. A look in Ensemble is purchasable, not a moodboard. The division of labor is the point. The person makes the taste decisions: which jeans, which size, whether the jacket earns its place. The agent does the cross-store bookkeeping: searching the catalogs you have browsed, resolving each choice to an in-stock variant with a real price, filling carts on multiple origins in one action. And the storefront draws the boundary, because its registered tools define exactly what the agent may touch. None of that was reliably possible when acting on a store meant scraping its theme. How we built it The WebMCP layer is a MAIN-world content script injected at document_start . When the browser exposes the WebMCP API (Chrome with the WebMCP feature enabled), it wraps modelContext.registerTool and captures every tool object the storefront registers. On stock Chrome, where no native API exists yet, it plants a minimal modelContext shim first; Shopify's storefront script feature-detects it and registers its ten native tools into the shim unchanged. Either way the extension ends up holding the store's own tool objects and serves listTools and callTool to the extension's isolated world over a postMessage bridge. Product lookups and cart adds go through the store's registered tools first: get_product for variant data, update_cart with variant GIDs (Shopify's global IDs), get_cart to confirm what actually landed. Storefronts that register nothing fall back to the public /products.json and /cart/add.js endpoints, so the same flows work everywhere and the supported surface is preferred wherever it exists. The overlay UI lives in an open shadow root so store CSS cannot touch it, and finds product cards by climbing from the hover target to the smallest container holding exactly one product handle, which survives themes that cover their tiles with overlay layers. Try-on renders and style suggestions run on Gemini with the user's own key. There is no server: the photo and the key stay in local extension storage. Challenges we ran into The tool-call contract has sharp edges the examples do not show. executeTool at the API boundary takes a JSON string and rejects a tool name in place of the registered tool object, but a captured tool's execute callback takes parsed arguments, because the native layer parses before invoking. Passing the wrong shape does not error loudly; Shopify answers with a polite "No line_items provided" and your cart stays empty. We also learned that update_cart 's top-level id addresses existing cart lines only; adds must nest the variant GID under item . On a product page, the store's own get_product returns only the currently selected variant, a single-element array. To honor the size a shopper picked we resolve variants catalog-first and match requested IDs in both GID and numeric forms, verified live by watching a stored look flip from the default US 0 to the selected US 2. Repeat adds taught us that Shopify dedupes them, returning updated: false with no item count, so cart confirmation falls back to get_cart rather than trusting the add response. And real storefront themes fight overlays: one of the live demo storefronts covers its product tiles with layers that swallow hover targets, which is what forced the container-climbing card detection. Accomplishments we are proud of The full loop runs against live storefronts: catalog in, look built, render on the shopper's photo, and both stores' carts filled with the exact variants, a dress from one catalog and wool runners from another under one total. The native tool path works on stock Chrome today through the shim capture, so the WebMCP story does not wait for a browser flag. And variant fidelity is proven end to end, the size picked on the page to the line in the cart. What we learned WebMCP's design carries real weight in practice: because the page defines the tools, an agent can act on a store it has never seen without guessing at DOM structure, and the same contract that serves a chat agent serves a product UI like ours. The gap between a demo and a product is exactly the sharp edges above, and the supported surface made them tractable to debug. What's next Tighter checkout is the obvious V2, exploring how far per-store checkout can collapse toward one action. Beyond that, the look itself wants to become a page: a shareable board that registers its own WebMCP tools, so your agent can discuss, edit, and price a look you were sent. At that point Ensemble both consumes the open web's tools and contributes surface back to it. Try it Open https://ensemble-dhf.pages.dev and download ensemble.zip (or clone github.com/sneg55/ensemble). chrome://extensions, Developer mode, Load unpacked, pick the folder. Paste a free Gemini API key in the extension options (aistudio.google.com/apikey). Visit any Shopify store, click the toolbar icon or just hover a product tile. Optional, for the native API path: run Chrome with --enable-features=WebMCP. Without the flag the shim capture keeps every feature working.
