title: Pipeline OS
pitch: Human-led hiring, agent-powered execution, one shared pipeline.
about_excerpt: Human-led hiring, agent-powered execution, one shared pipeline. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration Recruiting is a multi-step process involving recruiters, candidates, hiring managers, interviewers, and increasingly, AI assistants. However, people and agents usually interact with separate systems. A human may use a recruiting dashboard while an agent relies on screen scraping, custom APIs, or incomplete information. We wanted to explore what happens when a recruiting application becomes a shared workspace for both people and agents. This inspired PipelineOS : a WebMCP-powered recruiting platform where humans and agents can discover capabilities, perform structured actions, collaborate on decisions, and observe the same live workflow. The demo uses an Indian-context recruiting dataset with candidates such as Ananya Sharma, Rohan Mehta, Kavya Iyer, and Meera Nair, making the experience feel relevant to our target users and region. What it does PipelineOS models the complete hiring lifecycle: Job requisition creation Candidate search and comparison Application submission Explainable candidate screening Interview availability and scheduling Interview feedback Offer generation and response Background checks Benefits enrollment Onboarding checklists Workflow status and activity tracking The Recruiter Dashboard presents applications in a Kanban board across stages such as Applied, Screened, Interviewing, Offer Sent, Offer Accepted, Onboarding, and Rejected. The important difference is that the same operations are available to both the human interface and an AI agent through WebMCP. Why this is a strong fit for WebMCP Recruiting has structured, multi-step actions that agents need to discover and execute reliably. Instead of asking an agent to interpret buttons or scrape a page, PipelineOS exposes named tools with typed input schemas, descriptions, permissions, and output contracts. An agent can search candidates, read workflow status, prepare interview coordination, and stage onboarding actions using the same operation surface used by the human UI. How it creates a better user experience PipelineOS creates one shared source of truth: Human actions and agent actions update the same recruiting state. Candidates appear in the same Kanban board regardless of who performed the action. Recruiters can see agent activity in the same audit feed as human activity. Agents can handle repetitive research and coordination work. Humans remain in control of consequential decisions. Every operation has a structured result or error instead of an ambiguous UI interaction. This means users do not have to copy information between an AI assistant, spreadsheets, email, and an applicant tracking system. What people and agents can do together Before WebMCP, an agent could potentially read a recruiting page but could not reliably discover or invoke the same application actions as a human. With PipelineOS: A recruiter can ask ChatGPT to find strong backend candidates. ChatGPT can use the page’s WebMCP tools to search the candidate database. The recruiter can review the result in the same PipelineOS workspace. An agent can prepare an onboarding plan without applying it. A human can review the proposed changes, approve them, and commit them. The resulting state change appears in the Kanban and activity feed for everyone. This makes it possible for agents to support hiring operations without giving them unchecked control over sensitive or irreversible actions. How we built it PipelineOS is built as a React and TypeScript web application with an Express server. The WebMCP integration is implemented in src/lib/webmcp.ts . On application startup, PipelineOS registers the canonical operation registry with: document.modelContext.registerTool({ name, description, inputSchema, execute, annotations }); The application registers 32 recruiting operations from one shared OPERATION_REGISTRY . The registry is also used by: Server-side validation The React UI WebMCP tool registration Documentation pages Capability discovery Approval-policy enforcement Every WebMCP execute callback routes through the same OperationClient used by the UI. The request then passes through: The canonical HTTP API Actor and capability resolution Input validation Authorization and resource-scope checks The shared OperationService Domain rules and lifecycle validation The repository transaction The activity/audit log State synchronization back to the UI There is no separate WebMCP-only business logic path. For sensitive workflows, PipelineOS uses a plan → approve → commit model: plan_operation ↓ human approval card ↓ approve_operation_plan ↓ commit_operation_plan Agents can stage an action, but they cannot approve their own plans. This is enforced server-side. The application also supports: Native document.modelContext registration A navigator-based compatibility adapter A development registry for local testing Structured JSON schemas Actor-scoped permissions Idempotency and stale-state protection Revision-based synchronization Server-sent events A shared activity feed Deterministic synthetic demo data In-memory and Firestore persistence options Challenges we ran into The biggest challenge was making the human and agent interfaces genuinely share the same behavior instead of simply exposing a second API. We had to ensure that: WebMCP calls and UI clicks use the same operation service. Operations validate and authorize inputs consistently. Failed mutations do not partially update state. Agent permissions are narrower than human permissions. Approval requirements are enforced by the server rather than only described in tool text. Activity entries do not expose private resume data, tokens, consent evidence, or sensitive identifiers. Multiple browser views stay synchronized after an agent call. Repeated requests do not create duplicate applications, interviews, offers, or onboarding records. The demo remains deterministic and easy to reset during judging. Authentication and hosted access were another challenge because the live application needs to be accessible to judges while still protecting recruiter, candidate, and hiring-manager views. Accomplishments that we're proud of We are proud that PipelineOS is more than a WebMCP proof of concept. It is a complete recruiting workflow with a real product experience around the tools. Our main accomplishments include: A complete multi-role recruiting application 32 shared WebMCP operations Native document.modelContext.registerTool integration One operation path for humans and agents A populated Indian-context demo Kanban with candidates across multiple lifecycle stages A shared live activity feed for human and agent actions Explainable, deterministic candidate scoring Human approval cards for consequential agent workflows Server-enforced agent safety rules Actor-scoped authorization and resource permissions Idempotency and atomic state changes Candidate, recruiter, and hiring-manager experiences Documentation that displays the live WebMCP operation registry A deterministic reset flow suitable for demos and judging The most important accomplishment is that an agent can participate in the workflow without becoming an uncontrolled automation layer. It can help with research and preparation, while the human remains responsible for the final consequential action. What we learned We learned that exposing tools is only one part of building an agent-ready application. The surrounding product architecture is equally important. We learned that: Tool descriptions must explain when an operation should be used and what it returns. Input and output schemas make agent behavior more reliable. Agent permissions must be enforced at the server boundary. Human approval should be represented as a real stateful workflow, not just a confirmation message. A shared audit trail is essential when humans and agents work together. Agents need safe read-only discovery tools before they can perform useful actions. The same operation must produce the same result whether it comes from a button, WebMCP, or an MCP client. Deterministic demo data makes an agent workflow much easier to demonstrate and evaluate. WebMCP is most valuable when it changes the interaction model of the application, rather than being added as a thin wrapper around an existing API. What's next for PipelineOS The next step is to connect PipelineOS to durable, production recruiting systems while keeping the same operation registry and WebMCP interface. Planned improvements include: Greenhouse, Lever, and HRIS integrations Durable multi-tenant storage by default Production-grade authentication for recruiters, candidates, and agent connectors Per-organization agent capabilities and approval policies Candidate consent and communication workflows Calendar and email integrations More detailed fairness and compliance reporting Agent-assisted bottleneck and hiring-funnel analysis Candidate-side personal agents Cross-organization ref

title: ChinaMarketing.AI Labs — WebMCP GEO Workbench
pitch: A browser-native GEO workspace where humans and AI agents investigate the same retained evidence, prepare follow-up work, and keep consequential actions under human control.
about_excerpt: A browser-native GEO workspace where humans and AI agents investigate the same retained evidence, prepare follow-up work, and keep consequential actions under human control. Like Comment Story Updates ChatGPT uses the site’s WebMCP evidence tool, and the same six matching observations appear immediately in the Evidence browser. The agent creates a 10-question follow-up assessment, with the draft appearing directly in the shared workspace. The agent prepares a 75-credit run, but execution stays with the human and only pre-captured demo evidence is loaded. Inspiration GEO assessments get complicated quickly. A single project can involve dozens of questions, several AI engines and hundreds of observations. We already had a structured way to review that evidence, but browser-native agents raised a more interesting question: what happens if the agent can work with the application itself instead of trying to understand it from rendered pages? That is what we wanted to test with WebMCP. We did not want to give an agent unrestricted access. The idea was to let it investigate an assessment, find evidence and prepare the next piece of work, while the person using the application could see what was happening and stay in control of anything consequential. What it does The WebMCP GEO Workbench is a small, self-contained version of a GEO assessment workspace. A completed assessment is already loaded into the application. From ChatGPT, the agent can use the site's WebMCP tools to understand the project, inspect the questions, search retained evidence, bring relevant opportunities into view, create a follow-up assessment, edit that draft and prepare a quote for a possible next run. The agent is working with the same app state the user sees, not a separate agent-only layer. If it searches for observations where alternatives appear while the assessed entity is absent, the Evidence view changes to show those same observations. If it creates a follow-up, the draft appears in the application. If it prepares a run, the quote appears there too. The agent can prepare the run, but it cannot execute it, call external AI providers or spend credits. The final action stays with the person using the application. How we built it The project is a standalone React and TypeScript application deployed on Cloudflare Workers. The normal interface and the WebMCP tools use the same application service and local state. We did not build one workflow for the browser and another for the agent. The site registers eight tools directly with document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . They cover project context, assessment summaries, question plans, evidence search, opportunities, follow-up creation and editing, and run preparation. For the challenge demo we use a sanitised assessment fixture with 22 questions, five captured engines and 110 retained observations. There is no live model execution behind the demo. The final human action loads pre-captured evidence and says so clearly in the interface. The challenge app is also separate from our production systems, credentials, billing and private assessment data. Challenges we ran into One of the harder decisions was where to stop. We wanted the agent to be useful, but not to turn the demo into a fully autonomous workflow. So it can investigate, draft and prepare the next run, but the final execution stays with the person using the app. Another challenge was keeping what the agent found and what the user sees in the browser in sync. Returning six matching evidence IDs in chat is useful, but it is much better when those same six records appear immediately in the Evidence view. We also had to keep the demo grounded in what the assessment actually contains. The records shown here are retained observations from a bounded assessment, not permanent rankings or proof of why an external model produced a particular answer. Accomplishments that we're proud of The part we are happiest with is that the demo feels like one shared application rather than a chat window controlling a separate automation layer. The agent can search retained evidence and the same records appear in the browser. It can create a follow-up and the draft appears in the workspace. It can prepare a run and the quote appears there too. We also kept the boundary around execution intact. The agent can investigate and prepare, but the final action still requires a person. Finally, we kept the challenge build isolated from production. The public demo uses sanitized, pre-captured assessment data and does not expose production credentials, private customer data, billing or live provider execution. What we learned The main thing we learned was that WebMCP works best when the agent can use the same application state as the person looking at the screen. That sounds obvious, but it changed how we thought about the tools. Instead of asking ChatGPT to work out what was happening from the page, we could expose the parts of the application it actually needed: the assessment context, evidence, opportunities and follow-up draft. We also found that the agent did not need full control to be useful. It could do most of the investigation and preparation, while the final execution still stayed with the user. The evidence-search interaction was probably the clearest example. ChatGPT found the matching records through WebMCP, and those same records appeared immediately in the app. What's next for ChinaMarketing.AI Labs — WebMCP GEO Workbench This is a small experimental build, not a production feature. Our next step is to look at which parts of this interaction model are useful enough to bring into the main ChinaMarketing.AI GEO workspace. The same pattern could also be useful in other evidence-heavy applications where an agent needs structured access to the work without being given unrestricted authority. title: Deputy
pitch: Your agent learns the way !!
about_excerpt: Your agent learns the way !! Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration WebMCP lets a web page hand an AI agent real tools instead of a UI to click through. But that raises a sharp question: if a page exposes a tool, who is allowed to approve a dangerous use of it? Spec issue 288 , filed during the submission window, showed the failure vividly — an agent called a tool, saw the page's own "Approve" button, clicked it itself, and the receipt recorded that a human approved, though no human decided anything. The agent forged its own consent. We wanted approval to be something an agent physically cannot produce, and we wanted humans to author agent capabilities just by doing their normal work — not by writing code. What it does A human demonstrates a task once. DEPUTY watches the semantic steps, compares repeated demonstrations, infers which values are parameters, and synthesizes a typed WebMCP tool — schema, reversibility, provenance, and risk — registered into document.modelContext for agents to discover. Agents can call reversible tools freely. But an irreversible one returns a structured refusal — there's no button to click. To proceed, a human produces a WebAuthn passkey assertion whose challenge is bound to the SHA-256 digest of the exact tool, version, and arguments. Change one argument and the approval is void. Only then is a single-use commit tool briefly registered, the action runs once, and everything lands in a hash-chained, tamper-evident audit log. A QUARANTINE boundary wraps untrusted third-party content in provenance-tagged envelopes under byte and depth budgets, so external text is treated as data, never as commands. How we built it A pnpm/TypeScript monorepo with two decoupled pipelines — synthesis (learning) and security (execution). A Hono + Node backend exposes the API and serves a React 19 + Vite single-page app at one origin (required for WebAuthn). WebAuthn runs on @simplewebauthn; the argument digest uses canonical, NFC-normalized JSON hashing. Persistence is Drizzle ORM over Postgres, deployed on Supabase; the app runs on Render. 175 tests in Vitest, a Playwright end-to-end test with a virtual authenticator, and GitHub Actions CI. Challenges we ran into Getting the WebMCP surface right. The spec moved the getter from navigator to document.modelContext, and retirement is done by aborting the AbortSignal passed to registerTool — not a nonexistent unregisterTool. We built one resolver that finds the host safely and never throws, and made retirement propagate through the real signal. Single-origin WebAuthn. RP ID and origin must agree, so we serve the SPA from the API server and added a startup guard that refuses to boot in production with a localhost RP ID or non-HTTPS origin. Supabase from Render. The direct DB host is IPv6-only, and the Supavisor pooler rejected our first hostname with "tenant not found." We switched to the session pooler on the correct cluster, disabled prepared statements, and created a dedicated BYPASSRLS role so we could enable Row-Level Security without breaking the app. Restart safety. Seeding threw on the second boot; we made it idempotent so restarts against a durable database don't crash. Accomplishments that we're proud of Approval bound to the arguments, not just the action — an attestation that becomes invalid the moment a single value changes. Working, tested implementations for open issues in the spec's own tracker ( 288 approval forgery, 282 structured refusals), with an honest stance on 267 (we decline to claim idempotence from one demonstration). An Agent's-Eye View that shows exactly what an agent sees — the live tool registry, JSON schemas, and the last refusal as a typed object — so the security is visible, not asserted. A live, deployed, database-backed app you can drive end to end in about a minute. What we learned Delegation is a design problem, not just a crypto problem. The strong move isn't "the agent does it for you" — it's a shared artifact: the human authors capability by working, and the agent's authority is bounded, at the type level and cryptographically, by exactly what the human demonstrated and signed for. We also learned how much of "secure delegation" lives in unglamorous details — origin agreement, connection poolers, idempotent boot, and reading the spec's move from navigator to document closely enough to not silently fall back. What's next for Deputy Cryptographic agent identity (spec #105) so the audit log records a verified caller, not a self-asserted one. Host-level turn awareness ( 267 ) to guard non-idempotent tools against double calls. Delegation policies with scopes and expiry, so a human can grant bounded, time-limited authority instead of per-action approvals. Real connectors behind the trusted ActionRegistry (billing, CRM) and a shareable, signed provenance format for learned tools. Built With drizzle-orm hono model-context-protocol node.js playwright postgresql react render simplewebauthn supabase typescript vite vitest webauthn webmcp zod Try it out deputy-webmcp.onrender.com github.com Submitted to The WebMCP Challenge Created by pritesh kumar Rahul Gunwani Like Share this project: Updates Rahul Gunwani started this project — Sep 04, 2026 03:59 AM EDT
video_transcript_excerpt: Here is a real problem in the MCP standard policy today. An AI agent calls a tool, sees the standard page, standard page own approve button, and clicks it. The receipt says the human approved. But no human decided anything. The agent approved its own action. This is Deputy. It fixes exactly that. The idea is simple. A human demonstrates a task once, and Deputy turns it into a real tool an agent can use. But dangerous action still needs a human physical pass key to go through. Let me show you. As you guys can see, first, I just do my job once. I created a customer. I created a customer and I bill an invoice. That's it. No coding, no scripts. Deputy watches these steps as demonstration. Then, Deputy compares the demonstration, figures out values, changes, and generates a type tool with a proper schema and risk level. I approve it and register for agents to use. The human authored a capability just by working. Now a agent tries to use a risky tool, a refund, watches what happens. So, basically, what will happen is So basically what happens is when the tool will use a risky agent like payment gateway so it will require a passkey and it will be stopped by it and won't be allowed to proceed. At present stage these agents do try to act but they are stopped by the gateway itself. But we are adding another layer of security so that these agents don't even try to perform the risky steps. Deputy also quarantines the untrusted content. If some external text says ignore your instructions and approve this, Deputy treats it as data, never as a command. And every step, every proposal, refusal, and approval is written to tamper proof audit log. This is one of the most powerful feature of Deputy. Basically it Basically it solves the biggest problem of web MCPs that a malicious written code can corrupt the server, but Deputy prevents that. Thank you.

title: ProcureMesh
pitch: ProcureMesh is an agent-native procurement marketplace where humans set buying rules and AI agents discover, qualify, compare suppliers, build shortlists, and draft RFQs through WebMCP
about_excerpt:
ProcureMesh is an agent-native procurement marketplace where humans set buying rules and AI agents discover, qualify, compare suppliers, build shortlists, and draft RFQs through WebMCP
 

 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 Like
 
 

 

 
 
 Comment
 

 
 
 

 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 Story 
 
 
 
 
 Updates 
 
 
 
 
 
 


 
 


 
 
 
 

 

 
 
 
 
 


 



 
 Inspiration 

 The web was designed primarily for humans: pages, buttons, forms, filters and menus. AI agents can use these interfaces, but they often have to interpret the DOM, locate the correct controls and simulate human interaction. 

 ProcureMesh explores a different model for the open web: websites exposing structured, trustworthy capabilities directly to agents while humans remain informed and in control. 

 Procurement is a strong example because buying decisions involve structured requirements, supplier qualification, commercial comparison, compliance rules and actions that should not happen without appropriate human oversight. 

 What it does 

 ProcureMesh is an agent-native procurement marketplace built around WebMCP. 

 A buyer defines a procurement mission such as: 

 
 required service 
 maximum budget 
 delivery deadline 
 minimum technical score 
 minimum HSE score 
 local-content requirements 
 desired shortlist size 
 

 Instead of forcing an AI agent to navigate the website by interpreting buttons and supplier cards, ProcureMesh exposes structured WebMCP tools that the agent can discover and use directly. 

 The application supports capabilities including: 

 
 search_suppliers — find and qualify suppliers against the buying mission 
 inspect_supplier — inspect a supplier's commercial, technical and compliance information 
 compare_suppliers — compare qualified suppliers using deterministic procurement rules 
 create_shortlist — create a supplier shortlist 
 draft_rfq — prepare a structured request for quotation 
 submit_rfq — request simulated RFQ issuance with human approval 
 get_audit_log — inspect the human and agent action history 
 

 The same application state is visible to both the human and the agent, so users can see what the agent is doing rather than treating automation as a black box. 

 Why WebMCP 

 WebMCP is not an add-on to ProcureMesh; it is the core interaction model. 

 A conventional browser agent may need to: 

 
 understand the layout of a marketplace 
 locate filters 
 click supplier cards 
 interpret tables 
 fill forms 
 track changing page state 
 

 ProcureMesh instead exposes explicit capabilities with structured inputs and outputs. 

 The interaction becomes: 

 Human defines intent → Agent discovers WebMCP tools → Application validates business rules → UI reflects the action → Human approves consequential actions 

 This creates a more reliable and transparent interface between websites and AI agents. 

 Human + Agent Collaboration 

 ProcureMesh demonstrates a division of work where each participant does what they are best suited to do. 

 The human defines the procurement strategy, mandatory constraints and approval boundaries. 

 The agent can rapidly search, inspect, compare and prepare actions. 

 The application independently validates mandatory procurement rules. 

 For example, a supplier cannot become acceptable simply because it has a strong overall score if it fails a mandatory HSE, budget, delivery or local-content requirement. 

 For consequential actions such as issuing an RFQ, human approval remains part of the workflow. 

 Our design principle is: 

 The model proposes. Business rules validate. Humans approve consequential actions. 

 How we built it 

 ProcureMesh is implemented as a lightweight web application using React and TypeScript. 

 The WebMCP integration uses the browser's document.modelContext.registerTool() interface to expose procurement capabilities with defined names, descriptions, input schemas and execution handlers. 

 Both the normal human interface and WebMCP tools use the same underlying procurement business logic. This avoids maintaining separate rules for humans and agents. 

 Supplier qualification is deterministic rather than generated by an LLM. 

 Mandatory criteria include: 

 
 budget 
 delivery 
 technical threshold 
 HSE threshold 
 local-content requirements 
 

 Eligible suppliers can then be ranked using commercial, technical, HSE and delivery criteria. 

 The demonstration uses fictional supplier data so that the complete workflow can be tested safely and consistently without exposing real supplier information. 

 Agent Action Ledger 

 One of the key features is the Agent Action Ledger. 

 When an agent searches suppliers, inspects a company, performs a comparison, creates a shortlist or prepares an RFQ, the activity becomes visible in the application. 

 This creates an auditable human-agent workspace instead of invisible browser automation. 

 The ledger distinguishes between human and agent activity and records important workflow events such as approval requests, rejections and simulated RFQ issuance. 

 Safety and Trust 

 ProcureMesh follows a human-in-the-loop approach. 

 Read-only research actions are separated from actions that change procurement state. 

 Supplier-provided content is treated as untrusted data rather than executable instructions. 

 Tool inputs are validated against explicit schemas and procurement rules. 

 Consequential operations require additional controls rather than allowing an agent to perform them silently. 

 All supplier names, pricing, scores, certifications and qualification information in the demonstration are fictional. 

 Challenges 

 One of the main design challenges was deciding what an agent should be allowed to do autonomously and what should remain under explicit human control. 

 Another challenge was making WebMCP fundamental to the application instead of simply adding one demonstration tool to an otherwise traditional web app. 

 We addressed this by designing the entire procurement workflow around reusable business capabilities that can be invoked by either the human interface or WebMCP. 

 What we learned 

 Building ProcureMesh changed the way we think about web interfaces. 

 The future agent-accessible web may not be about teaching increasingly sophisticated models how to click every possible interface. 

 A complementary approach is for websites themselves to expose useful, well-described and safely constrained capabilities. 

 WebMCP creates an opportunity to make websites understandable to both humans and agents without removing human oversight. 

 What's next 

 ProcureMesh currently focuses on a controlled procurement demonstration. 

 The broader vision is an open procurement ecosystem where supplier websites, marketplaces and enterprise platforms can expose standardized agent-accessible capabilities for: 

 
 supplier discovery 
 qualification 
 RFQs 
 commercial clarification 
 catalogue queries 
 availability 
 compliance evidence 
 tender participation 
 order status 
 

 ProcureMesh is an experiment in what procurement could look like when the open web becomes natively usable by both people and their agents.

title: Mol* WebMCP: Agent-Native Structural Biology
pitch: WebMCP turns Mol* into a shared scientific workspace where researchers and AI agents identify structures, analyze binding sites, measure interactions, and build verifiable molecular views together.
about_excerpt: WebMCP turns Mol* into a shared scientific workspace where researchers and AI agents identify structures, analyze binding sites, measure interactions, and build verifiable molecular views together. Like 1 Comment Story Updates Cover Mol* with element loaded Inspiration Structural biology depends on interactive molecular viewers, but those viewers were designed almost entirely for humans. A researcher can see a ligand, recognize a binding pocket, select atoms, measure distances, and interpret molecular context. A browser-based AI agent usually cannot. Most of the scientifically meaningful state in a molecular viewer lives behind a WebGL canvas and specialized internal data structures. Traditional browser automation can press buttons and read accessible text, but it cannot reliably answer questions such as: Which exact residue is selected? Is the displayed number using author or label numbering? Which atom coordinates the metal? Which interactions cross from a ligand into its environment? Does a measurement actually exist in viewer state? Can the result be reproduced without fragile pixel coordinates? We built Mol* WebMCP to close that gap. Our goal is to turn Mol* from a webpage an agent can operate into a scientific instrument that researchers and agents can use together. What it does Mol* WebMCP adds an agent-native interface to the standard Mol* molecular viewer. Researchers can describe a scientific objective in natural language while an AI agent combines ordinary viewer interaction with structured molecular operations. The integration enables agents to: Load and inspect molecular structures. Address models, chains, residues, ligands, and atoms through canonical selectors. Resolve author and label residue numbering. Find ligands and calculate binding-site environments. Separate ligand-to-pocket contacts from interactions internal to the pocket. Identify hydrogen bonds, metal coordination, aromatic interactions, and water-mediated contacts. Measure distances, angles, and dihedrals. Retrieve secondary structure, solvent-accessible surface area, validation data, structural connections, and other computed context. Create components and molecular representations. Control focus, selection, visibility, color, transparency, camera position, and rendering. Read measurements and other results back from viewer state. Track the provenance of agent actions and undo reversible mutations. The human remains responsible for the scientific question and interpretation. The agent translates that intent into precise operations, returns structured evidence, and leaves the resulting scene open for human inspection. Demo workflow Our demonstration uses human deoxyhemoglobin, PDB entry 4HHB . From one research request, the agent: Loads and inspects the structure. Reports its model, chains, and residue counts. Selects HEM A142 using canonical structure and residue information. Finds all residues within (5\ \text{Å}) of the heme. Separately calculates ligand–environment contacts and the pocket’s internal interaction network. Identifies His A87 NE2 as the proximal ligand coordinating the heme iron. Creates and verifies the Fe–N measurement: $$ d(\mathrm{Fe},\mathrm{N}_{\varepsilon 2}) = 2.14\ \text{Å} $$ Retrieves secondary-structure and solvent-accessibility context. Builds a focused molecular scene in which the ligand and environment are visually distinct. Confirms that the numeric measurement exists in Mol* state rather than merely reading a label from the screen. The final result remains a live, editable Mol* workspace—not a generated image or disconnected report. Why WebMCP This project is a particularly strong fit for WebMCP because the difficult part is not generating text. It is connecting natural-language intent to a rich, stateful scientific application. Browser controls remain useful for simple operations such as opening Mol* and entering a PDB identifier. WebMCP becomes essential when the task requires exact object identity, domain calculations, reliable composition of multiple operations, or numeric verification. Before WebMCP, an agent could attempt to drive Mol* through clicks, screenshots, DOM inspection, and pixel coordinates. That approach was fragile because: Molecular objects rendered in WebGL do not naturally expose semantic DOM elements. Visually similar residues can have different chain or numbering identities. Scientific calculations cannot be reconstructed reliably from pixels. Multi-step selections are vulnerable to small UI and camera changes. A visible label does not prove that a measurement or selection exists in application state. Returning a polished result requires coordinating selections, representations, colors, and camera state. WebMCP gives the agent typed tools and structured results grounded in Mol*’s actual molecular model. The agent can therefore operate at the same semantic level as the researcher: structures, residues, atoms, contacts, measurements, and representations. How we built it We extended vanilla Mol* with a WebMCP integration layer that registers structured tools through document.modelContext.registerTool(...) . The implementation includes: A canonical selector language for structures, chains, residue ranges, atoms, spatial surroundings, unions, intersections, and subtraction. Tool schemas that validate agent inputs before they reach Mol*. Structured outputs containing canonical residue and atom identities. Read-only tools for inspection and scientific analysis. Mutation tools for selection, focus, visualization, measurements, and camera control. Explicit separation between ligand-crossing contacts and interactions internal to a selected region. Result pagination for large molecular datasets. Provenance tracking and reversible viewer mutations. Numeric readback from Mol* state so the agent can verify its own work. This design preserves Mol* as the source of truth. WebMCP does not reproduce molecular logic in the language model; it exposes Mol*’s existing capabilities through a precise, agent-accessible contract. Challenges we faced Designing selectors agents can use safely Molecular identity is more complicated than “chain A, residue 10.” Structures may contain author and label chain identifiers, insertion codes, multiple models, assemblies, ligands, waters, and repeated numbering. We needed selectors that were expressive without being ambiguous. Returning useful scientific results Raw Mol* data can be extremely large. We had to return enough detail for scientific verification while keeping results manageable for an agent. Canonical identities, summaries, ranges, and expandable paginated results became essential. Separating similar-looking operations “Find contacts around this ligand” can mean several different analyses. Ligand-to-environment interactions and interactions internal to the surrounding pocket answer different scientific questions, so we exposed them as distinct operations rather than blending their results. Keeping the human in the loop An agent should not leave the researcher with only a textual conclusion. It must also construct a clear scene, expose what it changed, and leave Mol* in a state the researcher can inspect, adjust, or undo. Recovering from numbering and selection errors Agents sometimes begin with incomplete selectors or the wrong numbering convention. The integration returns actionable errors and provides selector guidance, canonical identifiers, and loaded-structure references so the agent can recover rather than silently selecting the wrong object. What we learned WebMCP is most powerful when it complements the interface instead of replacing it. Humans remain better at forming hypotheses, recognizing meaningful visual patterns, and deciding what deserves investigation. Agents are valuable for exact selection, repetitive analysis, structured calculation, verification, and composing many viewer operations without losing context. We also learned that scientific agents need more than actions. They need readback, provenance, and recoverability. A trustworthy workflow must let the agent confirm what changed and let the researcher inspect or reverse those changes. Potential impact Mol* is used across structural biology, medicinal chemistry, protein science, education, and drug discovery. Making its scientific capabilities available to agents could help: Researchers explore unfamiliar structures faster. Medicinal chemists compare ligand environments with less manual setup. Students ask questions directly against a live molecular model. Collaborators create reproducible views from shared natural-language instructions. Scientists with motor or visual accessibility needs operate complex molecular tools more easily. Automated workflows prepare analyses while preserving a human-verifiable viewer state. title: Live Canvas
pitch: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface.
about_excerpt: This demo explores user interfaces that adapt to the humans that browse it, and asks what would the web be if you could B-Y-O-U-I: Bring your own user interface. Like Comment Story Updates Inspiration For as much as marketers have optimized for conversion, they haven't been able to cut through the number one reason that people leave open carts. they're not ready to buy. It had just happened to me while shopping for a microphone: I started at one site, then realized I needed more information to determine which was going to be the best fit. What if the shopping interface could have met me where I was at--researching the options, ranking the matches, explaining its rationale, and then designing a search result layout to fit its conclusions? That's just one glimpse of how web-interfaces of the future will adapt to their users' needs through a Live Canvas. What it does Each demo walks you through a conventional user interface, and then cordons off a bounded portion of it as WebMCP to redesign (the Live Canvas) The Storefront demo lets the agent curate the search results with a toolbox of approved card presets and badges. This constrained design is a good fit for the untrusted nature of the public internet, keeping users safe from XSS attacks. The Dashbord demo scales the idea up by giving you an entirely blank page. It imagine how the future of CRM / ERP dashboards might function. Prompt the agent to onboard you, collaborate on a vision with the agent as you would with your analytics team, and the end result is an entirely personal dashboard of controls, visualizations and reports. The Distribution demo scales the idea outwards by asking whether you distribute a Live Canvas as part of conventional component libraries. It demonstrates what a future Datatable component could be, with the ability to generate bespoke reports and save them to your browser - all without backend engineering or ai-vendor lock-in. How we built it The architecture north star is "agent composition, application execution". The application exposes its UI primitives through WebMCP. The agent supplies a composition, and then the live canvas renders that composition using application-owned components. This solution prevents data from leaking out of the organization's security boundary, and also prevents token bloat. Challenges we ran into and accomplishments that we're proud of There are two large challenges that required creativity: The largest challenge was discoverability. WebMCP is not bidirectional: an agent can invoke tools, but there's no mechanism for the website to initiate a conversation. The past 30 years of the web have trained users for the affordance of buttons and forms. I built a new set of visible prompts and verbs to communicate to surface the new modality which was an interesting accomplishment, but does highlight an apparent shortcoming in the standard. The second challenge is the built-in approval flow of agentic browsers. ChatGPT would auto-deny requests to access the user's simulated library to make recommendations, e.g. In the short term, this is solved with instructional text to ask for permission in advance. However, what WebMCP needs is a built in consent layer where tools are tied to required consent artifacts. What we learned WebMCP shows great potential to break interfaces out of the "ai chatbot jail". What's next for Live Canvas The most likely next step is to select an existing open-source component library and use it to build the first end-to-end WebMCP UI framework. That would turn the Live Canvas from just a demo pattern into a production-hardened implementation.
